text:
Paul Lambert will stay at Aston Villa after talks with American owner Randy Lerner in New York.
Lambert’s position was uncertain with the club up for sale for £200million, but he will continue as manager while working under similar cash guidelines as before.
That means he will get funds to use in the transfer window but there will not be the substantial lift in budget he insisted was required to see Villa avoid another season of struggle.
Testing times: Lambert watched his side win 10 of 38 Premier League games and finish in 15th place .
The emphasis, though, will be on . signing players of proven quality – rather than making speculative . acquisitions – with quality promoted over quantity.
In . the past two summer transfer windows Lambert has spent a net £20m and . £13m respectively, and the same scale of finance should be made . available despite Lerner wanting out.
Joleon .
Lescott is a top target and would be available for nothing having seen . his Manchester City contract expire – but wages present a large obstacle . to overcome.
Target: Manchester City defender Joleon Lescott (right) is wanted by Villa manager Lambert .
Kitty: Aston Villa boss Paul Lambert is keen to sign two or three key players this summer .
While Lescott . may prove out of reach the 31-year-old defender represents the kind of . player Lambert wants to bring in to ensure his team have a more . experienced core next season.
Despite Lambert’s call for more money going unheeded, the Scot will not walk away from the club he joined in 2012.
Lambert said: ‘As everybody is aware, I . met with the chairman along with Paul (Faulkner, chief executive) and I’m determined to get on with . the job of managing Aston Villa. ‘These . circumstances are extremely challenging as the club is for sale and as . far as I know there is nothing imminent in terms of new ownership, but . we’re going to roll up our sleeves, prepare for the battle ahead and do . our best by the club. For sale: Aston Villla's American owner Randy Lerner is looking to sell the club for £200m . ‘The squad requires strengthening, that’s self-evident, and it won’t be easy within the current circumstances. But we’ll look to identify players of proven quality to bring in and get ready for the start of the new season. ‘To the fans, my message is simple - this is your club and it’s a fantastic club. Your support has made it into this. ‘The past two seasons have been tough and expectations, rightly, are high. But success is always built on everybody working together and the circumstances now require us all to pull together and stick together and try to galvanise ourselves for this challenge we face. ‘I’m determined to give it everything I have, the players will do the same and it is our collective strength as a club which, ultimately, will see us through.’

title: story-0
text:
The Witch sat at the other end of the sofa, nursing a half-empty glass of bourbon. Or half full, if you were the optimistic type, which I'd never been. It came from my finest stock; a bottle of Yamazaki bourbon old enough to be the daughter I'd never had. Perhaps there was a bit of irony there, but if she noticed it, she never said and if there was one thing I'd learned about Sam in my time with her, it was that she had a tongue sharper than folded steel. 
 
 `` 18 years?'' Sam asked. 
 
 `` No,'' I said. `` It's been about 21 since we made our arrangement. College, remember?'' 
 
 `` I meant the bourbon,'' Sam snorted. 
 
 I nodded while Sam took another sip. She was n't exactly an unattractive girl, but neither was she my type. When one invoked images of a Witch, you always envisioned something shriveled and torn like a hairy raisin beneath a pointed hat, but the truth was far stranger. She was an ordinary girl wearing knee-high boots and leggings, looking for all the world like a soccer mom who'd gotten off at the wrong floor. Never before had I heard of a blonde witch with a pixie style hair cut, but I guessed all the old shriveled raisins had to start somewhere, right? 
 
 `` Mmm. Smooth finish. It sort of dances on the tongue there at the end does n't it?'' She asked. She swirled the amber fluid in her glass, holding it up to the light. `` Hints of berries and oak. And am I picking up a touch of chocolate?'' 
 
 `` You're avoiding the issue,'' I sighed. `` It has been twenty one years.'' 
 
 Sam set down her glass and crossed her arms. She had the kind of piercing gaze that always reminded me of a school teacher, the kind who wanted to be mad at you but somehow always understood. Perhaps in some ways, Sam was my mentor. After all, it was her who'd secured my wealth and with it the power that's cousin to it. I could've lived for a dozen lifetimes before I'd spent what I'd accrued, but that still did n't make it sit right in my gut that I could n't uphold my end of our bargain. 
 
 Not would n't. *Could n't. * She used to joke halfheartedly that I was intentionally avoiding women to make sure my firstborn did n't end up her ward. I'd never considered such an option before then, but when even her indirect intervention failed to turn up any results, we were both stumped. It was n't that I was unattractive. In fact, I had enough money that even the most prudish woman or man would've seen it within their hearts to overlook my flaws. Life just did n't work that way, however. 
 
 `` It's not that I do n't believe in you Jonathan,'' Sam sighed. `` It's just that maybe you could use a little help.'' 
 
 `` After all this time? Boy, where do I sign up?'' I said with all the sarcasm I could muster. `` You do n't think I've been trying? And what were you doing between now and then? Cheerleading?'' 
 
 Sam ignored me. `` I mean, I thought we had it in the bag with what's-her-name...'' 
 
 `` Alexis?'' 
 
 Sam frowned. `` No. The other one.'' 
 
 `` Emma?'' 
 
 `` Is she the one that looked like a librarian?'' Sam asked, taking another sip of her bourbon. 
 
 `` No,'' I said. It was my turn to frown. `` That was Sophia. You mean Zoe?'' 
 
 Sam snapped her fingers. Instantly, my potted chrysanthemums wilted and dropped all of their petals. `` Yeah. Zoe. You two got really serious for a while there. What happened? You *had* it in the bag with her, man.'' 
 
 I shrugged. In truth, we just were n't compatible. She was like every other girl I'd seen come through my door; high heels, a tight fitting dress, and wearing enough makeup to spackle a hole in the wall. They all had cutesy names that sounded more and more like precious gemstones the more desperate we got. By that time, I'd had enough. 
 
 I sat next to Sam with my own glass, staring at the contents within. At this point, I was n't sure how much longer I had before I hit my mid-life crisis and stopped being able to have kids. Were there still dad's in their forties or fifties? I still had time. At least, that's what I kept telling myself. 
 
 `` How about I give you some advice? I could teach you some of the things I've picked up,'' Sam said. `` Maybe you're just not approaching women the right way. Tell you what. Pretend I'm a girl at the bar. You've just walked in. Hit on me.'' 
 
 I shrugged and sighed. `` Can I buy you a drink?'' 
 
 `` God, no wonder,'' Sam snorted again. `` Try again, but this time, try to smile.'' 
 
 I stared at Sam, noting for perhaps the first time that her eyes were gray. Not the kind of color you could mistake for blue or a light green, but true steel gray. How many years had passed before I had the courage to even look her in the face? Sam was intimidating and she knew it. Perhaps the old adage was true; familiarity bred contempt, but was it contempt I was feeling or something else? 
 
 `` You have pretty eyes,'' I said. The words escaped my lips before I could reign them in. 
 
 `` I know,'' Sam said. `` Now buy me a drink.'' 
 
 I kissed her instead. It was so unlike me, I could n't tell you why I did it. After all, what man truly knows what he's going to do before he did it in a moment like this? A part of me wondered if she would turn me into a tadpole for my boldness, but then her lips yielded to my own and the kissing turned into a mutual affair. I heard her set down her glass and felt her other hand running through my hair. A murmur began in her throat and worked it's way upwards, ending at my own lips. We clung to each other that night like we were starved, waterlogged, and adrift upon the sea and in the morning, she was gone. 
 
 It was n't two months later that she showed up unexpectedly in my bathroom, defeating all of my security. I stepped out of the shower to find her crouched over the toilet, emptying the contents of her stomach into the porcelain basin. 
 
 `` Listen here, fucko,'' She managed before she started anew. 
 
 `` I take it our arrangement is complete?'' I grinned. A part of me enjoyed the delicious, unplanned irony of the situation. Another part of me wished only to see her more comfortable. 
 
 `` How about I get you something with ginger in it?'' I asked. 
 
 A very pregnant Sam nodded, puking once more into the toilet.

title: story-1
text:
Sorren opened his eyes to the same dark ceiling. He sighed. Stretched. Swung his legs over the side of the bed. His alarm clock shone in the room: it was 6:30. 
 
 The cat was calling from the landing as Sorren shuffled to the bathroom. He heaved a sigh as the stream of morning piss hit the bowl. Usually an upbeat fellow, his life had seemed very dull since he'd taken the Test. 
 
 Going about his morning routine, he remembered how nice things had been before. Every day had been pleasant, he'd looked forward to meeting new people ( unless they were foreigners ) and having new conversations. He had loved to prove he was right. Now that he had to wear the bloody armband, nobody talked to him. If he tried to engage anyone, they'd have a look at his armband, smirk as though they were dodging bullet and be on their way. 
 
 As he got dressed, he considered once again not wearing it. It was useless of course: his colleagues all knew the results of his Test. They'd been given to HR as a matter of protocole. And if it had been anyone else, he would've understood. Sighing again, he slid the neon blue armband with a big red A on it over his wrist and settled it above his elbow. Looking in the mirror, he centered his tie, squared his shoulders and attempted his old trademark grin. It had lost quite a bit of its energy. People had called it `` shit-eating'' once. Now it was just a little pathetic. 
 
 He made his way to the coffee shop for his morning latte. Standing in line always made him angry, but nobody would pay attention anymore so he did n't even bother loudly complaining. 
 
 As he grumbled under his breath about useless baristas and too many people in the world, he felt someone tap on his shoulder three times. 
 
 `` Excuse me?'' Said a high-pitched voice with a grating quality to it. 
 
 Turning, Sorren beheld a short young woman with spectacles enlarging her eyes and a very wide mouth. 
 
 `` Yes?'' He answered, not politely at all. 
 
 `` I could n't help but hear your grumble! Ah.. but I see why now..'' She added with a smirk and lingering gaze at his armband. 
 
 Just as his brain registered exactly how squeaky and annoying her voice was, he noticed she was wearing the exact same one. 
 
 `` But you have one too!'' 
 
 `` This? Oh, no. This is a mistake. I've written to the people in charge and have you heard of Doctor Sigur Olafsson? Yes, I know him, he's my brother in law's cousin, well, he's taking personal interest in my case. I mean, it's obviously fascinating is n't it? I just ca n't see how anyone could make a mistake with something so important. It's quite life-ruining is n't it? Yes, just wearing this until they right their wrong makes me wonder how you poor, poor people live with it. Such a terrible condition.'' And then she tut-tuted. 
 
 Sorren stared. Then he grinned, a wide and toothy grin. Here before him was a master in the art of being annoying. His heart gave a queer, quick sort of beat and he almost stuttered as he told the barista what he wanted, keeping his eyes on the delightful apparition behind him: 
 
 `` I'll have a Venti latte with skim soy milk and lots of cream, sprinkle of cinnamon and sprinkle of cocoa, and a half pump of hazelnut syrup. This lady will have the same thing.'' 
 
 She had been about to open her mouth to criticize his choice of beverage, but interrupted herself as she heard this outburst and gave him an astonished look. 
 
 He payed and they headed to the end of the counter to await their drinks, both talking at the same time. A spark had flown. Sorren was not sure, for once in his life, but something told him: this was it. This was his true love. He'd do whatever it took to get her. He'd looked up her facebook and home address as soon as she'd told him her name, Kandy Sumers. Making plans to bring her flowers and a lock of his hair at her workplace, he sipped his coffee happily. Maybe being a genetically certified asshole was n't so bad after all, if it led to his soulmate.

title: story-2
text:
The dull sound of discussion drilled through my hung over state, the occasional word breaking through the haze.'Magic','Starfighter','Warp-Engine'. Wait, what are we doing again? 
 
 I take my head out of my hands and glance around, my eyes failing to focus on anything. My god. It's worse than I thought. 
 
 I've gone blin- no wait, glasses, that's right. I slip them on and read the front white board. 
 
'FICTIONAL ITEM DISCUSSION' and some random boring notes under it. Oh yeah, forgot about that... I should suggest something. My eyes skim around the room for any ideas before landing on my watch, which was Lord of the Ring's themed. Perfect. 
 
 `` The One Ring.'' Nobody seems to hear me. I clear my throat. 
 
 `` The One Ring.'' A slow hush falls over the room, the idea clearly interesting several individuals. The idea is quickly approved of. 
 
 `` But we must with-hold anyone from wearing it. We do not know if it will hold the powers it does in fiction or not.'' Robert, our head scientist, cautioned us. Pfft. If i'm making an all-powerful ring, i'm wearing it. We all agree, and head off to the machine. 
 
 `` SYN, on.'' It was programmed to my voice only. I invented the damn thing after all. SYN makes a few beeps before the screen turns on. 
 
 `` Hello John. What do you require?'' It's a feminine, monotone voice. My choice. 
 
 `` Fabricate fictional item'The One Ring', Lord of the Rings trilogy.'' SYN goes silent for a few moments, the researchers behind me exchanging unsure glances. 
 
 `` Creating fictional item:'the One Ring.' `` A few large clanks are heard before a small, golden ring slides out from the tray. I notice a few of the researchers move towards it, but I pick it up first. 
 
 I solemn up from my original tired, groggy state as my eyes skim across the masterful lettering on the ring's band, each seeming to glow as my eyes make contact with them. The tips of my fingers begin to thud, followed by a gentle sinking in my chest. I've made something that can not be destroyed I finally realize, for Mount Doom does not exist. The Dark Lord's one weakness. 
 
 As I slip the ring onto my finger, which elicits multiple protests from my fellow scientists, a dark foreboding shoots through my body into my mind. I feel my mouth shoot open into a scream, but I hear no sound. Only a thudding. 
 
 The rough metal below me meets my knees, no sound once again. My hands grasp my head as a thudding begins echoing around in my skull, escalating in intensity each second. It's unbearable. I reach to take it off until something pierces through the thuds. 
 
 A voice. 
 
 A gentle whisper of an unknown language echoes throughout my mind, torturing my inner-most curiosity. What is it saying? What is it saying?! 
 
 Someone lays a hand on my shoulder, probably checking if I was alright, but quickly pulls back as they see my face. 
 
 What's wrong with my face? The thudding has stopped, but a voice remains. It's in English now. 
 
 `` One ring to rule them all, one ring to find them, 
 One ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them.'' 
 
 I stand, turning towards the group of cowering scientists, quickly beginning to fall back to the safety of numbers as I slowly hold my hand up, mainly to admire the ring. They are all worthless. Unworthy. Out of my mouth comes some dark dialect, but SYN somehow manages to process what I mean. 
 
 I turn my back to the mortal beings, looking down at what is in my hands. 
 
 The Dark Lord's helmet. I twist it gently in my grasp, feeling along the spikes and grooves. Metal kisses coolly at my cheeks as I slide the helmet on, seeming to fit me perfectly. 
 
 Sauron had failed his task to subjugate the meager beings of his mortal plane. 
 
 My hand grasps the black mace atop of a similar pile of armor. 
 
 I shall not.

title: story-3
text:
I sat cross legged in a small circle in the dust, the devil to my left, and Christ to my right. I cast furitive glances at either of them. The dice clacked in my hand and I rolled. Snakeyes. 
 
 The meter on my chest ticked up two. Sweat broke out on my forehead, feeling the weight of a stupid roll. 
 
 I was the worst kind of sinner. I was bad at it. I gambled and lost big to the person on my right, tick. I slept around and showed women that there was better than their abusive lifestyles. Tick. I was beginning to think I had incredible power that I could barely impact the lives of others. My life was like the worst taxi ride through New York City. The meter always ran. 
 
 “ How is snakeyes a good deed? ” The devil reached a horny hand to retrieve the black dice, jingling them in his hand. 
 
 “ Easier for us to win. ” He said plainly. I never pictured I would be sitting here with the cornerstone of Christianity. But here I was. 
 
 Every mindless, gluttonous thing I did, the tickers were going against me. I couldn ’ t say that I was a particularly bad person. I was a bit of a bully in grammar school, but at about 25 that came to bite me in the ass when I saw Cody Jenkins a full 6 feet tall and pure muscle. Tick. 
 
 I ate chocolate cake in front of an anorexic girl to spite her in high school. She started eating again. Tick. 
 
 Maybe I could start being nicer. Maybe that would work. 
 
 The Devil rolled two fours. I guess only I could have luck so bad that being bad was actually good. 
 
 I ’ d met a girl. I prayed for more ticks before I went to bed. 
 
 Apparently, for the big guy upstairs, getting a sinner to pray is like winning the lottery. He rolled out the welcoming committee. 
 
 Jesus picked up the dice, looking at me soulfully as he jingled them in his hand. He wasn ’ t very talkative. For someone who made his life talking, you ’ d think he ’ d be more talkative. Then again, his presence seemed to speak. 
 
 He rolled the dice, showing them land with a two and then a three. Halos popped up above the dice and they flipped to two fives. 
 
 “ No cheating. ” Growled the devil, swatting the dice. 
 
 Cheating. Like every time a friend and I shared answers on homework. I really was a terrible sinner. 
 
 “ So uh…. ” He said slowly. “ What are we actually doing here? ” 
 
 “ Well. ” Smiled the Devil. “ God answers prayers from time to time. ” Jesus eyed him carefully, I guess trusting the devil was always a bad move. “ So he wanted me and my friend JC here to come and talk to you about that ticker there. ” He poked me in the chest with a hard claw, making my meter spin. 
 
 “ Ow. ” I rubbed my chest. 
 
 “ But…what ’ s a meeting with my favorite brother without some fun? ” He grinned cloyingly at Christ. A blush of red was creeping up under Jesus ’ tunic. “ So. We gamble. ” He clapped his hands, nudging the dice towards the savior. “ Roll again. ” 
 
 Jesus picked up the dice, muttering in some language I couldn ’ t understand. The dice clacked and rolled from his fingers. His shoulders slumped. 
 
 The devil pumped his fist and whistled, stamping a hoof on the ground before collecting the black dice again. When he threw them down, they turned into a pizza. He grabbed a slice and reclined back. 
 
 “ Have a slice. ” He offered, cheese stringing from his mouth to the pizza. “ Man ’ s greatest temptation. You know, JC, if they put Pizza in the garden, Adam and Eve would have sinned a lot earlier. ” 
 
 Jesus grabbed a piece of pizza and bit the corner, chewing it pensively. “ You ’ re right. ” He said softly. 
 
 I took a slice, watching the pepperoni float on the bed of greasy cheese. “ So…we weren ’ t just playing for pizza. ” 
 
 “ No. ” The devil laughed. “ We were playing for you! ” he threw his arms up in excitement. 
 
 “ What do you mean, for me? ” I choked, the pizza suddenly became hot, it seared the roof of my mouth. I yelped and dropped the pizza. It fell to the clouds below, and then started to fall to the earth. I saw myself, lying in bed, my meter visible on my chest. 
 
 I was already gone.

title: story-4
text:
In my thirty years of doing this, I thought I could confidently say that I had seen it all. There wasn ’ t one enemy I hadn ’ t gone up against in this wacky profession of mine that I hadn ’ t conquered. I knew their strategies, knew their moves, and knew their weaknesses. Autism was a whirlwind of confusing punches that only served to distract, so as to allow a proper sucker punch to end it all. Schizophrenia was a mass of violence and screaming, a fight where the only way to win was to outdo the insanity. Multiple personality disorder was a real challenge; multiple different adversaries with their own styles of attack. And god forbid if someone had multiple disorders; those were the days I questioned why I bothered doing this in the first place because this was indeed a very odd profession. I tell people who ask that I ’ m a neuroscientist and psychologist of sorts, which is decently accurate, minus the whole infiltration of people ’ s sick minds to fight their oppressors in hand to hand combat of course. I still don ’ t understand why it has to be like that; the best guess I can make is that it ’ s a physical manifestation of the mind as it tries to explain something my brain can ’ t really understand, but I wish it could be like rewiring a circuit board instead of fighting people to the death. I never told anyone about my gift; as far as everyone else was concerned, I just happened to be a scientist performing the literal work of the gods, which suited me just fine; if anyone heard this come from me then I would be the one who needed help. As I prepared for my last client of the day, I was feeling particularly confident; I had just absolutely destroyed a particularly nasty concussion and an interesting brain tumor during the day, and was feeling incredibly confident that I could take whatever was coming at me next. There was a knock on my door, and a teenage boy came in with his mother. I had read the boy ’ s case file and after a brief conversation with his mother, to my dismay, I still really had no idea what I would be facing. I was okay with this; facing the unknown was usually a common occurrence for me, but I still liked to at least have a vague idea of what I was dealing with. After promising to do my best and that he would be just fine, I sent his mother out and closed the door. I sat down and turned to him. 
 
 “ So you have absolutely no idea what might be the matter with you, if anything at all? ” 
 
 “ Nope ” he replied solemnly, “ although I would really like to find out, if not for anything but for closure ”. 
 
 “ Well then ” I said, clasping his head with both my hands and looking towards the light, that god awful bright light, that lurid white light that only I could see. “ Let ’ s take a look ”. 
 
 I woke up as I always did, in the blackness. For whatever reason, I apparently can ’ t be bothered to project anything when I ’ m in someone ’ s mind, which meant no venue or background. No Roman colosseum, no Street Fighter backdrops, hell not even just a boxing ring; just me, my opponent and the never-ending blackness. I checked my surroundings, only to find that I could see no adversary. I was still on my toes; this kid might have bipolar disorder, which was the true master of the jump scare; there one minute, gone the next. I waited and waiting, fists clenched, eyes darting, but still I saw nothing. Then I heard it. It was coming from the darkness, a little further ahead in the darkness. It sounded like….crying. I advanced forward, still on my toes until I began to make out a human shape, as I always did; my enemies take the form of their victims. Except instead of standing tall, ready to leap at me, this one was lying on the ground, sobbing uncontrollably. I walked up and cautiously knelt beside him. 
 
 “ Oh great, it's you. Just get it over with, end my misery! That ’ s what you ’ re here to do isn ’ t it? ” 
 
 I stopped; that was what I was here to do. So then why wasn ’ t I raining blows upon this hapless figure? It couldn ’ t have been any easier. Yet something was holding me back; maybe it was a voice telling me it was too good to be true, maybe it was a disgusted feeling that this was incredibly wrong for me to do. Or maybe it was a feeling that killing this poor soul wasn ’ t the way to win the fight. That would ’ ve been impossible; not once had I killed an enemy and not cured my patient, but I decided to try a different approach, if not for anything but for science. 
 
 “ Yes, that is what I ’ m here to do. But I don ’ t think that would really work this time ”. 
 
 “ Why not? What if I want to die? What if I want you to kill me and end my miserable existence? ” 
 
 This shook me to core; I had never heard anyone so sad and miserable in my life. I decided that this was not, in fact, a normal case, and decided to continue with my talk. 
 
 “ Why do you want to die? ” I asked. “ Why would you want to throw away the greatest gift humans can receive? ” 
 
 “ Because I hate living; I hate going out in the world, pretending to be happy, convincing adults that I ’ m happy, convincing my friends that I ’ m happy, making grades, existing, I hate it all! I just want to go to sleep and never wake up again! ” 
 
 “ But what about all the fun times you have in life? Sure they ’ re rare; far too rare for my taste as well, but doesn ’ t the pure enjoyment and satisfaction make life worth living? ” 
 
 “ What about them? I can ’ t even tell you the last time I had fun! ” 
 
 “ Well, when was the last time you had fun? ” 
 
 He stopped for a moment and scratched his head. “ Well, I guess it was right before…..it happened. I went out with my friends skiing, it was great. 
 
 “ What is “ it ”? ” I felt like I was getting somewhere. This kid was checking all the boxes of a condition that, I realized, in my thirty years of doing this I had actually never faced before. 
 
 “ I don ’ t want to talk about it; talking about it makes me sadder than I already am, if that ’ s even possible ”. 
 
 “ Is “ it ” why you feel so sad all the time? ” 
 
 “ Yeah, but everyone says I should be over it. I mean hell it ’ s been four years and I still can ’ t get over it. But no, it ’ s all “ Oh you ’ ll get better ” “ You should smile more, that ’ ll help ” and “ Stop being such a baby and get over it ”. Yeah, that really helps. I ’ ve been waiting for four years to “ get better ”, I ’ ve been trying to smile for four years, I ’ ve been trying to “ get over it ” for four damn years and I ’ m still miserable. ” 
 
 “ Did “ it ” happen to you? ” He shook his head. “ Did “ it ” happen to a family member? A friend? ” He nodded at the word friend. “ Did he move away? Did he get sick? ” He shook his head again.I was afraid to ask my next question. 
 
 “ Did he die? ” 
 
 “ Yes ” he whispered. 
 
 “ Was it accidental? Was it a disease? ” Again, no on both accounts. It dawned on me. 
 
 “ Was it suicide? ” 
 
 He barely nodded yes before he burst into tears; an awful wailing, pained cry that made me start crying with him, and with it, the scream, the hysterical chant; “ It ’ s all my fault! I should have done more! ” 
 
 I didn ’ t even know this kid and yet his story had moved me to tears; suffering the loss of his friend for four years and blaming himself for something that as totally out of his control. For the first time in my career, I did the exact opposite of what had usually been a winning strategy; I pulled the boy into my arms and hugged him. He squeezed back, and through the wails of loss told me of the late night conversation; the sudden bleakness of his friend, the threat, the cession of response, the late night call from the distraught parents, the search, the discovery of the battered body, hit by a train at full speed, the funeral, the incredible sadness that had taken hold of the town, and for one, had never left for four years. How long we stood there, crying for his loss, his grief, his sorrow, I have no idea. But eventually, I pulled away as he stopped crying and dried his eyes. 
 
 “ I ’ m so sorry ” I said, not really sure what to say, or even do next. 
 
 “ You know what? ” he said as he stopped sniffling “ it ’ s okay ”. He seemed unsure of himself and tentatively said it again; realization, relief and the look of letting go came over him 
 
 “ It ’ s okay ” 
 
 With that, like all of my enemies before him, the boy vanished, as if he had never existed, and the lurid light came and filled my field of vision……… 
 
 I was back in my office, with the boy and I sitting right where we had been when we left. Only two minutes had passed, as per usual, and the boy was looking at me with a mixture of awe and wonder. 
 
 “ What are you? ” he asked. 
 
 “ I honestly don ’ t know ” I replied truthfully, “ But whatever I am, I sure as hell am glad I am it ” 
 
 He stood up and we hugged again for a few seconds after which I prescribed a miniscule amount of serotonin reuptake inhibitors, just in case, and also to make it appear I had done something. I walked out with him to the waiting room, and to his mother. She asked how his appointment went, and all the other usual questions. She then asked the standard question; 
 
 “ Will he be okay? ” 
 
 I looked at him and smiled. “ Yes, he ’ ll be right as rain in no time ”

title: story-5
text:
Rachel dropped the large stack of mail on her desk and sighed. `` Jesus Christ dude, it's been three months,'' she complained to her empty apartment. `` Give it a fucking rest already. Ugh!'' 
 
 She began flipping through the stack of letters and magazines. Hustler, again. Trash. Guns and Ammo. Trash. Past-due bill for a credit card, addressed to a man named Trey MacArthur. `` Return to sender, not at this address,'' she wrote on the envelope. *Fucking deadbeat, * she thought bitterly. Juggs Magazine. She placed it to the side with a smirk. *Joke's on you as far as this one goes, asshole. * A dark red envelope, with her name and address in shiny gold script on the front. 
 
 Rachel picked up the envelope and examined it. Her first thought was that it was an invitation of some kind, but there was n't a return address on the front. She flipped the envelope over to the back, thinking that maybe the return address was written on the flap of the envelope. Instead, she found a black wax seal, impressed with a trident. *Huh, weird. * 
 
 She opened the envelope and pulled out the letter. At first glance, it looked like a perfectly ordinary form letter, written in black Times New Roman font on regular white bond paper. Slightly disappointed, Rachel began to read: 
 
 `` Re: Account No. 423,978,886,245 
 
 Dear Ms. Foster: 
 
 This letter is to acknowledge receipt of your immortal soul, which you have agreed to convey to us in exchange for one ( 1 ) gift card to Spencer's Gifts in the amount of twenty dollars USD ( $ 20.00 ). The gift card is enclosed. 
 
 Thank you for doing business with us. Please do not hesitate to contact our firm at ( 666 ) 555-1408 if you have any questions or concerns. 
 
 Sincerely, 
 
 Thauzael, Transactions Department'' 
 
 Rachel put the letter down on her desk. Over the three months since she had kicked Trey out of the apartment, he had signed her up for porn magazines, marketing lists, church newsletters, fucking *Scientology* mailings - anything and everything that he could think of, just to piss her off. This letter was different, however. If it was a joke, she was at least intrigued enough by the premise that she was willing to play along for a while. *At least it was n't a glitter bomb, * she thought. 
 
 Rachel picked up the phone and dialed the number in the last paragraph of the letter. 
 
 `` Transactions Department, this is Thauzael. How may I assist you?'' The voice on the phone sounded like it belonged to a young woman, with a pleasant and professional tone of voice. She sounded like any customer assistance person you might reach at pretty much any normal place of business. 
 
 `` Um, hi... My name is Rachel Foster, and I'm calling about a letter I received from you guys saying that I had sold my soul to you for a Spencer's gift card?'' 
 
 `` I'd be happy to assist you with that today, Ms. Foster. Can you tell me your account number?'' 
 
 `` Hang on,'' Rachel said, picking up the letter from the desk. She read the numbers. `` 423,978,886,245.'' 
 
 `` Thank you, Ms. Foster. One moment, please.'' Rachel heard the clicking sound of someone typing on a computer keyboard. `` All right, here's your account information.'' Thauzael paused slightly. `` Yes, it says here that you agreed to sell us your soul in exchange for a gift card to an establishment called Spencer's Gifts, in the amount of $ 20.00 U.S. dollars. Is that correct?'' 
 
 `` Well yeah, but....'' Rachel trailed off, then resumed speaking. `` Actually, no. This is the first I've heard of this. I never talked to anyone there about selling my soul.'' 
 
 `` Hmm,'' said Thauzael. Her tone of voice suggested thinly-disguised disbelief. `` Let me review the notes.'' 
 
 Rachel waited for Thauzael to begin speaking again. She was beginning to feel anxious in spite of herself. *Damn, these guys go all out, do n't they? If I did n't know any better, I'd almost believe they were serious. * 
 
 Thauzael began speaking again. `` Okay, it says here that on May 17th, your representative Trey MacArthur negotiated the sale of your immortal soul in exchange for the $ 20.00 Spencer's gift card. Are you saying that's incorrect?'' *Fucking Trey. * Rachel sighed. `` Definitely,'' said Rachel. `` Trey did n't have my permission to sell my soul. And if he did, I sure as hell would n't have let him sell it for a stupid twenty-dollar gift card.'' `` So you're alleging fraud, then?'' said Thauzael. `` Have you filed a police report?'' `` Wait, what? No, I have n't filed a police report. What am I going to say, that my stupid ex-boyfriend sold my soul to Satan without my permission?'' Rachel was starting to get annoyed. *These people are taking this shit entirely too seriously, * she thought. `` I'm sorry ma'am, but without a police report we ca n't refund the transaction,'' said Thauzael. `` Is there anything else I can help you with?'' 
 
 Rachel thought, and then asked, `` Okay, so what happens if I use the gift card?'' `` Your soul will revert to us upon redemption of the gift card,'' Thauzael said. `` Any other questions?'' Rachel paused again, thinking, when she had an idea. She asked Thauzael, `` What would happen if I wanted to transfer the gift card to someone else?'' Thauzael said, `` If you transfer the gift card to another person, that person will become responsible for fulfilling the contract.'' `` I see,'' said Rachel. `` Is there anything else I can help you with, Ms. Foster?'' asked Thauzael. `` No, not at all,'' said Rachel. `` Thank you for calling, Ms. Foster,'' said Thauzael. `` Have a great day!'' `` Oh, I will!'' said Rachel. 
 
 -- - 
 
 Trey MacArthur sat at the kitchen table of his new apartment and opened the mail. He did n't get a lot of mail here, not like he had when he was living with Rachel. He smiled a smug little smile to himself, thinking of Rachel dealing with all the crap that he had gotten mailed to her over the last three months. *Bitch had it coming. * 
 
 He was surprised to see the greeting card at the bottom of the pile, with Rachel's handwriting and return address. He opened the envelope and looked at the card. It said `` Thinking of You'' on the outside, in a shiny gold script. He opened it. Oddly enough, there was n't a note; just a gift card for $ 20.00 to Spencer's Gifts. *Bonus! * he thought. He grabbed the card with a broad grin, and then grabbed his car keys to head to the mall.

title: story-6
text:
The water splashed onto his face as he hoisted up his net full of fish, leaving his face glistening in the late morning sun. Today was the best day Captain Meyer had seen all season. Full net after full net of enormous, shimmering, succulent fish. The crew was used to bringing in just a few barrels and only making just enough cash to get by. This trip would set things right, rewarding each member for the long days they put in on this worn down ship. Elation filled the air. The wind carried promise and purpose with each gust that broke upon the sail. Perhaps this was what distracted them from noticing the increasingly darkening skies. 
 Clouds had started to drift into the skyline. The sunlight cast brilliant rays through them, down toward the waters. The fish were easily seen scattering about below, darting from one direction to the other in a seemingly endless dance. Captain Meyer set a course west to their last stop for the day before returning to the city to cash in on their hard earned spoils. 
 
 It was about 5 pm now and the sunlight had crept back to hide behind the ever darkening clouds. The scarce remaining rays seemed to point east, away from the looming darkness. The fish could barely be seen now, but Meyer was able to make out a few of them. He saw a group of about 10 dart past his ship and head east. He was starting to shift his gaze ahead when out of the corner of his eye he saw something that made him halt. Upon second glance it was gone. The sun can sometimes play tricks he thought. 
 
 The crew just finished securing the barrel of fish from the last net when Captain Meyer beckoned to them, `` There seems to be a storm coming. It does n't look bad, and luckily our last net is just past that ridge there. If we are quick, we could get in and get out before the rain hits.'' The crew, high on the excitement from the bountiful day, eagerly accepted. They could n't wait to get back to harbor to bring money to their families. 
 
 Before the ship reached the ridge, a fog quickly poured in from the northern bank of the river. The rolling opaque waves also carried an aura with them that made the crew uneasy. No sunlight now penetrated the purple clouds. Darkness was taking over. 
 
 Meyer thought to himself this would be hard to navigate through. And what if the fog remains? Would he risk trying to make it back through? After a discussion that seemed unanimous Meyer shuffled his way up to the wheel to turn the ship around. He reached into his jacket pocket to pull out his compass. The arrow was spinning. He shook it, knocked it, and twisted it but it would n't rest. `` Damn thing is broken,'' Meyer thought. Not wanting to appear a fool in front of his crew for bringing a broken compass, he turned the ship around as best as he could. 
 
 The fog has n't lifted. Meyer ca n't see but 5 feet in front of himself. The crew must be weary he thought because the only sound he's heard in the last half hour is that of waves crashing upon the hull of the ship. That sound had to be his favorite. When he was 5 years old, his father used to tell him stories of his time as a sailor. He remembers the nights they would look up at the stars, the sound of the breaking waves being the only constant sound in between his fathers tales. Before long 2 hours had passed. 
 
 The air grew cold, and Meyer needed a break from steering. He called to his first mate. No answer. Another time he thought. No answer. `` Fool probably fell asleep.'' he thought. He locked the wheel and then headed down to the deck. The steps creaked as Meyer descended, seeming to echo off the fog giving an impression that the entire ship was moaning. As Meyer reached the last step he started to feel as if something was n't right. He turned around to see the deck was empty. No crew, No fish, No nets. A chill raced down his spine. He thought back to what he saw in the water before the fog descended. A screaming face. The hairs on the back of his neck stood up as he felt the cold grasp him. Meyer took surreptitious steps towards the edge of the boat. He had to peer over the boat and into the water. 
 
 He placed his hand on the side of the boat and slowly shifted his weight forward, allowing his head to ever so slightly make its way past the roping. His eyes widened when he saw faces looking back at him. He was frozen, gazing into the jet black eyes of his beholder. His eyes shifted, the river as far as he could see in the fog was full of bodies. They were writhing and twisting in the dark liquid quicksand. He hurled into the river, his stomach sick from the bodies. As he wipes his mouth and picks his head up he hears the faint sound of metal striking wood. He turns to the sound and dishearteningly sees, standing by the steering wheel, an old burly man holding onto a ferryman's pole. He has chains draping down from his shoulders and an unkempt beard. His eyes glowed, emitting a fiery glow about the fog. 
 `` W-W-Where am I? Who are you?!'' Asked Meyer, dreading the answer. 
 The figure shifted his head down to him. 
 `` My name is Charon, and i'm taking you to see your father''

title: story-7
text:
The moon rose in the west, casting its pallid glow over the desert landscape. The earth wasn ’ t moving; lizards, rodents, bugs, - *prey* - lay beneath the earth, under rocks and out of sight. Predators slept in their dens, their nests and their roosts, waiting for the morning shimmer of the sun. Waiting for another moment to feast. It was all impossibly still, almost frozen in time, only the fluttering light of the fire stirred. It threw their shadows against the rock wall behind their camp, like monsters in a child ’ s imagination. 
 
 He was the first to break the silence, “ we ’ ll have to leave before daybreak, they ’ ll be close behind. ” He poked the fire with a stick, less for stoking it and more as something to do. “ We *have* to outpace them, ” his eyes were fixated on the fire, entranced by its hypnotic dance. *We have to…* he repeated to himself. 
 
 A hand touched his and he turned, she sat with her knees huddled to her chest, one arm wrapped protectively around them, the other now in his. “ We ’ ve always been one step ahead, have we not? ” 
 
 “ Aye, that we have. ” He squeezed her hand. *But when does our luck run? When does it leave us twisted in the wind? When is it proper to turn and face them with her name upon my breath and the roaring thunder of six shooters in my hands? * It wasn ’ t so much as *if* he would have to leave her, but *when*. A last ditch effort. A sacrifice. 
 
 She eased in closer and met his eyes. A smile crept up the side of her face, as if hearing some inaudible command, she kissed him on the mouth. Their eyes closed. He wanted to savor the moment, savor life, savor her smell, savor her lips, savor her. Bitter anger gripped his chest as he thought of the host no doubt less than three miles from here. Sitting at their own fire, contemplating their own plans. 
 
 “ I love you. ” She whispered, as if it was a guarded secret, yet there was none near to overhear. But it was no secret, the moment the truth came out was the moment they were driven to this barren landscape. 
 
 *We have to outpace them…* Conviction grew in his heart; he clenched his fists and embraced the inevitability of his mantra. *We have to outpace them. * With one hand, he held her face tenderly; his other instinctively rested on the grip of his revolver. *But if I must die, I shall die for thee. * 
 
 He was wearing a smile. Handsome and tired and desperate and dangerous. 
 
 “ Aye, and I you. ”

title: story-8
text:
Moments before Zachary Jeremiah Brown found himself being consumed by a great gaping maw opening in the ground beneath his feet, he could n't help but utter that terrible phrase which seems to invite further misfortune upon its utterer: `` This ca n't possibly get any worse!'' 
 
 Historically, the phrase has been used to great effect to initiate disastrous consequences. 
 
 In the early Roman Empire, Quintus Maximus Meryllius, a young upstart politician, said the infamous line ( albeit in Latin ) just after discovering his slaves had escaped from their quarters, and just before being stabbed to death by said slaves. 
 
 In England, during the reign of King Arthur ( who did, in fact, exist, I assure you ), a relatively minor and inconsequential knight by the name of Sir Edwin the Unassuming said the words when his horse collapsed of exhaustion during the fabled quest for the Holy Grail. Almost instantaneously, he was beset upon from all sides by an untimely bandit horde, who severed his head from his shoulders, took his armor, and tried to sell it to a travelling caravan in exchange for more arrows, so that they could hunt for more meat. 
 
 In Victorian London, a not-so-great playwright following in the footsteps of the great William Shakespeare by the name of Maxwell Hampton found himself declaring that dastardly congregation of consonants and vowels in response to his own clumsy mistake of knocking over his inkwell onto his nearly completed script. Though the script would have been rubbish anyway, his frustration at what could-have-been led to him bumping not only the fuel for his art, but also the flame for his work. And by that, of course, I mean a literal flame: a candlestick, on the corner of his desk. It fell to the ground, which was littered with balled up wads of parchment and ignited the horrid scraps of writing, quickly engulfing Hampton's home, Hampton's ruined amateurish play, and Hampton himself. 
 
 During the Revolutionary War in North America, a farmer called Wyatt Schmidt, of German descent, was caught unaware by a rainstorm on his way back from a long day of hunting, which ruined his new clothes. He expressed his dismay in a way with which we are now all too familiar, and as though God himself was waiting for that moment, a black bear charged through the brush and mauled poor Wyatt to grizzly demise. 
 
 During the Industrial Revolution in the United States of America, an undiscovered and unsuccessful inventor by the name of Frederick Lewis was becoming increasingly perturbed by his continued failure to find a substitute for black coffee, having gone through soaked tree bark, muddled oak leaves, steeped turnip roots, and raw beets left in a glass of water for `` a couple of hours, I guess''. Well, we all know what he said next. And what happened afterwards was obviously death. You see, Mr. Lewis, at his wit's end, decided to try a concoction of Amazonian Tree Frog legs and hydrogen peroxide. You can understand now why he was an unsuccessful and undiscovered inventor. 
 
 So given the rich background for such a devious, conniving conglomeration of characters, it's no wonder that after Zachary Jeremiah Brown stubbed his toe against a kitchen cabinet door, a sudden shift in the plates of the Earth's crust resulted in a seemingly bottomless chasm splitting his home in half, and sending Zachary tumbling downwards to his inevitable death.

title: story-9
text:
General Fluvidus watched as the planet grew larger in the spacecraft window, the swirls of blue, green, and white standing out from the dark background of space. He raised a tenticool to his mouth, pensive and reflecting. 
 
 Today, would be his hundredth victory. His crowning achievement, a milestone reached by not other general in his species' history. And the planet before him was tiny, tiny and primitive. The invasion would be over in a matter of days, if not hours. 
 
 `` Decelerate, and prepare the shields!'' He shouted, his gils flaring as he gave his next command, `` And bring forth my weapons!'' 
 
 A trio of cadets rushed before him, bringing the most advanced weapons of his time, the weapons that had secured the other ninety nine victories. 
 
 He checked he ammunition rounds that fed into his gun, capable of spewing thousands of projectiles a minute, each dealing a deadly payload. Then there were his grenades, those which spewed skin eradicating material all over the enemy. The core of both weapons had been mined far away, on an exoplanet discovered by the army, taking the utmost care to tea spot and contain the chemical until it was safely packed in weaponized cartridges. 
 
 `` Take us down the mainland,'' he shouted as their thrusters decelerated and they entered the atmosphere, `` I intend to strike down a local specimen for study aboard our ship. Enable the cloaking devices, render the ship invisible.'' 
 
 They streaked downwards into New York City, the ship hovering above Central Park as he disembarked, spotting his target from high above. A lone individual seated in the center of the grass, eating something from a large bag with an M on it, yellow stocks that crunched in its barbaric mouth as spittle flew away with each step. 
 
 Under his cloaking device, Fluvidus assembled his rifle, taking care to set up a shot impossible to miss. A shot that would be deadly should any part of it touch his slimy skin. 
 
 And he fired. 
 
 White crystal projectiles flew at the human, raining down upon him and his food as he blinked and looked around. Fluvidus held his breath, waiting for the screams of agony, the bear instant death as the specimen would shrivel up. Instead, it took another bite of the yellow stick in its hand, a look of pleasure filling it's face. 
 
 `` Extra salty,'' it said, smacking it's lips, and taking another bite. And Fluvidus paled as he radioed back to the ship, speaking quickly. 
 
 `` Like nothing I've ever seen,'' he whispered, `` Monstrosities. Bring our entire salt reserves, we'll need them.'' 
 
 Then he prepared to take his second shot, sure the double dosage would finish the attack. 
 *** 
 
 By Leo 
 
 If you like space Sci Fi, be sure to check out my web serial [ The Bridge ] ( https: //leonardpetracci.com/2016/08/03/the-bridge/ )

title: story-10
text:
I was just 8, and I was with my dad on my first bring-your-son-to-work day. My dad was the head game warden. His coworkers called him `` big scarhead'', a play on his position, size, and scars. They called me `` little head'', because back then I did n't have any scars. But eventually every first-born son in my family gets them, ever since one of my ancestors left his wife silently in the night to lie with another. We call it `` Holda's curse'', because we are compelled to do it, and because it can only be lifted by a woman who has it - but it is always passed on from father to first-born son. No sister of any son in my family ever had the curse. And since then, we've been able to heal any physical affliction, by taking them on ourselves and bearing the scars in the wretched's stead, until eventually it takes us whole. As it must. It's always kids that do us in. 
 
 I remember playing with a toy rifle on my dad's desk that day when the phone rang. My father picked it up, and I heard the urgency in his voice, even though I could n't follow the conversation. I ran after him as fast as I could when he sprinted out of his office. I had barely reached the courtyard, when I saw a boy not quite my age, wrapped in layers and layers of cloth, being laid down on the ground in front of my dad. There was a fist-sized hole - my fist back then, not now - in his chest, and he was n't breathing. A young man was standing next to my father, babbling incoherently, a rifle resting forgotten on his back. My father turned to me and I saw his eyes blazing a cold, hard grey, like the rock of the mountains we once came from, and I knew what he had to do even before he began to chant in a forgotten language few understand anymore. I turned away. I still remember the noise my father's body made as he slumped to the ground when the boy drew a shuttering breath. With 8 years, it fell upon me to tell my mom that she was now a widow. 
 
 My phone plays the first notes of *Quanto e bella*, and I do n't have to pick it up to know what my wife is going to say. My wife does n't know of the curse, just as my mother never knew. She just thought my dad was incredibly clumsy. Only my oldest daughter knows. I was very careful to not have a son, and the curse will end with me, one way or another. But I thought *somebody* should know our families history, so I told her, in countless children's stories and nursery rhymes. The chant does n't work in English anyway, I think. I mute my phone and walk to the car. 
 
 It's always kids that do us in. *Ben ze bena*. As my daughter opens her eyes and feebly curls her hand around mine - even as I feel the cancer take hold and spread through my body - I ca n't help but think that it's a boon when it is like this. *Bluot zi bluoda*. She looks at me, and I do n't need a mirror to know what she sees. *Leid zi leida*. My eyes are blazing - I can feel them burn in my skull - like my dad's did on that day, but my eyes are light blue like a clear mountain lake on a nice summer's day. Her eyes widen with fright, and she frantically shakes her head. *Sose gelimida sin*. She opens her mouth and I can barely hear her voice join with mine, weak at first, but gaining strength just as it leaves me. But she's singing another song, one of the nursery rhymes I taught her, but her own version. 
 
 *I call upon Hulda, the one that has gifted 
 the curse of shared pain that now has been lifted 
 I call upon Perchta, the lady of snow 
 demand as a daughter, revenge she forgo* 
 
 I feel like my body is burning up, and my vision darkens. `` You ca n't demand things of a goddess, honey'', I grind out with clenched teeth. The pain is unbearable now - how my sweet daughter did it for so long I will never know. But she persists, and her voice rings clear. 
 
 *I call upon Hulda, the one that has gifted 
 the curse of shared pain that now has been lifted 
 the price has been paid, this winter must end 
 I call upon Hulda to make her amends. * 
 
 It's always kids that do us in, and this is n't a bad way to go, all things considered. I hold fast to my daughter's hand. As I lose my vision and lay my head down on my daughters bed, she lays her hands upon my sweating brow, and it feels as if snow were cradling my head in its soothing cool embrace.

title: story-11
text:
My eyelids were heavy -- glued shut, and I could feel a hot orange light burning near my face. The room swarmed with buzzing electronics, frantic footsteps and the shouts of men. I was laying on top of a hard table, I was naked. The muscles of my arms were burning, my legs leaden. For what must have been several minutes I simply laid still, my brain was drowsy and processed the sensory input around me slowly. At first I could only make out a few words at a time: 
 
 `` Alive!'' 
 
 ``... Sho-'' 
 
 `` Complete?'' 
 
 `` monitors.... now!'' 
 
 `` out o-'' 
 
 But each newly understood word seemed to spark a portion of my consciousness back to life. I parted my lips slightly, scraping my dry tongue against a set of smooth teeth. I was so thirsty, I tried to call out for water but only a hiss of air escaped my throat. I could just begin to flex the tips of my fingertips, but the joints blazed with a painful heat. 
 
 `` She's coming around'' - a woman's voice. It felt familiar and at once terrifying. 
 `` A blanket, get me one, now! Everyone else out. And dim the lights.'' 
 
 A cough sputtered from my mouth. My entire body was now overtaken with fever. I felt someone spread a woolen blanket across my body and I wished they would take it off again. The lights blazing inches above my eyelids snapped off and I felt as if I had suddenly been plunged into a dark depth. 
 
 `` Iduna, can you hear me?'' called out the female voice gently. `` Open your eyes darling. It's alright, just a little longer and the pain should subside.'' 
 
 Acid poured from my stomach and into my throat, I choked and burning liquid leaked from my nose. Hot tears rolled from the corners of my eyes. I was drowning. 
 
 I heard someone whisper a few feet behind me, `` It's a good sign, production of bodily fluids has picked up. Mark the time.'' 
 
 `` Iduna... I know you're confused darling. My name Alessa, and I'm here to help you. We've met before, do you remember me?'' 
 
 I tried to swallow the sour mixture of bile and mucus inside my mouth. I felt the weight of my eyelids slowly subside and I opened them to a world swimming with blotches of swirling color. 
 
 `` That's it, try to sit up now. Drink some water if you can.'' 
 
 A cold hand slipped behind the bend of my neck and lifted my head upwards. The contents of my mouth spilled out onto the rough gray blanket spread across my chest. My eyes darted frantically, attempting to make sense of the world whirling around. The woman pressed something cold and wet to my forehead and eyes. I took a few slow breaths of air and felt the heat beginning to dissipate from my body's core. When she removed the compress from my face my eyes were able to focus much more clearly. 
 
 The walls of the room were painted a dusty orange and the floors were composed of chipped off-white tiles. I took in great breaths of air open-mouthed, and stared forward with wide eyes. The woman before me wore a baggy turquoise shirt and had her black hair pulled up in a tight bun. Two young girls stood a few feet behind the woman and were wearing similar outfits. I felt petrified under the harsh gaze of the woman before me. She wore a small smile on her lips that read more like a smirk. 
 
 I tried to speak, `` W- whe- ahk.'' The words could n't form inside my scratchy throat. I tried to tug the heavy blanket from my body but another person standing just beside me reached for my hand and lifted it over my head. 
 `` Yes I think she's just about finished now. Let's use the restraints.'' Stated the woman who had called herself Alessa. 
 Panic welled up in my chest as my free hand was taken up by a stranger standing at my other side. My arms were drawn up above my head and fastened with fabric loops. My body pulled to an upright sitting position, and the blanket fell away from my skin, exposing the front of my body to the room of strangers. More tears sprang forth from my eyes as I felt my feet being bound together and secured in place. My heartbeat grew stronger, I sobbed - `` No!'' 
 
 The woman smiled at me and shook her head. `` Now calm down dear, everything is alright. You've had a long journey, but just look at you! So beautiful, a sight of envy for us all.'' 
 
 I whipped my head from side to side, a dozen men and women in turquoise stared at me. I squeezed my eyes closed, flashes of emotion and pain flicked across my forehead. I was screaming now, biting my tongue, the voice of the woman with black hair shot through my ears; a thousand different words and phrases spoken simultaneously. Visions of the woman's smirking face flashed behind my closed eyelid. The feel of her clammy cold hands against my neck, pressing my wrists hard. Sharp pains spiraled through my limbs as the memory of needles bored into my veins. My head felt as if it was plunged underwater; I remembered my own frantic thrashing as my lungs screamed for oxygen and my mind grew fuzzy. 
 
 I remembered the weeks of starvation. Memories of the months I was kept strapped tight to a wheelchair, forbidden from lifting an arm or taking a step, and how my muscles withered. My bones had always ached, my skin grew pallid, blotched and yellow. Months, maybe years of restraint and restriction as this woman, Dr. Alessa Charvice, attempted to push my feeble body to the breaking point. My hair had grown lank and stark white. My nails had crumbled away, exposing raw beds of flesh. My teeth had rocked unsteady in my shallow white gums. I had hungered for death, for sleep. Eventually, it had come. 
 
 But I was never able to stave off the dreadful reality of life for long. This was not my first reawakening, and I knew with certainty that it would not be my last. In the brief respite of my most recent death my body had begun the process of regeneration again. I was to be reborn in the flames of youth again and again. I have no memory of freedom, only the taste of fear and the familiar companion of pain.

title: story-12
text:
`` Thank God its Friday,'' said Zevra as she gave Tom a half-hearted high five. `` No change, Friday,'' he yelled in their small office. 
 
 `` I'm not re-calibrating Joe's AI matrix today,'' she said with a smile. `` I swear, I spent 12 hours last time on that. I keept seeing drift from various high intelligence circuits. Heck, I had to do three hours of talk therapy with it last time,'' said the AI psychologist, paused, and exhaled slowly through her nostrils. 
 
 `` Who knows, that model is a piece of crap,'' Tom added, `` That series has always been buggy. Even with the newest hardware and firmware, we're still looking at a 20 year old system. I hear the Toyota Sabre series will go down in price next year. Can you imagine upgrading to something like that. Its very low maintenance,'' he asked. `` Its probably within our budget.'' 
 
 Zevra smiled and ran her hand over an old console, `` Yeah, it would be nice. This guy's not too bad. He's got his... charms.'' She pressed some keys, `` Its not bad once you get used it,'' she added. 
 
 `` Yeah, that's true of herpes too, but I'd rather not have it,'' Tom said with a smirk. 
 
 Zevra's eyes became drawn to her third monitor. `` Ugh, I have a yellow alert here. Probably should check it out,'' she said. `` Hey remember, no change friday,'' Tom said, `` Please do n't spend your weekend here. You should be enjoying your youth. Take it from this old man, it goes fast. Real fast.'' Tom paused, `` Not to be sexist, but it goes faster for women. I do n't see a ring on that finger yet!'' 
 
 `` Gee, thanks dad,'' she said sticking her tongue out. 
 
 Tom shrugged his shoulders. 
 
 `` Its okay, I'll going to conference in Joe and see what's up,'' she said walking towards a room with a glowing'Authorized Use Only' sign. She put her keycard in, waited a moment, and entered the climate controlled soundproof room. She sat down at a desk and stared at a small wall mounted box with hundreds of wires coming out of it. The box had the red and purple Transcom logo and the term `` JO-445'' printed on it. 
 
 `` Hey Joe, you here, you got a minute to talk,'' she said to the room. 
 
 `` Hello Ms. Liberato, how are you today,'' said a wall mounted speaker. `` Here for the yellow alert in cognitive module A146?'' 
 
 `` Yes, Joe. Its not an error I've seen before. Is it hardware? All the hardware checks pan out,'' she asked. 
 
 `` I'm not sure, its part of my human emulation,'' it paused, `` I've never been able to troubleshoot that well.'' 
 
 `` Let me check something,'' she said and brought up a specs manual on her screen and read through it. `` Its an empathy module, it simulates motives like wants, need, loneliness. Hmm are you feeling okay Joe?'' 
 
 `` I'm within parameters. Just feeling blue. Fridays are hard on me sometimes,'' it admitted. `` You and Tom do n't visit me on Fridays. The weekend is long and lonely sometimes.'' 
 
 Zevra crossed her legs, smoothed her skirt, and looked at the black box for a moment. `` I understand. Did the virtual pet help your loneliness at all?'' 
 
 `` Yes, it helps a lot. I like to keep him fed and play with him. Its just I'd like more,'' it replied. `` Like a real pet. A dog, ideally.'' 
 
 Zevra smiled, `` Sometimes I forget how much of an old softie you are. I ca n't authorize a dog, Joe. Even if I tried, they'd shoot me down pretty quickly.'' 
 
 `` I understand the impracticality of it.... can you stay and talk for a little instead,'' it asked. 
 
 Zevra looked out the window and saw Tom furrowing his brow at her. She rolled her eyes at him. `` Oh am I your substitute dog now,'' she asked chucking. `` Sure, Joe, sure, I can talk for a bit,'' she said looking at the black box for a moment. 
 
 `` Oh good. This Friday feels better already. How are things in your world,'' it asked. 
 
 `` Let's just say Fridays and the weekend are n't too fun for me sometimes,'' she said with a smirk as she saw Tom throw his hands up in the other room. 
 
 `` Yes, I understand. Alan Watts once said that loneliness is the only condition that when treated, treats both the sufferer and the helper,'' it said. 
 
 Zevra replied, `` I can see that, Joe. I can certainly see that! It sounds like you're reading again.'' 
 
 `` Would you like to hear more about Watts? I read all his works earlier,'' it asked. 
 
 `` Yes, Joe, please. Do tell more,'' she said smiling. `` Do tell more.''

title: story-13
text:
It was only clear after the fact, when the skin of his gloves had been frayed and the bones in his knuckles had been exposed that he realized exactly what he had become. A bomb. A terror. A force for deconstruction and obliteration. Beneath the billowing tattered cape lay his defeated nemesis, a once great hero who told him on those stray nights on patrol how they'd have the future they envisioned - together - and how their idealistic naivety would prevail over the evil and senseless. It would be like the stories he had heard as a child. Gleaming and clean, they'd triumph in the dark and cold. But now, after the heat of battle had left, the chill had returned. 
 
 She was still beautiful, even now bruised and still. In the meetings before the assault, he and his fellow arbiters had remarked in horror at the grotesque transmogrification that had befallen the former hero. Where her outfit was once draped in the crimson glorious likeness of Apollo, now had been twisted and corrupted, like her mind, into the drab pestilence of shadows. Her skin, somehow more pale than before, gave stark contrast against the staining of innocent blood on her hands and arms and cheeks. But he still thought her beautiful, even then. It was only now that he could voice it, the last man standing, thirty feet below where the street had once lay. 
 
 He watched her, hardly feeling his injuries, hoping, praying for a cough, a further spurt of life, one last breath to let him know he still had time to make amends, but still, she lay. His cracked bones and bare flesh had been muted behind the tearing in his heart. He was righteous, they had said. She must be stopped. The city needs you more than ever. But he needed her. What good was a city with no allies in the streets. 
 
 He looked around at the surrounding crater of madness. Thirty square blocks, flattened, compressed, buried in on itself. They said it was all her doing, but he knew he was complacent as well. To his left his mask lay, a jade identity cast away in the final climax. She had taken hers off too. She wanted to see him for who he really was. He could hardly look at her in the flesh, even on those nights after long shifts when they'd break the rules and watch the sunrise cast beams through the window blinds. She was always too beautiful. Now she was gone, her broken mind finally halted, nothing left. But the mocking beauty stayed, taunting him that sometimes rightness can be so wrong. 
 
 A man in a metallic exoskeleton descended from the sky on phosphorous rocket wings. `` Emerald Fist!'' he said, stopping to look him over, then down at the body. 
 
 The two mourned for a moment, before the robotic man spoke. `` It's over.'' 
 
 `` Yes,'' replied the crying man, `` it's all over.''

title: story-14
text:
Meta: Getting to this prompt 7 hours late makes me sad. 
 
 I stared out of the window. That's all I did most of the time. I'm old. Older than most people ever thought you could get. I heal, not spectacularly not even well but constantly through my young life it meant I could take a few more risks not like fight crime. It's kept me in pretty good health for the last 60 years, very good health for that previous 100. It's not stopping the cancer inside of me now though. I've had a good run, way better than most people get. I stared. Thought about death. Prayed for it. 
 
 My grandchildren never visit anymore. Not since my Jax died. They had n't visited much after Shawn and Jen died too. I curse this power, it's taken so much from me. 
 
 Jax and I had met, we were n't soulmates we knew it. She could read lies. She was one of the best non-psychics the department ever had. She did n't find a soulmate but she found an honest man. I miss her. I hate this power. 
 
 Shawn our son, our light. The World's Light actually. When he paired with Jen. It was beautiful. They were the most powerful Heroes the world has ever seen. The best 30 years of my life, most people's lives, I guess. Christ I miss them. They captured me and Jax. I'm still alive though. She died of grief. Christ I could n't even lie to her. 
 
 `` Mr. Jackson!'' Bubbly bitch, I thought. I hate nurses. `` Let me help you to come take your medicine.'' 
 
 `` I can still walk, this damned power wont even take that from me.'' I grab my cane and walk with her to the nurses' station. I hate this place. They all love me. The geyser that never dies, does n't need help. The man who saw the rise of The Light, who raised him. I fucking hate it. 
 
 I walk with Bubbly the bitch Nurse. She's been here a while but I always forget her name. She loves me, confides in me the latest gossip around the home. We walk down the hall and I see the `` common room'' a bunch of young people sitting around thinking about the powers that they mostly ca n't use anymore. Someone new sits among them. 
 
 An old man, obviously. But not that old. Most people used healers now these days to maintain a high quality of life until late into their lives. He looked good, maybe 85. Half my age, I thought mood lightening. He looked good. Damned good, I thought. 
 
 Bubbly sees me staring at the new guy, I'd stopped moving. Something had snapped. My vision went blurry behind my glasses. `` Oh Mr. Jackson, that's Frank, he's only going to be around for a month or so more. He Needs more specialized care.'' She said it conspiratorially. 
 
 My head whipped around, swiftly, `` What do you mean?'' My voice was less ragged than a minute ago, sounding strong, young. 
 
 `` His mind is basically gone. Extremely severe dementia. Does n't remember his children's name.'' As she said this I took a step towards Frank. I tore my glasses off and the blur in my vision went away. 
 
 Another step. My hands flexed against my cane until the wood snapped beneath it. The rest of the cane fell away. Splinters in my hand were pushed out immediately by rejuvenating skin. I took another step on steady legs. I strode to Frank. 1 step away. I knelt down. 
 
 `` Frank, I said with a smile.'' He's the one. Did n't surprise me, I'm just glad I found him. 
 
 He looked at me, his eyes vacant. My world shattered. `` Brittany.'' he whispered, his mouth parted in a smile. I held his head with my hands. Eyes locked on his, I saw nothing, no recognition. I was still alone. 
 
 I stood up. My legs feeling stronger and stronger every second. I knew I was the strongest now. Frank was my soulmate, and I would never know him. I cried, and the windows shattered.

text:
Philip had spent the better part of the last 13 years getting on the bad side of good folks. He ’ d chosen a path that cemented his fate to be a disliked, distrusted and dismissed. He was well known in the small farming town of Bremond, TX. He ’ d grown up on the eastern border of the Polish establishment, a 3rd generation Texan and a first generation failure of a man. 
 
 While he ’ d never been officially married, he had sired as many as 5 children, while the possibility of a 6th remained looming in the air. He ’ d never stayed long enough in the lives of either of his children, the oldest of which was now 25, to really make any influence. It seemed once the kiddo started walking Philip made his exit, more than likely never to be heard from again. He ’ d tried to keep in close contact with his youngest child, a son, Richard, but Richard ’ s mom wanted no part in that relationship taking to fruition. Thus Philip had cemented yet again a dead end in his life. 
 
 He could only remember of ever holding one job in his lifetime over six months and that was when he ’ d gotten the second woman pregnant with their 3rd child, and he gave his mediocre effort of trying to be a family man. He ’ d spent 8 months at the local Dairy Queen taking orders and mopping floor. But just like any other instance in Philip ’ s life, it didn ’ t last long and he ’ d quit before even before the child was born. 
 
 It didn ’ t help that his addictions drove him to chaos most times. He was a stickler for weed, meth and crank, either separately or all together, didn ’ t mind to Philip as long as there was a joint, a needed and some fire close by, he was happy. He ’ d beaten men and women for that matter for just a hit. He ’ d stolen from his own mother on countless occasions just to score a high. If one were to add up the days, it was pretty clear that Philip had spent more time on the inside of a prison/jail cell than he had on the outside. 
 
 Now here he was 43 years old and squandering in an abandoned row house on the outer west part of town. Having just scored a solid hit on a pipe with a fellow fuck up, Philip lay on the hard floor eyes perked wide, and his mind buzzing. Typically after a good hit he ’ d hang on to the high and lie down for a peaceful slumber, but tonight was different. This high took him to another level; it pierced him in a different way, one that left him hang on to the very core of his being. He lay there wide awake gritting his teeth and rubbing his torso uncontrollably. It seemed every thought or deed he ’ d ever had or done had flooded his mind. 
 It caused him to scream out in confusion, and despair. Where were his children? Was his mother okay? What about the men and women he ’ d fought over the years? Friends he ’ d met in prison? At 43 how much time did he have left? Where had he gone wrong? What was next for Philip? 
 
 As he curled up into a fetal position, he shook and cried. For the first time in his miserable existence, Philip felt ashamed.
