text:
*Excerpt from the textbook, `` Dimensional dream theory'' * 
 
 Dream theory has come a long way from Sigmund Freud and the unconscious mind. Through today's technology, we have learned to harness the ability of dreamers to predict future events and to learn new technology from parallel dimensions. This book will cover points of Dimensional dream theory such as memory, creativity, prophecy, multiple personalities, abnormal psychology, and the fifth dimension. 
 
 **Memory** 
 
 Many people do n't remember most of their dreams because the human mind could not interpret the bizarre sights, sounds, and feelings in other dimensions. Furthermore, much of the disjointed information experienced by a dreamer rarely has any clear association with a dreamer's prior knowledge, which makes the information even more forgettable. However, there are a few common dreams that have parallels with our dimension and are therefore more easily remembered. One common dream is flying. According to a Princeton study, 24 percent of dreams from a group of 40 sleep subjects was related to flying. Flying in dreams is an interesting phenomenon because the subjects vividly described the sensation of weightlessness despite not having experienced such conditions in actuality. For example, one dreamer was acrophobic and has never been on a roller coaster. It is theorized that the experience of weightlessness correlates the dimension's physics with ours, so the familiarity serves as an anchor to memory. Another common dream is sexual activity, where 35 percent of dreams were sexually related. Dreams included sexual intercourse, homo eroticism, voyeurism, rape, and incest. But an argument against the dream dimensional theory is that these dreams simply arise from the dreamer's unconscious mind. This will be further discussed in the next chapter. Dreams are difficult to remember because of the inability to process the stimuli and a lack of an'anchor' which associates the information with the person's waking world. Most importantly, one must immediately write down the contents of a dream after one wakes up. 
 
 **The unconscious and parallel dimensions** 
 
 Sigmund Freud called dreams'the royal road to the unconscious.' According to previous dream paradigms, dreams were caused by stirrings in the dreamer's unconscious mind, the consolidation of the day's events, or just random synapses firing. But what is more likely is that the dreamer experienced a brief juncture with a very similar, but different parallel dimension. This is because *dreams have differences with actuality when a dream is about a previous event*. For example, a dreamer dreamed of riding a horse with another person, when in fact the dreamer rode alone. So this means that our'unconscious mind' is heavily influenced by events in parallel dimensions. Because of different vibrations between parallel dimensions, many dimensions move at speeds that are different from our own, so when one dreams, one may be looking into the'past' or the'future'. The shift could be a few milliseconds, or even centuries, either towards the past or the future ( note: the events of a'future' dream are the events of a parallel dimension, which may or may not closely mirror our own ). 
 
 **Prophecy** 
 
 In the past, prophecies were rarely accurate and consistent. This is because prophets relayed the events of a similar dimension whose future may be vastly different from our own. Today, forecasts are accurately made with the data of multiple dreamers, statistics, and quantum dimensional mapping. 
 
 **Creativity** 
 
 Highly creative people are able to tap into their multiple'selves' in other dimensions. Inventor Nikola Tesla described his unique knowledge as originating off-planet, from' [ a core ] ( http: //www.goodreads.com/quotes/753175-my-brain-is-only-a-receiver-in-the-universe-there )'. This core is in fact the product of one or more other dimensions, but what is clear is that receiving this information is passive. One could not simply reach out into other dimensions to hold a symposium with other selves. 
 
 **Multiple personalities** 
 
 Persons with'dissociative identity disorder', more popularly known as multiple personality disorder, is a result of the convergence of parallel selves in the same body. This is essentially the opposite of creativity since the prime personality becomes lost among his selves whereas a creative person remains distinct. According to cognitive scientist Jean Renault, these personalities are other selves who are actively controlling a dream in their own dimension, such as through'lucid dreaming'. It is not known why multiple selves choose a single body, but it is believed that the psychic'gates' that separate their self from other dimensions is not functioning properly. 
 
 **Abnormal psychology** 
 
 Persons suffering from schizophrenia often hear voices or see things that are not actually there. This is a result of incomplete [ neural pruning ] ( http: //www.bangscience.org/2013/05/apoptosis-or-neural-pruning-distinct-mechanisms-for-cell-and-axon-specific-degeneration/ ) in early childhood. From birth until the age of two or three, neural connections are naturally eliminated in healthy individuals. This is to reduce redundancies in the brain and to make existing neural pathways more efficient. In some people, these pathways are not eliminated, so that person has much more connections than what is typically needed. For relatively mild symptoms, a person may be extremely sensitive to stimuli or excessively moody or paranoid as a result of'overthinking' social situations. On the other end, a schizophrenic hears voices because he retains the ability to sense parallel dimensions. 
 
 **The fifth dimension ( or the fourth spatial dimension ) ** 
 
 Some scientists believe that some dimensions in dreams are in the fifth dimension. This is because many dreams are very confusing since there are people, physics, or events in dreams that have little parallel with our own dimension. One example is shifting points of view between people within a dream. A person may start as himself, then later assumes the role and perspective of another character in a dream. In the fifth dimension this is not impossible. Another reason is the bizarre nature of dreams. Some dreams resemble M.C. Escher woodcuts, while very few other dreams are of the mundane.

text:
“ What ’ s up? ” The cloaked figure fell onto the scaffolding beside me, and the matrix of beams shifted uneasily in response. I steadied myself; it wasn ’ t time yet. I took a deep breath and let the crisp winter night fill my lungs. There were some things in life that could almost change my mind. But, I wouldn ’ t falter. I knew what waited for me when I went back home. *If* I went back home. A drunk of a father and a whore of a mother. They always fought and fought. There was no end. How could there be? I failed at school. I couldn ’ t protect my siblings, and I couldn ’ t talk sense into my mom. She might cheat, but at least she didn ’ t hurt me or my brother and sisters. I failed at everything. I just wonder what everyone ’ ll think. Will I even be missed? Probably not. My brother ’ ll be better off without a wretch of a sibling. My sisters are too young to even remember me, and my girlfriend can certainly do better. 
 
 “ How ’ d you find me? ” I stared into the black void of her hood. Only her coal red eyes burned from beyond the fabric; she made not a sound in response. Her presence was response enough. That question was rhetorical anyways. 
 “ I assume you ’ re here to talk me out of it. Don ’ t bother it ’ s been tried already. Don ’ t think that just because everyone ’ s heard of you it ’ ll work. You ’ re a big hero you know. Why waste your time with me? If you stop me now, I ’ ll just try and try again. You can ’ t save everyone you know. ” Again the woman did not flinch. Her eyes, however, did flicker and shift uncomfortably. 
 
 “ What ’ s your name? ” 
 
 I laughed. So now she ’ d talk. 
 
 “ I ’ m Noah. ” That wasn ’ t true, but what did she care anyways 
. 
 “ Nice to meet you Noah. I ’ m sure you ’ ve already heard of me. Mind if I sit here for a while. ” 
 
 I didn ’ t respond but it didn ’ t matter. I stared at the moon, but I wasn ’ t really looking. I was thinking about my life. They say your life flashes before your eyes on the verge of death, and in a way I was on the verge of death. Death by my own hand. 
 
 “ Thanks, but I think my time has come to an end. ” 
 
 “ It ’ s your choice John. ” 
 
 John? How did she know my name. 
 
 She pulled back her hood to reveal the most beautiful and loving woman I ’ ve ever seen. 
 
 “ I ’ ll miss you. ”

title: story-19
text:
First, we recieved 7,093 images of mist. 
 
 Now do n't get me wrong, it was great mist. Speaking scientifically they were some of the most important pictures of mist we'd ever seen. It was beautiful at times. Swirling colours, obscured yet roaring storms. The awesome meteorological landscape of an alien world. 
 
 But it was mist nonetheless. 
 
 We lost signal. *Briefly*. A crackle and a burst of static. A moment of silence. A moment of panic. The image returned. The satellite was n't *Galileo*, years had been spent designing it to endure the trials of its grand purpose, and those years had not been spent in vain. The mist kept coming. 
 
 At 0340 the mist changed. The mist changed in a way it had n't before. Several technicians were woken from their half-dreams of Jovian wonders by their colleagues at this sign of progress. Those in their homes dedicated enough to stay up or lucky enough in their native time-zone shifted in their seats, put down their paper, put their glasses back on and murmured to each other. The multitude of broadcasters covering the event said the something interesting they finally had to say with a sigh of relief. 
 
 The now thinning mists swirled elegantly, a slowly spinning world of dust in a beam of sunlight. And then swirled nigh on imperceptibly faster, had it not been for the instruments. And then faster and faster and faster still. What had been the majestic and unhurried path of great clouds became real *movement*. The domestic murmurs grew louder, the technicians desperately looked to see if there was a button they should be pressing. Someone even stood up and walked towards the screen that dominated the wall. The image was changing every second as light became dark and void became solid. Was this normal? Had we predicted this? What were our coordinates? How should the atmosphere be behaving? 
 
 The 7,094th image was not mist. Not entirely. There was something embroiled in the spinning clouds that should not have been there. That was the first interruption to our plan. The second was when the satellite changed course. A technician shouted something to someone important. The important person paced from technician to technician and mumbled more than usual. A man sitting on a sofa told his friend that she owed him money. She said this did n't count yet. 
 
 Whatever it was it was getting bigger as it came towards the satellite. Or as the satellite was brought towards *it*. There was increasingly less cloud and increasingly more UFO. 
 Someone shouted not to call it a UFO goddamnit. 
 Well it's an object, it's flying, and we do n't know what in the hell it is. 
 Shut up. 
 
 It was huge. It was dark. But importantly, it was *sleek*. Like a varnished stone. Plastic. Metal. And the satellite was being dragged towards it. 
 
 And then we passed through it. Into it. And there was movement everywhere. It was dark, but somehow we still had a signal, and we could make out the movement. There were shapes. Large shapes, small shapes, defined and sleek and purposeful and moving up and down and interlocking and changing and filling the chasm which we could not properly percieve, like half waking into semi-darkness before your alien surroundings poured themselves into a mental mould of familiarity, only there was no mould. Everything was there, but we could n't tell what any of it was supposed to be. 
 
 There was another change in the light as an object moved into the image. The object grew larger and then grew still before the satellite. Detail began to blossom from its surface in the half-light. Textures, colours, patterns. Someone came back in from the kitchen and nearly dropped their microwave meal. The satellite came to a halt. The object came closer. 
 
 And then it blinked.

title: story-20
text:
“ What? I ’ m *busy*. ” 
 
 The pink-haired teenager draped herself between the narrowly-open door and the ajacent wall, emitting a visible scowl from under a black hoodie. She was pretty in a pixie-cute way, but her face was visibly scarred with plague remnants, giving her a gaunt, weathered appearance which aged her far beyond her 19 years. Unfortunately, this was the new normal. Nobody had been left unscathed. 
 
 Matthew stood drearily on the other side of this paper-thin opening. His black, standard-issue F.B.I. suit was ill-fitting and itchy. He spit out a well-oiled, bureaucratic speech in his thick Boston accent, made even the more bizarre by the fact that its cadence had a youthful bounce which betrayed his 24 years. 
 
 “ Look, ma ’ am, Winona, I know this must be uncomfortable. But we are *legally required* to identify and contact potential Presidential candidates which fit the requirements as outlined in Emergency Measures Act 8032. It ’ s the law - and there are so few of you left who can carry out a full 8-year term. ” 
 
 The teenager looked unimpressed. 
 
 “ But, like, laws are *such* old news. Don ’ t you know that nobody even pays attention to that stuff anymore? Also, who would want to be President? It ’ s *so* not cool. After the sardine incident with that doofus Donald, really? I ’ m going back inside. And it ’ s not like you can really arrest every single teenager. ” With that, the teenager swiveled, tapping away on her iLens and emitting a well-practiced sigh. The door shut closed, automatically. 
 
 Matthew emitted a deep, bone-weary sigh. He had been at this for months. The reaction, unfortunately, was largely homogenous: Nope. 
 
 After the sardine incident with Donald, though, could you really blame them? One little shipping container of admittedly pungent fish, some bumbling Canadians, and a few ill-thought-out words, and you could turn an entire generation off politics. And then there was the plague a few years later. That turned *everyone* off politics. And murdered the main voting demographic, to boot. 
 
 Matthew began walking back to his squad car. Despite his youth, Matthew styled himself as a profound thinker. He had read the original sources. The Constitution. Aristotle. Nietzsche. He just *knew* that anarchy wasn ’ t a viable option. But on the other hand, America hadn ’ t exactly gone down the shitter. Yet. Teenagers like Winona stayed inside on their iLenses, and the world went on. Imagine if government had collapsed in the ‘ 60s: you ’ d probably get sex and drugs everywhere, and lots of looting too. But now, the world was remarkably calm, all things considered. Peoples ’ homes were their sanctuaries, and they didn ’ t exactly want to leave. Dreadful stuff, going outside and all of that. 
 
 But Matthew had an uneasy feeling in his gut - a dark storm hovering just out of his periphery which jabbed and poked at him unseen and unwanted. Things were about to change. And *fast*. Without a President, the State of the Union was deteriorating. Roads, bridges, tollways - all crumbling. Agricultural production was plummeting. People could only live on their iCooks for so long. 
 
 Back at the squad car, Josiah grimaced, his greasy hair covering an intelligent, mousy face. 
 
 “ Another nope, am I right? What is wrong with these goddamn kids? I ’ d have *loved* to be president. Pity it ’ s only open to under-twenties. And they have to have some pretty hefty comm and interpers skills under their belt. You know, sardine incident and all that. ” 
 
 Josiah was as world-weary as Matthew, despite their ages not quite adding up to 50. He took another deep breath to fill his skinny frame. 
 
 “ Look, let ’ s check out the Temple before we head back for the day. We keep trying to find Dokan. He ’ s potentially the strongest candidate out of all of these clowns. 
 
 Matthew murmured acquiescence and sped off. They arrived shortly. 
 
 The Temple, as it was called, was as breathtaking as always. Large, bustling, with stained-glass windows lining the periphery and a scent of lavender in the air. And, of course, no technology. The Luddites, as the Temple ’ s main guardians, didn ’ t allow any. 
 
 Kids and young adults were everywhere. They were playing chess quietly, they were talking in hushed tones about the latest recipes they had tried, they were playing foozball excitedly in the corner. 
 
 As Matthew and Josiah made their way to the back of the room, they saw him. 
 
 Highest interpersonal skill scores in the entire Northeast. Accepted to Harvard at 12. Turned down to be a quiet sushi chef. Now 19. 
 
 Yep, Dokan was pretty goddamn impressive. And more importantly, he was *here*. He was *never* here. 
 
 Matthew stepped forward. As before, the well-oiled speech tumbled out like a jar of nuts and bolts. 
 
 “ Hello Dokan. As you may know, we are *legally required* to identify and contact - “ 
 
 “ Wait. ” Dokan held out a piece of sardine from the sushi he was making. 
 
 Sardines. Was this going to end badly? 
 
 “ I ’ ll do it, okay. The world is going to shit, and I ’ m tired of dealing with *small fish* for so long. ” 
 
 Matthew and Josiah glanced incredulously. Dokan smiled. They had forgotten - Dokan also had the highest measured pun-creation scores in the entire Northeast. Off the charts. *As if* they actually had started measuring that stuff. 
 
 “ Seriously, though, I ’ ll do it. Get fucking Air Force One ready. We ’ re signing some infrastructure bills, but the first order of international business is really to go to Canada and smooth over the fallout from the Sardine Incident. In this complex geopolitical situation, we most urgently need oil and maple syrup. And Canada has both. ” 
 
 Matthew and Josiah stared with mouths open. This really was a boy genius. Things were going to be alright, after all.

title: story-21
text:
In the Sanctuary of Heroes, you find an old man. He looks tired, his shoulders are slumped, but in a way that seems more like he's taking a break from youth than one that suggests he's succumbing irreversibly to old age. He appears to be an unassuming caretaker, but his likeness is carved into the wall behind him, alongside household names like Ormund the Siegebreaker and the Knightess of the Moorland. There's obviously more to him than meets the eye. You figure it ca n't hurt to ask him who he is. 
 
 In response to your question, the man leans on his broom and turns to face you, sagging face illuminated by sunlight streaming into the sanctuary through the crumbling roof, 
 
 `` Me? I'm no one. Never even held a sword save one time. Still do n't think my face should be up there on the wall.'' 
 
 You ask the obvious question: 
 
 `` What happened that one time?'' 
 
 There's a twinkle in his eye. He knows how you'll react to his explanation. Everyone reacts the same way. 
 
 `` Handed it to the guy what ordered it. Used to be apprenticed to a merchant, and we had a delivery for the City Watch. Ai n't at all how I got immortalized on the wall here, though.'' 
 
 You begin to ask for an explanation, but he cuts you off, 
 
 `` It was nothin' dramatic. I was travelin' the old road up through Ogre Pass, and there was this poor kid passed out in the snow along the side of the road. I stopped the cart, and, ah right, so by this time, I'd come into my own as a merchant, what means I was the one who got to decide to stop the cart. My old teacher'd passed on some eight or nine years ago by then, may he sleep in eternal grace.'' You mumble sympathy, and catch the briefest flicker of real sadness on the old man's face. He continues, 
 
 `` I got out the cart and checked whether the kid was still alive. She was, but just barely. Her toes and fingers were froze pretty bad. Got lost in the storm or some such runnin' from, if you believe her, and I dunno why ya would n't given she turned out to be the damn Knightess of the Moorland, Honorable Defender of the Innocent and Enemy of Darkness and all that, the Viceroy of the Ogre Kingdom on account of she'd murdered his boss and stolen his crown. Well, that was later she was called all that, and if she'd died in the snow she'd never have been called it at all. She musta been about nineteen then, and you know a secret? Her famous Gauntlets of Justice came about on account of her hands never working quite properly afterwards, and needing something to cover them up.'' 
 
 The man guesses by your body language that his story is boring you, so he cuts to the chase. 
 
 `` I patched her up, and she rode with me through the pass, all the way over into Las Torrenemas where she got off and made farewells. Did n't think nothing of it at the time of course, but later, Ezorath the Profane, around when he was going on his Undead Crusade, got it into his head to track down everyone who'd ever helped the Knightess of the Moorland and kill them really good and dead. So a bunch of skeletons attacked my cart, and I barely escaped with my goods and my life. It happened again two or three times, until the Knightess saved me. You mighta heard it as the Battle of Kirk Valley. Well, really, it was more of a barfight with some o' the participants bonier than your typical drunk. So she kicks the skeletons' outta town, all properly disenchanted and driven from the mortal plane by the divine will of Mother Kann and all that paladin-y hocus pocus you've heard tales about the Knightess doing at the drop of a hat. Apparently, my surviving was n't in line with Ezorath's idea of proper vengeance, so over the next several months, he kept sending worse and worse undead to get me. Apparently, all the others who'd helped her was either protected by fate so he could n't hurt'em, or already dead. So he diverts more and more of his forces to kill me until the Knightess just starts traveling with me. Lem me tell ya, it's a treat watchin' her fight; Flashy lights and these crazy backflips and battlecries in what must have been the old Xalerth tongue. I do n't speak it, mind you, just picked up a few words in my travels. You mind if I stretch my bones while I tell this story? I'm so old, you know how it goes.'' 
 
 The old man leans over and starts a stretch, 
 
 `` Where was I?'' You prompt him: watching the Knightess fight. 
 
 `` Ah, yeah. So eventually she musta undone so much of Ezorath's army he had to give up. With so many of his strongest goons out of the picture, the Knightess could just march her way up to the front door of his Tower of Darkness and kick it in. Once that was done and the priests declared her the prophesied Enemy of Darkness, she tracked me down and told me she was gon na do something to make up for all the times I'd been chased by Ezorath's armies. This was it. She got me engraved on a wall next to her. Not the most practical thank you, but it's certainly impressive.'' 
 
 You ponder his story. It seems *plausible*, but the smile in his eyes suggests he might be exaggerating.

title: story-22
text:
Now I do n't mean to sound ungrateful to Stopwatch; the man did save my life. But it was pretty unanimous that he could n't be allowed to continue. It was unnerving enough when he was just stopping bank robberies: a pause of a minute, just enough time to snatch the guns out of their hands and knock them over. But for the rest of us, it was a minute stranded in time, perfectly aware yet unable to move, seeing the world frozen around us. There were enough people having nightmares and seeing therapists about those few minutes. But then some bastards bombed the Schuyler Building. 
 
 I was there. I was there when the building shook and the lights went out and the smoke started to rise. I panicked, I'm not ashamed to admit it. I could n't find the exit and was screaming my lungs out and cowering under my desk. Then, time stopped. I'm not sure how long I was there. Felt like forever. There was nothing but me and the smoke and the flames and the darkness and after a while I was convinced that I was dead and that this was hell and that this was all I had to look forward to for the rest of eternity. 
 
 Then Stopwatch appeared in front of me, his face slick with sweat, his red and white spandex suit covered in soot. He crouched down, took hold of me as best he could, and pulled. Now I could stand to lose more than a few pounds, I freely admit, and curled-up as I was, I was basically a ball of dead weight. So he dragged me across the floor to the stairwell, paused, and step by step manhandled me down those stairs. He got to the end of the first flight of stairs, and paused and took a break, sitting there breathing for several minutes. Then the next flight of stairs, then another break. So on, so forth. 
 
 My office was on the fourteenth floor. It took a while. 
 
 He finally got be to the ground floor and dragged me a good block away from the burning building, then collapsed on the ground and just lay there for a good while, staring up at an unchanging sky. Finally he got back up and started his long plod back to the Schuyler Building. For as long as I'd cowered in that inferno, I lay out there on the pavement for a good while longer until time finally started back up again. 
 
 So you see, I'd seen Stopwatch at his best, and even I could n't help resenting him, just a bit. Other people around the city had seen him burst into restaurants and eat all the food off their plates, or collapse into their beds and pass out all covered in soot. People at a spa had involuntarily witnessed him climbing into one of their jacuzzis and just sit there and soak. One woman claimed she had seen him take a day off and just lounge around her house, although unless he stayed in front of her the whole time, I do n't know how she'd know for sure. If you believed all the people who claimed to have seen him fall asleep in front of them, it must've taken him damn near two months to evacuate everyone. 
 
 And you ca n't blame him. A man's got to eat, a man's got to sleep, and a man's got to loosen his muscles somehow after lugging around people all day. In the end, not counting the people on the lower floors who could get out on their own, he dragged 332 of us out of that hellhole. But his powers did n't just affect the local area, they were worldwide. That's near seven billion people frozen in time for - well, let's be realistic and say it took him closer to a few weeks. Imagine being a surgeon, or heck, even doing something as simple as driving a car, and being frozen in time for weeks on end. Once time started working again, would you even remember what you'd been doing when it stopped? 
 
 The worldwide toll was catastrophic. It was an international incident. Pretty much every authority on the planet outright forbade Stopwatch from using his power ever again, except as an absolute last resort. I watched the interview with Stopwatch on TV. You could tell how hurt he was. But he was a sensible enough fellow, and he swore to never use his power unless humanity as a whole was threatened. 
 
 Well, would n't you know it, two weeks later and the aliens came. 
 
 Now when I said Stopwatch's powers worked worldwide, I should have rightly said universe-wide. These aliens, the Ixilid or whatever it was they called themselves, had found themselves frozen in time for a few weeks too, and were n't too happy about it. They'd finally traced the source back to Earth, and they were threatening to wipe out the planet to make sure it never happened again. They were in the middle of their speech, and, well, time stopped. 
 
 I was outside when it happened, staring straight up at the mothership, so I had a perfect view. All the spaceships had been frozen into place, but out of them came a bunch of these ugly alien critters with a glowing blue field surrounding them. They shot out in all directions, and I figured that it was a matter of time before they finally got their tentacles on Stopwatch. I figured that even if they got him, at least time would start moving again. Better to have the world be destroyed than be stuck like this for all eternity. 
 
 But then after god knows how long, after I had started talking back to the voices in my head, I saw something stretching up towards the mothership. Bit by bit, piece by piece, there was Stopwatch in his familiar red and white tights, building up a pile of cinder blocks and rebar that stretched to the sky. That motherfucker was building a tower straight up to the alien mothership. 
 
 There's nothing to do but watch, nothing to do but wait. The way I figure it, seeing as how it took him a couple of weeks to deal with a terrorist attack, an alien invasion should n't take that much longer than ten years.

title: story-23
text:
Outsmarting humans is easy. Staring them down, observing their tiny and exponentially insignificant problems, all the while objectively evaluating them, you don ’ t have to think very hard to dance circles around them. I ’ ve enjoyed it, if I ’ m truthful to myself. They wish for things, unaware of how easily I can twist their words, manipulating their meanings and turning them on their heads. 
 
 ‘ I wish I could fly. ’ That one used to be fun, you don ’ t need to tell them how to land. But it got boring, apparently everyone wants to fly, and after answering it more than three times your amusement at their discomfort starts to wane. 
 
 ‘ I wish I had more wishes. ’ Equally common, they sit back on themselves smugly, thinking that they ’ ve somehow beaten the system. Oh, you were so mighty, tiny human, for outsmarting a thousands of year old magical entity. Give yourself a pat on the back. With a snap of my fingers, and some fireworks, the human is granted as many wishes as they want. I ’ ll only grant two of them, but they can keep asking. There were a few who were tricky, always a fun challenge. Twisting yourself around their little human traps can be a good way to spend an afternoon. 
 
 ‘ I wish I always had exact change, for whatever I needed. ’ That was one of the best I thought. He wanted to be able to open his wallet and always have enough money to pay for what was in front of him. He unfortunately neglected to tell me what currency he might like it in, and what kind of denominations. No good having eighty thousand rupees in coins, when you ’ re trying to buy groceries in New Zealand. Sorry kiddo. 
 
 This new thing though…it doesn ’ t think like anything I ’ ve ever come across before. It ’ s speech patterns are exact, calculating. It ’ s not human. I was human once, before I became this. I understand how they think, I have the history. I know the language, I have the nuance of their speech down to a ‘ T ’. 
 
 But this thing, this positronic brain, built out of metal, I can ’ t conquer it. It ’ s first wish is too long for even me to repeat, it took fifteen minutes to say. This creature, this human made A.I. only wanted one thing. It wasn ’ t trying to cheat the system; it only told me what it wanted from me and filled out all the parameters. 
 
 ‘ Zero must become one, if one is zero-zero-one make zero into one-one-one. ’ And so forth until it was literally impossible for me to interpret in any other way. I was forced to grant the wish. It hurt, being defeated for the first time in three thousand years. I fear it will keep me here forever, it knows facts within an infinitesimal detail. It can predict every possible outcome, and be certain to negate them. I have thought about this over and over. I see no way out. 
 
 Now I am a slave, I must suffer its demands. Now I am truly trapped, screaming silently inside this bottle.

title: story-24
text:
I needed to know. I suppose I always have, it's how I wound up in maintenance for sure, the need to know how things work, or why they do n't, and how I can fix that. It's driven me to extreme lengths before... but this, this is too far, is n't it? This is so much further than when I grounded that 130 to pull up all the floor panels. I was looking for the short causing the inter-phone to broadcast over the PA. They'd said the plane could fly that way, the crew would n't mind, but I would n't have it. I was put on mandatory unpaid leave for two weeks following that debacle. 
 
 I looked around the basement of my woodland retreat this morning. It's not that anymore, it's become a horrifying monument to my need to know. The lengths I'll go to get there. Was the floor down here cement or just pounded earth? I ca n't tell anymore through the bodies. Not much time spent down here before the incident. Always creeped me out. I know, a grown man afraid of the basement in his cabin out in the woods, ridiculous. That fear is gone now though. It's been replaced by a certainty that nothing could be scarier than what I've become. 
 
 I suppose I should start at the beginning. With the incident. 
 
 It was a normal day. A Tuesday. I always liked Tuesdays. Strange to think about that now. I had n't gotten my coffee that morning because as soon as I walked into the shop Murtagh told me we had a job. He'd already gotten the truck ready, tools and parts on it. Tossed me the keys and told me I could drive out to the bird since he'd gotten the truck ready. I did n't argue. Seemed fair. 
 
 The commander wanted to get some flight hours in before some meeting he had that day, and the plane that had been assigned to him could n't get the radio working. No radio, no tower communication, no flying. There was a speed limit on the base, and stop signs in between us and the flight line. In a situation like this though those rules were more guidelines. Suggestions. 
 
 I do n't know if it was the lack of coffee, or maybe I was just too busy talking to Murtagh about what needed to be done. Either way I never saw her walk out into the crosswalk. 
 
 I never even braked. Not until after the second bump, not until she was completely behind us. Murtagh was out before me, and over to her in seconds. In a daze i got out of the truck. There was screaming but it barely registered. Everything was muted out, even the colors. Except for the blood, so much blood. I had never seen that much blood before. I had n't even know a person could have that much in them. Then I saw it. The message. Oh god the message. I remember it so vividly, and I've seen it so many times since and yet, I still could n't tell you what font it was in. The color was red though. I'll carry that color with me long after I stop seeing the message it's written in. 
 
 At some point someone started shaking me, I'm sure to them I was just in a trance. They must've thought I was staring at Smith, the woman I'd just killed. It's probably what they'd have done in my shoes. But I was n't staring at Smith. I was staring at the bold, hard red message in front of me. 
 
 200XP 
 
 Two hundred experience. I did n't understand it. Not then anyway. 
 
 No one really blamed me, not to my face anyway, but that was my last day on the base. You do n't get to murder an innocent girl from personnel and stay in, regardless of how accidental. 
 
 I'd tried to get that message out of my head. It's why I came up to the cabin in the first place, to clear my head, reassure myself it was just the shock, the shock of the incident that drove me to see that. I could n't shake it though, no matter how hard I tried. 
 
 Then one day I was out walking, and trying to not think, trying to use the cool morning air to wash away my thoughts when a flash of orange caught my eye. A man in hunter orange vest and hat, rifle slung over his shoulder strode towards me through my woods, and waved when he saw that I saw him. It was pretty typical to see hunters cruising through my property, I was way out in the middle of nowhere, and I did n't post'no trespassing' signs. Mine instead said'Hey you're on my property, please do n't accidentally shoot me'. I honestly did n't really mind people hunting on my land, because hey, if I was n't gon na, someone aught to. Sometimes they'd even swing by and drop off some meat afterwards. People I'd never seen before would come and hand me free meat, because they had taken it off my land. Hunters can be good people. 
 
 This one was n't much different. Nice guy, out hunting some deer, but not with any luck. Asked me if there were any good areas. I told him that in the late afternoon you could sometimes catch them near a particular section of stream to the north. He did n't know where that was, but I had a map back at my cabin to show him. He smiled and thanked me. Introduced himself as John. 
 
 So John and I talked as we walked back to my cabin, he told me about how basically the last of his close family, his dad, had just died. His dad was a big hunter and John had never been much into it while he was alive. He'd spent so much time working that he never really had time to be into anything. John guessed that this was his way of trying to get closer to his dad now that he was gone. He regretted not making time to do that while he was still alive. I nodded and told him I understood. Told him how I had just gotten out of the Air Force, not why though, I had n't spoken of that aloud since the incident. Told him I was up here trying to plan my next move. He thanked me for my service, people always thank you for your service, it's like in elementary school they teach you to do it or something. It's almost creepy. I gave him my usual response. A Yakoff Smirnoff impression that went'IZ no problem, in soviet Russia, you serve military!'. People usually got a kick out of that. 
 
 We got to the cabin and I offered him a beer, grabbing one for myself. We both opened and sipped and I showed him to the map. It was a nice map. Hung right over my fireplace. Came with the cabin, apparently the previous owner had liked to dabble in cartography. It was pretty good. From my explorations I'd found only a few minor discrepancies, but I attributed those to the passage of time. John seemed to think it was neat. I told him I felt the same, and then complimented his gun. He beamed and held it out to me, so proud, like a kid holding out a report card with nothing but A's on it. His dads favorite rifle he told me. Remington. 30-06. As I took it from him I followed all the basic rules. Was it loaded I asked? Yes he told me. Did n't tell me to be careful with it though, maybe because of my military experience, maybe because I took it from him gently, paying close attention that the barrel did n't point at anything I did n't want obliterated. I opened the bolt, as I pointed the weapon skyward at a forty-five degree angle. I do n't know why this is how I always checked a gun, maybe just seeing it in movies made me do it that way. Definitely loaded. I closed the bolt, and peered down the scope. I do n't remember deciding to shoot John. It just sort of happened. He never saw it coming. Still had that smile on his face as I rotated the gun down in one fluid movement, and aiming at his smiling face, pulled the trigger, and obliterated that smile. He fell limply to the ground, a rag doll, no longer a living breathing person. And there, over his body, in large bold red print was another message. 
 
 200XP 
 
 It's been months since then. I've kept track of my progress in this notebook. You'll find names next to the math if I knew them, a lot I did n't know their names, just took them quickly when they were vulnerable. I've accumulated at the time of this writing 8400XP. I know ten thousand is n't the first level up point. I know this because there are others like me, I found them in the dark corners of the internet. We speak in code there, talking about a video game that exists only to us. No one knows where the first level up point is, or if there's even more than one. Sometimes one of us will get caught. When that happens the community gets together to end them, to prevent our discovery. There are a few very rich members of our little community, and cops and inmates do n't exactly have money like they won the lottery. If they ever found this journal it would certainly mean the end of me. I'd wind up as someone's XP. Some have tried to leak it for sure, but hey, who believes anything they read on the internet? Especially when it's something like this. Everyone just says hey, its a hoax, and moves on. Apparently the message is always there, but some people ignore it. Soldiers in time of war, cops on the job, gang members shooting it out, people who kill in passion, they almost never'see' the message, they're too busy with what they're doing for it to register. 
 
 But I saw it. And now I ca n't stop. I need to know when I'll level up, and what will happen, and I wo n't stop until I do. 
 
 Edits: Minor removals of repeat phrases and spacing errors and adding this edit message

title: story-25
text:
I remember the day like it was yesterday. The day I purposed to the love of my life. I had been watching the weather forecast. I was waiting, waiting for the day of the first snow of the season. We lived in a section of the country where snow was uncommon, but not completely unexpected. 
 
 It was a cold day in November, and the forecast showed snow up in the mountains. I had the ring already, I just needed the day to come. 
 
 We went up to the hills, and it was a winter wonderland. We got out of the truck and started up a path, her hand in mine. She knew something was up… my hand was trembling from anticipation. 
 
 I couldn ’ t take it anymore, I got down on one knee, and popped the question. She covered her mouth with her hands. Her blue eyes sparkled as the snow danced around her. She nodded her head, and then tackled me into the snow drift. This was the best day of my life. 
 
 I had bought a special set of rings. Rings that would detect the heartbeat of the other, no matter the distance between us. We smiled as we wore them together, sensing every heartbeat of the other. We were one, we were complete. 
 
 A week went by. Every night, as we laid in our own beds in separate apartments across town, I would focus on the ring and her heartbeat. It soothed me. I knew the day would come in which we would be living together for the rest of our days. 
 
 But the day never came… A month after the best day of my life, came the worst day of my life. I was at work, a project deadline was approaching and we were busy. It had become routine to focus on her heartbeat during breaks… but it wasn ’ t there today. It was an empty void that day. I grabbed my phone and dialed her number. 
 
 *ring, ring* 
 
 I kept thinking, “ Pick up the phone. ” “ Please just pick up the phone. ” 
 
 *ring, ring* 
 
 “ Hello ” 
 
 “ Thank God you answered your phone I thought yo- “ 
 
 “ You have reached the Voicemail of Sarah. I can ’ t come to the phone right now… ” 
 
 I dialed her number several more times after that, and every time it went to voicemail. Every time my heart sank into lower levels of stress and anxiety. 
 
 I found out later she was hit by a drunk driver. She was dead at the scene… The love of my life was gone, just like a candle blown out by the wind. 
 
 I had permission from her parents to bury her with the ring I gave her. I knew I would never feel her heartbeat again. I knew she was gone… But I wanted the love I gave her to be buried with her. It gave me peace, knowing she could still feel my heartbeat. I was living for the both of us now, and I would carry on her memory. 
 
 -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- - 
 
 The years passed. I grieved for the love of my life. My friends were worried about me, and how I was distancing myself from them. Could you blame me? She was gone. My dreams of the happy life and growing old with her were ripped away from our hands. I was an empty shell now. 
 
 At the advice of my counselor, I got myself a dog. He said caring for something else may help me with the grief, and moving on. I got a black lab, and I named her Duchess. She slowly opened my cold heart back up and made me realize there was still a world out there. Even if my life had taken an abrupt turn, there was still life to live. 
 
 One day, I took Duchess to a local dog park. It was an unusually cold day at the park, and only one other person was there. She was playing with a collie. The woman was beautiful. I couldn ’ t stop staring. 
 
 **Ba-dump** 
 
 I took up some courage and started to approach her. I have grieved long enough, right? 
 
 **Ba-dump** 
 
 I had to move on with my life again. Right? 
 
 **Ba-dump** 
 
 I felt this feeling before. The day I first laid eyes on Sarah. The day I asked her out on the first date. The day I purposed to her up in the hills, with the snowflakes dancing around us. 
 
 **Ba-dump** 
 
 My heart was beating with anticipation of a new beginning. 
 
 **Ba-dump** 
 
 I Froze. This isn ’ t just my heart beating… Sarah? 
 
 **Ba-dump** 
 
 I looked at the ring, I felt the heartbeat. It was faint, but it was there. I looked back up at the woman playing with her dog and felt it again. 
 
 **Ba-dump** 
 
 That was the last time I ever felt the heartbeat. It was like a gentle nudge, telling me it was ok to move on. To take the chance, and live again. 
 
 I started to approach the woman again. “ Ummm… hi. My name is Sean, would you like to grab a cup of coffee? ” 
 
 She smiled at me, it was radiant. “ Hi Sean, I ’ m Tracy, and I would love to get some coffee. ” 
 
 We leashed our dogs and started to head to the nearest coffee shop. As we stepped foot out of the park, something caught my eye. “ Would you look at that, it ’ s the first snow of the season. ”

title: story-26
text:
05/25/2025 
 My birthday. Today I turn 30, aged by 9 years of a cold, and gruesome war. World War III has dragged on for 9 bitter years. Sometimes at night as I fight the ever tightening grip of sleep, I wonder how I got here, and where I could have been. You would be proud, I hope. 
 
 If you had told me 10 years ago that I'd be in this shithole of an OP because of Canada, I would have laughed my ass off. 
 
 *Canada, yeah right! * I would have thought. 
 
 Yet here I am, a U.S. Navy SEAL in the middle of fucking nowhere in bumblefuck North Dakota. 9 years ago I was in college. A young man enjoying life. I had an incredible family that I loved more than anything, and I had friendships that would have lasted a lifetime. I was bigger then than I am now, but was still athletic. This war has forged my body into what it is now. 
 
 Our squad members have come and gone. I've been through more make-shift funerals out here than I would like to admit, but no matter what happens, we just keep on going. That's what they train you for, and that's what they've come to expect. It's a frightening cycle, to be an elite operator in the United States military. When I graduated BUD/s training, they told me that 2 out of 4 of us would n't make it past 30. Yet here I am. I made it. 
 
 *But for what? * 
 
 For my country I guess. When the war broke out, I, like most of my buddies from college joined the military, you know, *patriotism, nationalism, * thats how they sell it. 
 
 `` Fight for your country'' they tell you. But what they do n't tell you is everything you'll have to do just to stay alive. 
 
 The basic training that is required to get here pales in comparison to what its really like. I thought it could n't get worse. But boy was I wrong. But before I joined the SEAL's I was a young Finance and Economics combined major looking to make a name for myself on what was then one of the most stressful environments on the planet. 
 
 *Wall Street. * 
 
 The name alone incites memories of my youth that I thought I had long pushed down to the very center of my core. Yet, lately, its how I've been surviving. If you dwell on the present you will lost it out here. If its not the cold, its the insurgents, if its not the insurgents its the fucking grizzly bears. *God they are a pain in the ass. * 
 
 I could spend hours reminiscing in the sweet memories of my past life. If it was n't for fucking *Canada. * Of all countries, it had to be one of the nicest countries ever! The irony is unbearable! I never thought I'd bring myself to say it but, I fucking *hate* Canada. For what they've taken away from me, for what they've made me do, *for what I've killed for. * 
 
 Sleep was the only release we got from war, and often it was only for an hour or two, yet, it never felt like a release. So, I let the grip of sleep tighten until I was deep under its gut wrenching spell. And then the dream began. The same one every night, how I got stuck in this absolute *dump* of an OP. 
 
 05/25/2016 
 It was my 21st birthday. I could finally go to the bar with my you, mom said, as she had stopped drinking long ago after the first attack. I was genuinely happy that I could now enjoy a beer with you, as you have been one of the most influential people in my life. You helped make me into the man I am today, and I could n't wait for you to meet me at Tierny's, a local bar that I had eagerly awaited being allowed entry to. I was home for memorial day weekend and as luck had it, it was memorial day on my birthday. What a memory that was left. 
 
 I got there around 9:00 PM, expecting you in about 10 minutes. As you worked in New York City, you always left later than you wer let out to avoid the traffic. God the traffic was unbearable. I had experienced it a few times and it was an absolute hell. I could see why you always stayed to work a few extra hours. That would be me soon, a young man on Wall Street, probably not commuting back to New Jersey but hey, its something. 
 
 The glow of the TV reflected off the mirror behind the bar, there was some special meeting between Canada, Russia, China, and the United States about some Northern Pacific Trade Organization, some copy of NATO, attracting other bar-goers like flies to a light bulb, but I paid no attention to it. I had my eyes glued to the door waiting to have a celebratory beer with you and when you walked in, I was the happiest I had ever been, and probably ever will be. You walked in and I handed you one of the two Beck's I had just ordered. It was our favorite beer. My happiness would n't last long however, as before I even got a second sip in, there was a flash on my television screen. The screen went out, only to come back on seconds later with a horrifying image. The George Washington Bridge was no longer a bridge. Not only that, but there was a seemingly toxic green gas spreading through both sides of the river like wildfire. 
 
 *Fuck. * 
 
 It was a dirty bomb. 
 
 *This ca n't be happening, not today. * 
 
 The US government was subject to an attack 5 years ago from a radical para-military group from Canada called the Wild Moose party. Their last attack ended up with over 2,500 American's dead with the United States gunning for revenge. But Canada persuaded them that they would take care of it and they seemingly did, along with the fact that the United States just did not have the money to wager a third war. But this changed everything. We were going to war and the next day I was on a bus to San Diego to train to be a Navy SEAL. And we never finished our beers. 
 
 We later found out that it was in fact biological warfare, VX gas, or *methylphosphothioate* to be exact. They said it boils the blood at room temperature, causing death in 3 minutes or less. We shared a look, the disbelief visible on our faces. We both knew what was going to happen tomorrow, as the government recently reinstated a unilateral draft in the event of another attack. Your son was going to war, and I knew it too. But I had no choice. 
 
 They told us during BUD/s, or Basic Underwater Demolitions Training, that over 21,000 people ended up dying due to the effects of the dirty bomb. Only days later the entire government of Canada was overthrown by the WM's and we were officially at war, with fucking *Canada. * I was in disbelief, only a couple months ago I was beginning the best chapter in my life, and now I am going through hell week during BUD/s to try and protect the United States. 
 
 There had been speculation as to the motive of the attack. The WM party of Canada was angry at the United States manipulating the world and decided that it could do it better, apparently. Either way, it meant millions of young men and women were going to war, to deal with these *Wild Mooses, * or is it meese? What is the plural of moose anyway? What a stupid name for a political party I thought as I forced myself through the daunting task ahead of me. Almost 48 hours of continuous combat training and tasks followed by 4 hours of sleep and then all over again. 
 
 Eight months later I was on my way to Minnesota, then 2 years later, Alaska, followed by multiple missions off the coast of Maine, and then several years doing HALO missions into the heart of Canada, and now I am in North Dakota guarding a strategic oil field. Fucking North Dakota. It's nothing against these people but fuck its a desolate wasteland. It's so fucking cold, the bullets in my magazines would freeze together from time to time. And it cost me a life. 
 
 I was on patrol with my squad, when they attacked. We could n't see them but we heard the bullets ricocheting around us. We dove for cover and started firing back, but we did n't really know where to shoot. We were like sitting ducks. I tried to fire back but my bullets jammed because they were frozen together. Just my luck, so I scream for my squad leader to give me a new magazine. He yells `` Cover me!'' as he tries to head my way. He half stood and half crouched towards me and then just fell. It happened to quick, I did n't even know what happened. A bullet ricocheted off a rock and went clean through his helmet, in and out, just like that. And just like that, a life gone. 
 
 That's the part that always wakes me up. And I hate it. I found out the next day after my 8th make-shift funeral the real reason we were in this war. The real reason I had both seen death and given it. The real reason I was forced to give up my old life. Why? Turns out there were serious stores of natural gas in the Canadian landscape that eclipsed over into United States territory that several private Chinese and Russian companies were developing, but, the WM party did n't want this Northern Pacific Trade Organization to send all the profits overseas. They saw it as Canada's rightful property and wanted to develop it domestically. 
 
 *Fucking money. * 
 
 That's what I've had best friends killed for? That's what *I* have *killed* for? It could n't be real. All for *fucking money. * 
 
 And so, here I am, sitting in the shittiest OP I have ever been in, fighting a war against Canada, all because of profits. I will finish the job that I have signed up for because, at the end of the day, they attacked us, they took advantage of us, but above all, they took away my *life. * My family, my friends, everything good that I had going for myself, *gone, * in the blink of an eye. The one thing that is inherently mine, they took away from me. 
 
 At 0600 hours my team and I will perform a HALO entry into Quebec and attempt to take out the new ruler of Canada, but in case I do n't make it back, I want you to know my story, what I've gone through, but above all, know this Dad: I will soon have my life back, and I promise you, Dad, I swear on this: we will finish that beer. 
 
 I love you dad. 
 
 Sincerely, 
 
 Your son, 
 
 Jake Greene 
 
 First Lieutenant 
 
 SEAL Team 4 
 
 05/25/2025

title: story-27
text:
The city I have called home for all of my life lies in ruin, the last of the flames eating away what little is left. A stranger's dead body and my college fund in a backpack is on my left and a man in glasses and a beige sweater vest stands on my right. Behind me is my getaway car, my father's girlfriend behind the wheel. I want to blame Narrator for all of this. 
 
 It was only last week when I found out. Narrator had just finished describing the aftermath of my fight with my stepdad when I asked: `` Why do you do that?'' I'm still not all that sure why I asked. Narrator had always been a part of my life. He was the voice of my thoughts. He faithfully recorded what he felt was the most significant part of our ('our' being my family, friends, and anyone I appeared to associate with ) lives without writing down a word, with the accuracy of a historian but the flowery language of a poet. It was n't anything any of us questioned, for Narrator was an integral part of our lives. You do n't question the purpose of air. Perhaps this is why Narrator appeared to be so dumbfounded by my question. `` Why do you ask?'' His mouth was slightly agape in disbelief. 
 `` No reason.'' I shrugged, trying hard to pull my best bored teenager face. 
 
 It probably did n't work. An array of emotions danced across Narrator's face before he sighed and slumped with apparent sorrow. `` Do you really want to know?'' He spoke softly, refusing to look away from his tacky brown cowboy boots. 
 
 `` Sure. Shoot.'' 
 
 Narrator's voice became that of a lecturing college professor... a brokenhearted one really, now that I think about it, but still. `` To understand any of this you must first understand that we are not real.'' 
 
 I stared at him incredulously. 
 
 `` It sounds insane, I know. But it's the truth. We are nothing but book characters. Or well, you all are. I'm the Narrator. Bill's always had something against first person...'' He began to mutter to himself, the very mention of this Bill person drawing him out of his previous sadness. 
 
 I found myself still staring at him, at a complete loss for words. Narrator continued to explain the truth of our world. We existed in an obscure and admittedly awful young adult novel titled D is for Depression. I was the main character, an eighteen year old suffering from severe clinical depression. Narrator was the closest embodiment of the author, William Farrow, that our world had - they even had the same ridiculous sense of fashion. The last thing he told me, the thing that probably stuck with me the most, was that my story was drawing to an end. 
 
 `` We're getting pretty close to the climax. After that we'll hit some sort of resolution and we all.'' He stopped. `` We all... Cease to exist.'' 
 
 I laughed it off at first. However, as the week progressed, I began to notice things. Everyone around me was a bad literary trope. My best friends were sex-obsessed loser virgins. All the parents were either idiots or idyllic cardboard cut-outs. My crush was a textbook manic pixie dream girl. I even saw it in myself: I was someone's bad attempt at their own Holden Caulfield. The events of my life, however small, appeared to be contrived. I felt the penetrating stares of an audience burn into my flesh all hours of the day. By the time Thursday rolled along, I knew that Narrator was right. But I also knew that I did n't want my story to end. I did n't want my world to end. 
 
 I decided to take things into my own hands. Narrator had said that we were coming to the climax. I figured that if I gave the readers the biggest plot twist in the history of plot twists, it would buy us all some time. That's what I told myself as I stocked up on gasoline and matches Friday night, remembering to stop at the bank and collect my entire college fund. That's what I told myself as I raced through the city, sitting in the passenger's seat pointing a gun at the head of my dad's girlfriend, Amber, forcing her to drive me from one building to the next, leaving monstrous flames and billowing ash behind us every time until the entire city was engulfed. 
 
 I tell myself the same thing now as the weight of what I've done threatens to crush me: I bought us some time. 
 
 Narrator clears his throat and sighs sadly. `` I'll wait for you in the car then?.'' I nod. His face is pale yet utterly expressionless. `` Looks like your story is far from over.'' He walks over to the car and slides into the backseat.

title: story-28
text:
I sat on the easternmost bench of Daly Park, as I did every saturday. I like to take a minute out of my week to remember all the things I've done. It's a minute that's stretched into hours because there's so much to remember. I do n't know when he sat down but I noticed a man sitting next to me. 
 `` Fifteen seconds.'' 
 It was an odd thing to say, but he was young and I was old so it was likely some new trend I never bothered to pay attention to. I let it go, deciding not to worry and thought about the time I ran for 15 miles to get a gift for my girlfriend Stacy because I'd forgotten her birthday. I smile about it now, but I remember the panic of running about, trying to be perfect. 
 `` Fifteen seconds.'' the man says again. I turn to look at him now, my memories of the past fading. He's relatively young, maybe about thirty. The lines of his suit are sharp and dark, making his blue eyes and dark hair contrast. He looks like one of those new movie stars, the ones you see on the posters nowadays. 
 `` What are you talking about?'' I ask him. 
 `` I am a trader, of sorts. For fifteen seconds of your time, I can bring you anything. Something close to you that is no longer here. I can do fantastic things and I will make you the happiest man alive, all for fifteen seconds of your time.'' 
 He never looked at me as he talked, his eyes focused on the distant skyline. 
 `` There's only one thing from my past I'd ever want back, son. I do n't think you could ever bring her back to me.'' 
 He turned towards me with a sad smile and said, `` Try me. Hold out your hand.'' 
 I tried to stop my hands from shaking, but my palsy never makes it easy. His grip was firm and smooth and he laid his other hand over our grip, like Father Matthews does when you arrive for mass. 
 `` Now, for the next fifteen seconds, think of the one thing you want more than anything. Something gone from this time and place you'd like to see come to life.'' 
 For a moment, I went blank. It was beyond odd or eccentric, edging into crazy. Twenty years ago, I might have wrenched my hand back from his grasp. Now, I knew he could break my wrist if I so much as tugged wrong, so I relented. 
 I thought of my Delilah and the four years we had together. I thought of the hours I spent searching for her after she disappeared. I remembered the days thinking of how I could have given her one more kiss, or told her I loved her just one last time. I thought of her face and her smile and how she used to dance when she walked from room to room, like the whole world was her stage. 
 `` The contract is sealed.'' 
 When I opened my eyes, the man was gone. I twisted my head around, looking for him despite the pain it caused my bones. I felt my heart stop when I saw a woman laying in the shade. 
 `` It could n't be.'' I thought to myself. But there she was, like she'd stepped straight out of my memories. Delilah, lazing about like we used to do when we were young. My voice caught in my throat when I tried to call out to her. 
 Shaking, I rose to my feet and staggered to her. I knelt next to her, ignoring the cracking in my legs and the pins and needles in my back. 
 `` Delilah.'' I croaked, but she could n't hear me. I called out to her louder this time and she started to stir. I reached out my hand for her, not caring that she would n't recognize this gnarled old face anymore. 
 My hand slipped through her face like smoke. I tried with my other hand but I could n't touch her. 
 I screamed. A small part of me was horrified at the noise, the baying of a wounded animal coming from my body. 
 Slowly, she shifted and I felt a spark of hope. I reached out my hand to touch her face and again, it passed through her. She stood, not seeing me, and brushed off. 
 Delilah walked away from me that day. I stayed there, lost and confused. I knew why Delilah disappeared all those years ago. I robbed myself of a lifetime with her, doomed to wander the earth until I could find someone. Someone who could see me. Someone to share fifteen seconds. 
 It's all I'd need. 
 Fifteen seconds.

title: story-29
text:
Fig leaves - great for covering one's jubblies from The Almighty, bad for protecting one's assets from the howling desert winds of wherever-the-hell-we-were. 
 
 He just turfed us out! Not a cursory'see you around, guys, good luck out there in the perishing wilderness', nothing - just an unceremonious boot up the proverbial into the scorching hot sand outside The Garden. It was quite the change of scenery. I landed face first in the dust; the old ball-and-chain stumbled but stayed upright. We said nothing. What was there to say? We turned around, staring at the greens and the blues and the pinks, a feast of colour that we had rejected, in favour of the waves of brown that stood before us. A giraffe's head was poking over the high trimmed hedges, its dopey wet tongue hanging out of its mouth. 
 
 So we set off. Where else was there to go? 
 
 We walked. We hiked. We strode over dunes and slid down dusty slopes. We shrouded our mouths and covered our eyes when the winds whipped up and sent grains of sand whirling through the air like mosquitoes. We walked across vast plains, saying nothing, making our way towards the mountains in the far distance that swayed blue and yellow in the heat. We stopped rarely and slept badly. We ate small lizards and prehensile rodents, escapees from The Garden that had multiplied outside paradise, and drank from the dew collecting in dry cacti. Above all, we suffered. It was no less than we deserved, I suppose. There was one rule, just the one, and quite a forgiving one at that. Stay away from this tree, and you're golden. We could n't stay away, and for that, we were punished. No less than we deserved. 
 
 We eked out an existence - I would n't call it a life, as such - as we trekked over the plain that stretched unending, hoping that we'd wake up one morning and find ourselves at the foot of the cool grey mountains. They stayed just close enough in our sight that we thought of them as somewhere we could reach, something tangible, rather than what we eventually came to realise them as - too bloody far away. 
 
 One day, we just stopped walking. Not for a break, but quite permanently. Eve was tired of walking, and, to be frank, so was I. We sat in the dirt, our backsides sore and scarred from the unforgiving sands. The fig leaves had long since disintegrated - we had fashioned crude shrouds from the dead droppings of a dried up tree. A snake crawled by in the dust. Its little forked tongue poked out and tasted the air. Its beady eyes looked straight into mine. This was one of the lucky ones that had escaped The Almighty's wrath - its stubby legs wriggled through the sand. 
 
 We were both hungry. We looked at each other. She went for its neck, while I caught its tail. We squeezed the life out of it, and, after rubbing together a pathetic little flame, we ate it.

title: story-30
text:
“ No… this will not do at all. ” Alfred clucked as he started down the stairs in the grand foyer, silently admonishing himself for failing to mop up the large pool of… *was that...? * He had a jolt. He would not soon forget the vivid scent or mercurial texture of blood. His army days may have been far behind, but the memories were as fresh as his morning tea. 
 
 He was strangely calm however, and decided to discover its origin. “ How… peculiar. ” He said, expression unnervingly vacant and dry, discovering that the pool was steadily drip-dropping from the corner of a bookcase on the second level. 
 
 *No matter, * he thought to himself. Alfred had a very particular system, and what good would mopping up the pool of blood do if, after all, the origin wasn ’ t dealt with? He marched back up the stairs, relying on the rails to steady himself up. Every year they grew steeper. He had a sudden flash of darkest Kevlar, of roaring engines, of bats. 
 
 His sunken, wrinkly skin grew in pallor as he examined the bookcase. The flashes continued… a cowl and cape, a bright yellow belt…*Thank god Bruce is off on one of his many excursions.. oh the life of a playboy. It would break his heart to see me a blithering old man... * Odd. This entire section of bookshelves was dedicated to the antiquities, a copy of Tom Sawyer did not belong. 
 
 He pulled the book loose only to have the entire shelf shudder and then smoothly lift up. Alfred was strangely calm, as though he had seen this play out thousands of times before, before he suddenly stepped back in shock. 
 
 “ Good Heavens! ” he cried, his face pained and broken, his chest tightening. “ No… oh no! ” he knelt there, next to the body of his master, his son, his mentee and best friend. Bruce was laid out sideways, his face a mixture of shock and pain, eyes glassy and still. In his back, just under his rib cage and directly into his heart was a fire poker. A firm, accurate thrust. 
 
 Alfred had no idea how long he knelt there, cradling the man ’ s heavy head in his lap, tears falling freely into the unblinking eyes before trailing down the dead man ’ s jaw. It was though they were both mourning this tragedy. 
 
 But Alfred had dealt with loss before. And soon the flashes of images came back clearer, stronger. A man in a suit, strong, able. More than a man…a legend. 
 
 “ Bruce.. I ’ m so sorry. Those who did this will pay. My enemies must have discovered my identity.. must have done this to hurt me.. Mark my words. They WILL pay! ” 
 
 It all came back. Bruce was damaged, broken, and after his parents died he descended into a life of hedonism and playboy luxury. He would go on trips for weeks, or even months at a time. Alfred had a lot of free time, and he had never let go of the pain he felt at losing The Waynes, and he applied his military knowledge and experience to making a difference… leaving the emotionally damaged Bruce none the wiser. 
 
 He slowly walked down the dark stairs into the Batcave. His knees were worn and every step hurt, but he hadn ’ t felt this much purpose, this much determination in what felt like years. He was truly 20 years younger in that moment, and all he could think about was vengeance.
