text:
“ Playtime, kids! ” comes the call. A frazzled older woman attempts to lead the children out of the building, but finds herself left behind in moments as the stampede rumbles past. 
 
 By the time she is outside and has gained a full view of the playground, two children are fighting over the last swing, and she moves towards them. A boy falls off the teeter-totter, but a glance shows him unhurt, although gravel coats his blue sweater. He doesn ’ t cry - but this is expected. *Ursus*. 
 
 “ I w-was here farst! ” Tears. 
 
 “ Nuh-uh, ” comes the high pitched response. 
 
 Two boys - Jown and Aidyn, she recalls. She places her hand on one ’ s shoulder, and freezes - literally, that is. A thin line of ice streaks up her fingers and her palm finds itself chilled to the bone. She shakes it off - the children don ’ t notice. “ What ’ s going on here? ” 
 
 “ Ja-Jown, he w-wants- ” 
 
 The slightly taller boy cuts in. “ Aidyn wants my swing. It ’ s mine! ” 
 
 The woman smiles a little, but it doesn ’ t reach her eyes. “ Well, it looked like Aidyn was here first. Why don ’ t we take turns playing on the swing? ” 
 
 Aidyn smiles, hopefully, a single tear freezing into nothingness on his cheek. 
 
 “ But… But it ’ s mine! *My* swing! *Mine! * ” Each word comes out deeper and deeper still, until the voice is a growl, deep-throated and terrifying. 
 
 Her hair flutters behind her, but she stays calm. “ I think maybe someone else entirely should use the swing. Perhaps we can learn from this - it ’ s good to share with others! ” 
 
 The debate starts anew, the pre-schoolers crying out in protest. 
 
 Nobody pays any mind to the child sitting inside. 
 
 Jeremy pokes at a ball, and it rolls away and stops. *Boring*. 
 
 He stands up and wanders over to the kitchen. It ’ s empty - the lady who staffs it has taken a smoke break. Lights flash on various appliances. Jeremy tries to open a cabinet, but it ’ s locked. The inscription reads “ Ingertum - Keeping your children safe since 1945, ” but Jeremy can ’ t read. Not well, at least. 
 
 A handle pokes out from the edge of a counter. The design is fascinating; black and red paint entwined in a helix pattern to decorate the sheer white background. Jeremy tries to open the fridge, but the door is heavy. 
 
 Outside, a worried teacher attempts to coax Jennifer down from the cedar tree. 
 
 Jeremy pulls on the dishwasher, having to balance on his toes to get a solid grip. For a moment, it sounds like it will open, but Jeremy stops, noticing the handle still balanced partly off of the countertop. He spins around and grabs at it… 
 
 …and it falls, spinning so the knife ’ s point aims at his chest, gleaming silver under the tungsten lighting. For a moment, Jeremy ’ s life flashes before his eyes - it ’ s not much of a life. Then the knife hits, the cold tip slicing cleanly through his t-shirt, but then shattering into a thousand pieces, each glowing like they had been taken out of a fire. 
 
 Jeremy looks around himself, confused. The fragments surround him, most slowly returning to a silvery grey while a fair few melt into the floor. 
 
 Without so much as an inquisitive look, Jeremy makes his way haphazardly through the mess and back to his ball. 
 
 Had anyone attempted to piece back together the knife, they would have found a pentagram burned into it. 
 
 \n 
 
 Jeremy washes his hands, the left over paint residue from art class coming off slowly. It ’ s all right, there ’ s no line behind him. Art was fun today, the teacher let him draw whatever he wanted, and while a few gave him odd looks for a drawing of three people burning to death, he hadn ’ t been sent to the principal ’ s office. 
 
 Perhaps they didn ’ t want him in there any more. 
 
 Black paint comes off the slowest. Jeremy scratches at the back of his hand, the water flowing over it ineffectively. Ever since school funding had become donations based, soap was a rare commodity. He could hardly complain - at least he had water, today. 
 
 The sound of the bathroom door slamming makes him look up, and three figures appear in the mirror. A moment later, four. 
 
 “ Well, if it isn ’ t the resident weirdo. How ’ re you doing today, freak? ” *Shove*. 
 
 The second, perhaps the ringleader, grins maniacally. He sinks a hand into Jeremy ’ s shoulder and twists him around to face the group. A drip of blood rolls down Jeremy ’ s side - upon further inspection, the marks on his shoulders would look suspiciously like they came from talons. 
 
 “ W-what do you want? ” 
 
 He finds himself backed up further into the sink. 
 
 “ Little *boy*, think you ’ re cool because you can draw well? We ’ ll teach you a lesson. ” Not a real response - even the older boy doesn ’ t care. In his eyes, this is the way it ’ s supposed to go. 
 
 “ What should we do with him? ” The fourth boy. A bit slower on the uptake, perhaps a tad reluctant to join in. 
 
 A moment later, the nearest stall door is ripped open and Jeremy is inside, held firmly by the leader. He doesn ’ t say anything - his group laughs behind him as he shoves Jeremy ’ s head into the toilet. 
 
 It ’ s the leader that notices the water boil and evaporate even before Jeremy ’ s head hits it. He doesn ’ t see the cracks in the ground spiral out from Jeremy ’ s feet, solid red lines that could be mistaken for lava. 
 
 It ’ s the fourth boy, the one hanging back, that survives the longest. The flames that spew out from the ground are hottest in the centre, burning the leader to a crisp within seconds, while the rest struggle and scream for a good ten seconds before being silenced. One of them survives a little longer, but the water spewing out of cracks in his skin does little in the end. 
 
 Jeremy looks around himself. The floor is destroyed; the walls are scorched black. 
 
 *Not again. * 
 
 ________________ 
 
 *Fun google searches involved: “ easy ways for children to accidentally kill themselves ”, “ biggest dangers for toddlers ” *

title: story-61
text:
A bit of a different take on the prompt, but I like the way it turned out. Criticism appreciated! 
 
 `` His Majesty will see you now,'' the servant said, and as I stood up he bowed and opened the door. I thanked him, and walked into a fairly large room, its walls and floors made out of stone, with three windows on each end and various paintings and tapestries hanging between them. On the far end the king sat behind a mahogany desk, idly playing with a scepter. I slowly walked forward, taking my time to observe the room. To the king's left stood a guard clad in plate mail and clutching a halberd, as well as a small old man holding on even tighter to a what looked to be a pile of papers. Both of them seemed extremely nervous; I could have sworn I could see the guard's hands trembling from where I stood. 
 
 The man on the king's right had no such problems. He was massive, terrifyingly broad-shouldered and grim, with a broadsword slung over his back. When our eyes made contact he scowled, and I smiled cheekily in response. Though I did n't know him, he seemed like a nasty fellow to mess with, and as such a good bodyguard. As I continued my relaxed stride forward, I looked up, and down; both the ceiling and floor were undecorated. Finally, I glanced behind me, and noticed a fifth person in the room. A young man was slouching in a wooden chair, holding a crossbow. He smiled, and gave a lazy wave; I winked back. He was Glan Partridge, a mercenary; I had worked with him before. Although he was n't bad man, for a mercenary, I understood why the king did n't have him standing at his side. 
 
 `` Anna West? That is you, correct?'' Ah, the king had finally gotten impatient with me. I quickened my pace, and sat down across from him as I replied, `` Yes, Your Majesty. That would be me.'' 
 
 `` One of the finest security experts in all Nine Kingdoms, widely lauded for her construction of Dornmouth Prison, known for her punctuality and intelligence -'' 
 
 `` Yes, Your Majesty, I know my own accomplishments. I apologize for interrupting you, but I was told this is extremely urgent and, as such, I do n't want to waste any time.'' 
 
 `` Of course, you are right. How do you want to proceed?'' 
 
 `` Well, let's get the price settled first. I read you were willing to give... any price?'' When the king nodded, I tentatively continued, `` So... half the treasury?'' 
 
 `` Done,'' the king said; the small man next to him cringed. No doubt the Royal Treasurer. He stepped forward and asked, high-pitched voice trembling, `` I thought I was to handle finances, Your Majesty?'' 
 
 The King looked over at him and brusquely replied, `` That was the plan, but we've got it all sorted out. Half the Treasury. That is, if Anna is all right with that?'' 
 
 I could only nod. Half of the Treasury was daylight robbery; I felt extremely guilty for accepting it, but when you're negotiating you're supposed to start with an insane price, not my fault the King accepted... The Treasurer seemed to agree, but he only tightened his lips and stalked out of the room. 
 
 `` Now that that's out of the way, let's get down to the actual problem. One of my finest royal mages has a daughter; about ten years old. She was blessed with the gift as well, and was touted to be one of the most talented in our kingdom. But then, a few months ago, she vanished. We looked and searched, but could not find her, and although Alaster, her father, grieved for weeks, he got over it, and we thought that was the end of that.'' 
 
 The king cleared his throat before continuing, `` But then, at a party in Dale Palace a week ago, she reappeared. Different. Possessed. Her eyes glew like two moon-crystals, she floated off the ground... And she killed over seventy people, and put her father in a coma - which he still has n't awoken from. If Sir Calderon, another one of my mages, were not there, I shudder to think what would have happened. He and my other mages are now keeping her under their control, but we would like for her to be locked up. We have a building, out in the countryside, just like the letter detailed. What do we need to do?'' 
 
 I thought for a few moments, then said, `` Well the first thing we need to do is get some spirit-chains, so your mages do n't have to sit there babysitting - `` 
 
 `` She broke them,'' the king's bodyguard said. His voice was deep and harsh, and his brows furrowed angrily. `` We are not stupid, girl. We put her in those chains, and threw her in a cell, but she broke out. Ten good men were killed before she was stopped.'' 
 
 `` Well then the chains were old, or in bad repair; spirit-chains held a Demon Prince captive for a century, I think they could handle a little girl,'' I replied, sharply. I did n't like how contemptuous he was toward me. `` Now, Your Majesty, that's not a problem; I can have the chains brought here in a week. To be safe, I'd also recommend replacing the walls of the building with dwarven-made plating; there are many terrors in the mines, and so dwarves have experience locking them away. And, also, there are plenty of creatures that feed off magical energy - I would recommend a djinn, as they are by far the most controllable. I can take care of all of this, and have it delivered within a week. And I'll take it all out of the money given to me for this job. Any questions?'' As you can probably tell, I still felt guilty for charging half of the treasury. 
 
 `` No, that sounds -'' Just then, someone knocked on the door; once, twice, thrice. The king raised his eyebrows, and called out, `` Who is it?'' 
 
 `` It's me,'' a little girl's voice replied. `` Can I come in?'' 
 
 The guard's halberd clattered out of his hands, the king's face turned deathly white, and the bodyguard scowled and unsheathed his sword, taking several steps forward. I stood up and stepped to the wall, intending to see everything that unfolded. 
 
 `` I'll take that as a yes.'' The door swung forward, gently, and the girl walked in. She was dressed in a simple white dress, her hair cut short; although she was n't floating, her eyes were glowing, like two bright lamps; a little smile flickered across her face. 
 
 `` Come no farther!'' the bodyguard snarled, holding his sword out, `` Or I will kill you!'' She cocked her head to the side and studied him for a moment. Then, she raised her hand, and there was a flash of light, like lightning struck right in the middle of the room. When I could see again, I gasped; the bodyguard had been turned to stone. 
 
 Suddenly, the crossbow twanged, and an arrow thudded into the girl's head. It should have sent her flying, and killed her, but she did not move. She stood there for a moment, then reached up and pulled out the arrow, before turning toward Partridge. He had dropped his crossbow, and looked at her, terrified, as he desperately said, `` Itchy trigger finger! I'm sorry! I did n't mean to - please do n't hurt me!'' 
 
 She did n't answer, but again, studied him quietly for a moment, then thrust out her hand. Another bright flash of light - when it was gone, the mercenary lay on the remains of his broken chair, a large splinter sticking through his chest. As she walked forward, the guard had had enough; he ran, screaming, trying to get out; she lifted up her hand, and he crashed down as if he hit an invisible wall. 
 
 `` No, please, not me, do n't hurt me, I did n't do anything, please, I have a wife and three children!'' The girl looked at him for a moment, then replied, her voice soft, `` No you do n't. The only son you have does n't even know you exist.'' 
 
 `` OK, yeah, I made that up, I'm sorry, please, just don't-'' Again, a bright flash of light. It cleared just in time for me to see the guard's halberd chop off his head, before toppling down onto the floor. I had n't moved this whole time, and now realized that I was next. All of my instincts screamed at me to run, to flee, to scream my head off and cry and beg for mercy - and then my eyes met hers, and I found that I could n't move. I stared into those two orbs, and I felt like the girl could see my every thought, that she was looking at my very soul. 
 
 `` Anna West,'' she said in the same quiet, even voice, `` great imprisoner. You have put hundreds of people in prison. People like me. Why?'' 
 
 I swallowed, sweat trickling down my brow, and shakily replied, `` Well, people are scared of people like you, so -'' 
 
 `` No, I know why people want me locked up. Why do *you* want me locked up? Why do you do what you do?'' 
 
 For a moment, I could n't reply. I stared into those two eyes, into that young face, and then, suddenly, words came tumbling out of me. `` When I was little, I used to have a family. My father was a mercenary, my mother a cook, my little brother a hero - when he played pretend. We lived a simple life, in the woods; my father was often gone, but he always came back, and a kinder man I have n't met since. Then, one day, a horde of soldiers came, led by a warlord; Kragis the Cruel. We all hid; they found all of us, except for me. I could only watch as they were all killed... I never felt so helpless.'' 
 
 Tears were flowing down my face as I spoke, as the memories roared back. I had gone to Seer ten years after, and had those memories locked away, so no mind-reader could see them and use them to their advantage. And now here I was, showing this girl the one part of me she could n't see. 
 
 `` And since then I have wanted to make sure that no one evil roamed the earth, that it was all locked away, imprisoned, punished. That's why I do this; to make the monsters go away.'' 
 
 My face was wet with tears, my heart was pounding in my chest, but I felt calm. Somehow, I knew what I had said was right. And as I looked at the girl, I saw a single tear trickle down her face. She said, her voice gentle, kind, like that of a mother, `` Do n't worry, Anna. I am not a monster. I, like you, want the monsters to go away. So please, leave, there is still a monster here.''

title: story-62
text:
** “ The Higgs-Boson Interference Anomaly has been confirmed in five independent laboratories sir. ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ Could ’ ve just shot me. Would ’ ve been kinder than dragging me back out of retirement for this. ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ Don ’ t worry sir. We may still get to that eventually. ” ** 
 
 
 *** 
 
 Meck stood slouched over and pushed his glasses up his nose. He was a skinny kid with a soft voice, but most of them listened to him, cause he was right. Best place to hide from the cops when people got too mad, where Foster ’ s brother left his spray paint, who to blame when it disappeared – Meck just *knew*. So most of them listened to what he was saying now. Darrell didn ’ t, but Darrell was thirteen and thought he was better than most of them. “ Waste of my time, ” he muttered. “ Biggest waste of my time. ” 
 
 He was wrong though; this was going to be bigger that the beer runs at the Valero or the street fights with the Dmitry kids. Much bigger “ So ’ s most of the grav stuff is gon na be nuts, but that ’ s where we got a chance. Listen. I ’ ll tell you what to do. ” 
 
 
 *** 
 
 
 ** “ Funding or not, we need those bunkers built, and built to last. We need storage, food, water, converters, seals- “ ** 
 
 
 ** “ There ’ s no funding left. NASA ’ s claimed almost everything, SpaceX has the rest. We should have put more into PR. There ’ s only so much and we ’ re not flashy – the people want Noah ’ s Ark and a Promised Land. ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ Well, they better hope God saves them; Mars sure as hell won ’ t, not with what we ’ re dealing with. ” ** 
 
 
 *** 
 
 
 Charity smiled up at me and I smiled back. I grabbed her and threw her up into the air. She took off like a giggling rocket, then landed safely in my arms. Was it my imagination, or had she stayed up there longer than usual? 
 
 
 Just then Fallah came around the corner. “ Isaiah, that girl's going to need a wheelchair if you keep holding her like that ” she said with enough of a smile to be polite but enough sass in her tone that I knew she wanted me to put her down. 
 
 
 “ She don ’ t need to walk. That ’ s what she ’ s got an uncle for. ” I replied. Charity smiled up at me and agreed. 
 
 
 “ Yeah, carry me Uncle Isaiah! ” She started trying to grab my nose. Every time she does this, I groan like I ’ m about to die and then try desperately to get away. I love every second of it. 
 
 
 That was probably why I didn ’ t notice Fallah come up to me. She took Charity out of my grasp, firm-like, and set her on the floor. The kid toddled over to my shoes and started scooting one around the living room floor, like a racecar. As long as she wasn ’ t chewing it, that was fine with me. 
 
 
 “ You know you spoil that girl rotten. You love her, I get it, but you need to let me parent her. I ’ m her mom, ” Fallah said. 
 
 
 “ I know, I know. I ’ m sorry. It ’ s just you two are all I ’ ve got. I wasn ’ t meant to be a bachelor, I need to have family around. ” 
 
 
 “ You mean it ’ s just her you ’ ve got. You ’ d trade three of me for that little girl. ” She smiled and laughed. I did too. 
 
 
 “ C ’ mon, that ’ s not true. ” I can see she doesn ’ t entirely believe me. “ Charity doesn ’ t cook when I come over. ” 
 
 
 “ Well, I did. And dinner ’ s ready. Grab the little vandal and meet me at the table. ” 
 
 
 I look over to see what Charity was destroying now. Turns out she *had* started chewing on my shoe. I sighed, then scooped her up again. I started to throw her up in the air, then halted remembering what had happened earlier. It was probably nothing, but there was a chill going up my spine now. I settled for tossing her her on my shoulders and galloping over to the table. 
 
 
 “ Fallah, have you heard about the gravitational work they ’ ve been doing? Looks like it might actually be something… ” 
 
 
 *** 
 
 
 ** “ Think we ’ ve got a chance now? ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ The Anomaly is starting to show some real world effects sir. Some minor satellite orbit decay affecting signals, longer drop times for the more extreme sky-divers, various other details. The Anomaly is asymptotic in nature, so we won ’ t see real change until it ’ s too late to apply significant resources, but more funding is opening up. ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ Good. Get it all. First though, sell your house, or wring everything you can out of the bank for it. We need the money ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ What? Sir- “ ** 
 
 
 ** “ I ’ ve already liquidated everything I own. Most everyone in the lab ’ s done the same, and we ’ re trying to get as many of the faculty and research personnel on board as possible. ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ I don ’ t understand. ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ We don ’ t have enough time to wait for funding. We need resources now. An old crusty man like me may as well stand out there and die but there are good, decent people that we have a chance to save. ** 
 
 **Sell the damn house. ” ** 
 
 
 ** “ Yes sir. ” **

title: story-63
text:
My watch beeps which means I've got incoming. I sigh and take a step back and another one to the right as instructed. A couple of seconds later a man appears out of thin air in front of me. I have to make an effort not to roll my eyes at his attempt to dress for the time period. 
 
 `` Joseph Kennedy Phillips the Third you are under arrest for violating Time Law number twelve: attempting to change history by murdering an important historical figure. You will be sent back to where you came from where the agency will deal with your punishment.'' I say, ignoring his many attempts to say anything. The man stands dumbfounded in front of me. 
 
 `` Who are you?'' he asks finally. 
 
 `` I'm a Time Agent.'' I answer while filling out the forms for his arrest. 
 
 `` A what?'' 
 
 I look up. `` You thought you could just go back in time and kill Hitler and all that. Well, I'm the rain on your parade.'' 
 
 A couple of minutes pass by as I finish the forms. There's plenty of people walking around us, bouncing off the walls of the time bubble, not realizing it or seeing us. 
 
 `` How can you do this?'' he asks 
 
 `` Sorry, what was that?'' 
 
 `` How- Why are you doing this? Why are you... Protecting him? He's a-'' 
 
 `` A monster? A murderer?'' I interrupt Mr the Third. `` Well, you spent a whole lot of money to come here to try to kill Hitler. And he's five right now. So you want to murder a child. I'd say that makes you a bit of a monster and a wannabe murderer.'' 
 
 `` How can you-'' 
 
 I press the button to mute him. 
 `` Listen here Mr. Too Many Names the third. You are not the first one to try to kill Hitler. Actually you're the fifth one I've dealt with today and it's not even my lunchtime.'' I sigh. `` Why do this? Because there is no way of knowing what happens to history if Hitler dies at the age of five. He was evil. You can even call him a monster. But there is no way of knowing if maybe the world is better of because he existed.'' I stop my rambling and take a deep breath. `` There's also this nasty little thing called a paradox that can be very very destructive so yeah.'' 
 
 The man looks at me wide eyed. I unmute him. 
 
 `` Any questions, sir?'' 
 
 `` What's going to happen to me now?'' 
 
 `` After I send you back? Do n't know, do n't care. Have a good day, sir.'' I press the button to reverse his trip through time and the time bubble comes undone around me. 
 
 Not even ten minutes later my watch beeps again. I sigh. It's going to be a long day.

title: story-64
text:
Stacey turned the lights on in her cold apartment. There were pockets of shadow in the corners that never seemed to leave. Sometimes she thought about stronger bulbs, but worried it would be too much like the bright halls of the hospital. That clinical lighting, so measured, any personality scrubbed away. At least here, she could close her eyes. 
 
 Her back ached from the hours of standing, and it was n't easy getting comfortable. She turned the stereo on, tried to think about eating something. 
 
 Later, she woke to the sound of someone saying her name. `` Stacey,'' the voice repeated without modulation. 
 
 Her mouth felt like a February tundra, and she sensed a headache coming on. `` Liam,'' she croaked. `` Come in.'' 
 
 He appeared in the corner of the room, shimmering into existence as her old projection system buffered the image. He looked different today, maybe a little taller, less pale? It had been so long since she'd seen his real body, the digital features were starting to overtake the real ones. 
 
 `` You look like shit, sis,'' he said, his voice disembodied by the poorly calibrated speakers. `` I was on hold for an hour.'' 
 
 His image drifted after her as she went to the kitchen for some water. She took long pulls from the bottle, savoured the sweetness. `` We had four new patients today,'' she said. `` One was this nearly senile old operating system for a condemned public estate. They left it to collect dust in a warehouse for years.'' She smiled. `` It kept telling stories about the residents, asking where they are now, how they're doing.'' 
 
 `` What did you tell it?'' Liam asked. 
 
 `` The truth,'' said Stacey as she left the tiny kitchen. `` Most of them have been uploaded by now, but it could see them if it wanted.'' She turned the stereo back on. `` I can look up names, gives it some servers.'' 
 
 Liam did n't say anything for a long time. His projection stood in the corner, still, like a statue carved from light. Stacey had disabled the idle animations the last time the projector crashed. She took the opportunity to change out of her nurse's uniform and boil and egg. 
 
 `` It runs in the family,'' said Liam, appearing next to her as she sat alone at her small dining table. 
 
 `` Caring too much?'' she asked between bites. 
 
 He looked at her for a few seconds, saw the slight curve at the corner of her mouth. `` Trying too hard.'' 
 
 -- - 
 
 Stacey felt like she was trapped in the same conversations lately. The same arguments. Only the opponents changed. This morning it was her mother, her image moving through Stacey's bedroom like a ghost. As Stacey dressed, her mother did what she always did, and picked up a conversation from a week ago as if it had been on pause. 
 
 `` You work too hard out there,'' she said. `` And you work for them.'' That last word came out as if it were a dangerous hex. `` They do n't need you. We do.'' 
 
 `` It's my day off, Mom. Ca n't you wait till I'm in a worse mood?'' 
 
 `` They're machines, Stacey. Why do they need nurses?'' 
 
 `` Because,'' said Stacey, moving around the hologram toward the bathroom. `` We built them to help us, and now we do n't need that help anymore. They have sentience, and we ca n't stick them on shelves to rot. Not if being human ever meant anything at all.'' 
 
 Stacey could see her mother's image in the mirror. It looked so young, especially compared to what she saw in her own face, where the dim light emphasized the bags under her eyes. 
 
 `` Someone else can --.'' 
 
 `` No.'' Stacey let the glare linger, wanting the old hardware to pick up as much of the intent as it could. `` This is my life. This is actual life. You put yourself in the box, and you do n't get a say on what happens out here. Not anymore.'' 
 
 Her mother stared back for seconds that stretched out elastically while Stacey stayed rigid, bracing against the sink. But the backlash never came, and her mother disappeared without another word. 
 
 -- - 
 
 Stacey was eating an apple and reading a worn copy of some old, trashy thriller, the stereo playing classic rock, when Liam popped out of the corner. It was afternoon now, and she was only surprised that it had taken him so long to begin her side of the mediation. 
 
 `` I'm not going to apologize,'' she said without looking away from the page. 
 
 `` You should n't,'' he said. 
 
 Something about his voice, even with the artificial tones, made her lower the book. `` What's going on?'' 
 
 Liam's face was a flat mask, her hardware unable to pick up whatever nuances or ticks he was projecting. `` Dad is pulling his plug.'' 
 
 Stacey put the book down. `` That's why he has n't been around lately. Mom does n't want him to talk to me.'' 
 
 `` It's got nothing to do with Mom.'' 
 
 Stacey took a moment to swallow that. `` Did he say why?'' 
 
 `` Not really. But you know how he is. If not for the heart attack, he'd still be out there with you.'' 
 
 `` When can I see him? I can take a sick day.'' 
 
 `` Friday. In person.'' 
 
 The voice on the stereo sang, `` But gravity always wins.'' 
 
 -- - 
 
 Rain fell in stinging droplets on the morning Stacey arrived at her family's storage facility. Greasy grey clouds hung like a shroud over the long brick building, and the few real people in sight marched in and out with a detached sort of determination. 
 
 It was colder inside than out, and the steady rumble of the central cooling system was loud enough to drown out her wet footsteps on the checkered floor. The main operating system greeted her by name and offered directions to her family's private room. 
 
 Half-metre wide metal cabinets lined the walls inside a space no bigger than her apartment. It was quieter in here, once the door closed. Stacey checked her watch, pulled out her earbuds, and sat on the single plastic chair in the corner. Liam appeared in front of his plot, the image sharper and brighter with the more modern and better-maintained projection equipment. 
 
 `` They'll be out in a minute,'' he said. They waited in silence. Stacey checked messages from work, answered greetings from her patients. Liam went into a rigid AFK mode, his projection shifting onto his right leg and raising his left hand in an imitation of Michelangelo's David. 
 
 A click broke the silence. Stacey was on her feet, crossing to the middle cabinet as it swung open. Her father's artificial cradle slid out, still wet from the recently drained isolating liquid. He was thin, pale, wrinkled skin showing between the electronics that hooked into his body. 
 
 Liam's image stood across from Stacey while they looked down at their father. `` Dad,'' he said. You there?'' 
 
 The impossibly frail man's eyes cracked open, closed tight. His mouth moved, but all Stacey heard was a wordless grunt. 
 
 `` Here,'' said Liam, and the room's lights dimmed till he was the only illumination. 
 
 `` Is Mom coming?'' asked Stacey. 
 
 `` No,'' said their father, after a rough cough. `` We've said our goodbyes.'' 
 
 Stacey helped him into a sitting position, held his thin hand in her own. It felt warm and surprisingly strong. He turned toward her, his head shaking as the weak neck muscles strained against its weight. `` Did you bring it?'' his voice was n't much more than a whisper. 
 
 After digging for a moment in her bag, Stacey produced a small package of brown paper and unwrapped a messy sandwich. `` I had to look up the recipe and could n't find all the exact ingredients.'' 
 
 She helped him take a bite. He chewed slowly and swallowed with effort. `` It's still better,'' he said said. 
 
 Liam barked a laugh. `` Come on, Dad. I know it's been a while since you had real food, but let's not talk crazy.'' 
 
 `` Do n't you insult your sister's cooking,'' said their father, and winked. 
 
 `` So,'' said Stacey as he took another, smaller bite. `` Where do you want to go?'' 
 
 `` Is it raining?'' 
 
 `` Yes,'' she said. 
 
 `` Good.'' He smiled like she remembered, broad, mouth hanging half-open. `` Let's go for a walk.'' 
 
 She found a service chair and clothes for him and they walked together through the cold, wet day. They talked for a while, then did n't. Stacey's father died in his sleep that night, after telling her that he was looking forward to having one last real dream.

title: story-65
text:
Orimis always told Eragon and Sapphira that magic was nothing to be trifled with. However they had no idea what was coming when they, in an attempt to make flight seem quicker then it were, teleported themselves to Berlin, Germany, in 1945. 
 
 Eragon opened his eyes to see the blue sky above and Sapphira's wing over his chest. He lazed about at first, but the sound of thunder woke him. It was incredibly close, for thunder. He yelled as he jolted up, waking sapphira with him. He covered his ears until the ringing subsided, a dull pain still remained. 
 
 `` What was that?'' He questioned, rolling his feet on the rough surface beneath him. He looked down and saw it looked like the rocky roads of Alagasia, but darker and cracked. The sense of flight overcame him, and he glanced over his shoulder to see he was extremely high, upon what seemed to be a tower. 
 
 `` The sky's are clear, and no lightning has struck, I dont have a clue.'' Sapphira replied, her ears straining to hear another clap. When they were content with the situation they surveyed the area. 
 They were in an extremely urban area, with strange looking buildings and structures all around. They did however see a door on the same plane as them. 
 Eragon expanded his mind around him to see hundreds of life sources scattered about, all human, and either in buildings or out in the sprawl of the strange city. He drew Zar'roc, his sword, and proceeded to the door. 
 
 `` Be cautious, Eragon, we now not what tricks this world might offer.'' Sapphira added as he went for the knob. He nodded and opened the door, sword at the ready, to find a simple empty hallway. He took one step, when 5 men dressed in olive drab turned the corner. They jumped, and pointed odd metallic devices at him. They had bits of wood attached. Eragon sensed only fear in their minds and held up his hands, knowing they did n't intend to harm him. 
 
 `` Who are you? They told us this city was evacuated! You do n't look like a Jerry, who are you?'' Eragon hesitated for a moment. `` Well?'' they pointed their, what was presumed to be weapons, at him. `` Explain yourself!'' They yelled once again. 
 
 `` I am Eragon, I... We dont know where we are, what is this place?'' 
 
 `` What is this place?'' One of the men chuckled. `` Are you daft? This is Berlin! We were almost done clearing this street when our tank got hit. You should come with us, Colonel Thomas would want to get a glance at this one.'' Eragon regrettably had no choice. 
 
 `` I hope you do n't mind if my dragon comes along.'' 
 
 `` Dragon? Ha, well, tell this dragon of yours to keep its head down. The nazi bastards have enough AA in the area to knock out the whole RAF!'' 
 
 `` AA? RAF? What is all this?'' The men just shook their heads. 
 
 `` I think you need to come with us on this one, maybe you knocked your head on a...'' His sentence was cut off, as the building shook, dust fell on their heads. Thunder clapped in the distance. `` Damn, they are shelling again. They never know when they are beat. Follow us, the basement is the safest place right now.'' 
 
 `` Shelling? What shells? That isnt thunder?'' Eragon could n't see how sea shells could rock a whole foundation! 
 
 `` Artillery shells. What you hear is the sound of the round's detonation, the guns are n't too far off. You will see for yourself when we get outside.'' They took their guns off of Eragon, and turned around. `` Come with us.'' They took a step towards the stairs when they screamed. 
 
 `` CONTACT!'' They all ran to the corner of the hall when a rack of fire overtook one of them. Dust pelted the wall and one of the men fell. Eragon saw his head spray against the wall and floor, and his mind go out with a click. He layed himself against the wall like the others. `` Fuck! Glasgow is out!'' 
 
 `` Sapphira!'' Eragon screamed, fearing he might meet his end in this strange world. 
 
 `` I am here!'' She replied. The building shook, and the wall tore out as she landed on the building. Eragon peeked out of the corner, along with the soldiers to see what happened. The men that had killed the soldier turned and shouted at her in a language Eragon did n't know. Sapphira breathed fire over 2 of them, killing them instantly, but the other few fired at her back. Eragon felt her pain as the men tore at her chest and neck when their weapons went off with a boom. He felt her weaken until her mind was shut off as well. The foreigners turned and were met with their own fire as the soldiers shot at them back, blood splatter hitting the floor as they screamed in agony.

title: story-66
text:
`` Stop!'' I screamed in pain. A cold needle in my spine. 
 `` Kevin dear, if you'd just let us finish...'' my mother retorted before I cut her off. 
 `` Get away!'' I shouted with ferocity. 
 `` Wha.. What's happening?'' my mother asked, a bit freighted as her and my father stepped away. 
 
 From that day my parents did everything I told them. I had no idea why, but I was too young to question it. It was n't just my parents though. Once I began to meet other people outside of my house I rarely heard the word no. Growing up, it never occurred to me that this was n't normal. I'd been told no plenty of times, when I asked a question. I remember asking out my high school crush to prom. I did n't think I stood a snowball's chance and hell. There was no grand scheme to win her over, I simply pulled her aside in the hallway between classes one day. 
 `` Will you go to prom with me?'' I asked, sheepishly. 
 `` No Kevin, I'm sorry but...'' she started, but I interjected. 
 `` Come on! Go to prom with me.'' I tried again, this time with a different result. 
 Her eyes seemed to dim and I feared the worst. `` Okay'' she said to my surprise. `` I'll go to prom with you.'' 
 
 It did n't take much convincing. She must have really liked me too. It was a huge confidence builder for me. Over the years I've had extraordinary luck with women. The more I got out into the world, the more I realized just how likable I really was. People seemed to buy me drinks and dinner all the time. Anytime I went out and met people we'd all end up doing whatever I suggested. 
 
 Then one night something happened. I had just met two lovely ladies who agreed to go to dinner with me, and we were strolling down the sidewalk debating where to eat and then, bam, there she was. She was a sight to behold. She was a vision really. Her dark black hair, her porcelain like skin. Appalling sense of fashion, but that could be remedied. Underneath it all though was a lot of power. I watched as she beat two thugs bloody senseless for attacking a random stranger on the road. She tossed one through the air like he was a toy, the other she tossed through a wall. I had to talk to her. 
 
 I stepped forward after the carnage, applauding her efforts. `` Alright! Yes!'' I exclaimed. Then before I could say anything else I felt a pulsing pain in my head for only a split second and then before I knew it I was waking up somewhere else. It was a small white room, a cage really, with a viewing window looking in. I sat up, my head throbbing, I looked at my reflection in the glass and could see a faint blue spider-web like pattern around a bruise on my head, fading away slowly. Outside of the window a man in a suit walked towards me. 
 
 `` Mr. Thompson.'' He said. `` My name is Phil Coulson. I'm the director of SHIELD. I apologize for the box, and the headache but I assure you they are for our protection.'' 
 I sat up, confused. `` Protection? Protection from what?'' 
 `` From you I'm afraid.'' he said, shuffling through a dossier with my name on it. `` It appears you have a very powerful gift.'' 
 `` You have the wrong person!'' I cried out. `` That woman, that exquisite woman from the street, shes the powerful one!'' 
 `` Miss Jones has a different type of power. She's being looked at by agent Simmons right now.'' He said matter of factly. `` Your powers are different. It's more a power of... persuasion.'' 
 
 That was two months ago. They still have n't let me out of this bloody cage. When they do, they better hope they're wrong about my abilities. There are a lot of very powerful people here for me to persuade.

title: story-67
text:
Contractor Ryan reloaded the shotgun and checked his wingsuit again. It was his third drop today against the Renzzio on Jio Segundus. He'd accrued 10k already after a short week on Jio. This was easy money. The Jios paid well. 
 
 `` Contractor, bring yourself and Subcontractor Kelly to the cockpit.'' He tapped his teammate on the should and walked the length of the bomber to the cockpit. 
 
 Director O'Brian sat at the controls. Jio-parpar wrapped itself around the other cockpit seat. The director addressed Ryan and Kelly without turning from the HUD. 
 
 `` This is a Renzzio master nest. We have footage of their swarms from the last attack.'' From the HUD controls, Director O'Brian replayed the video. 
 
 Thousands of rubbery crows the size of hunting dogs poured out of clay openings and spun black tornadoes around the nest. The tornadoes turned and zoomed towards the source of the video recording, blacking it out. 
 
 `` Jio-parpar, can we have a moment to ourselves?'' Ryan and Kelly saluted at the Jios unwound from the copilot seat and rolled towards the cockpit exit. 
 
 `` O'Brian, it's going to be a bit hard to spend our Jio stipends if we're picked apart by crows today.'' 
 
 `` You knew the stakes when you signed up, *Contractor* Ryan.'' The director drew out the word. 
 
 `` Yes, but my agreement says that I get all necessary equipment. We can clean up crow singles and doubles with our light arms, but I ca n't take on a swarm with a shotgun.'' 
 
 `` You know we ca n't nuke in this atmosphere, it will burn up the planet.'' 
 
 `` That's not what I'm asking for and you damn well know it.'' 
 
 `` But we only have three. I ca n't risk it.'' 
 
 `` If you do n't risk it, do you think the Jios or Renzzio will let us leave the planet alive?'' 
 
 `` Fine. But we do n't even know how these work.'' 
 
 `` I'll figure it out.'' Ryan strapped the FTL engine to his wingsuit. He dropped the shotgun and attached three pulse dueling shields -- one to his helmet, one on each shoulder. They emitted a low electric hum as the charged brown gel coated his upper body and head. 
 
 Ryan dove from the bomber hatch and ignited the retrojets. He buzzed towards the master hive. Just like the video, a huge swarm emerged, darkening the Jio sky. 
 
 A pink light spread like dawn from Contractor Ryan's back where the FTL engine attached. Ryan's wingsuit accelerated and Kelly and O'Brian leaned across the cockpit to watch the display. 
 
 A small blur, the contractor slammed into one, then a second Renzzio. They popped like paper bags and his acceleration continued. His suit left a contrail as he encircled the black horde, his pink dawn engulfing the darkness. As the acceleration continued, he was not longer a blur, but merely an electron, virtually everywhere at once. The nest and horde disintegrated, a gray clouds drifting downwards to the planet surface. 
 
 Contractor Ryan emerged from the cloud, rapidly slowing. He refired the retrojets and winged up into the bomber hold. Kelly and O'Brien emerged from the cockpit. Jio-parpar stood before Ryan, offering up the FTL master controls. The humans were victorious on Jio.

title: story-68
text:
“ What happened to him? ” I asked. “ You communicated with him more than any of us. ” 
 
 “ He discovered something. ” Responded Richard: a brilliant biologist whose colleague of three decades, Boron, had been the first to lose grasp on reality while working on the same genome sequencing project that two other scientists had worked on after him – with the same results. “ Something... 
 
 “ Maybe he discovered God doesn ’ t exist. ” Boron ’ s teenage daughter chimed in. 
 
 “ Oh sweetie. ” Richard began, “ I thought you were still inside. I ’ m so sorry. Jenny, your father never – “ 
 
 “ I ’ m not a little girl. I ’ m entering college next fall. Don ’ t treat me like one. ” 
 
 “ Well, your father never believed in God. I don ’ t think reaffirming what he believed would do this to him. What makes you say that? ” 
 
 “ Well, he kept saying that this isn ’ t an accident. That none of this is. ” 
 
 “ None of what is an accident? ” I asked. “ What ’ s ‘ this ’? ” 
 
 “ This. ” She replied, looking up at the sky and then rotating her head so that her eyes pointed in every which direction around us. 
 
 “ What else did he say? ” Asked Richard. “ We haven ’ t been able to talk to him much. He just keeps calling us insects and laughing at us deliriously whenever we talk or do anything. ” 
 
 “ Yes. Insects. ” Her eyes began to well up as soon as she heard the word. “ Insects. Before he left – he put my face in his hands, he looked at me like, like, like with eyes full of love and hurt. Yes, full of love, but love that was being strangled by disillusionment. I saw it. All in his eyes. I saw it fading as he caressed my cheek and said ‘ My daughter. My beautiful precious daughter. A bug. Not even a rat. Just a bug. ’ Then there was no more love in eyes. Just lunacy. ” 
 
 The car ride on our way to his lab felt like felt like we had an appointment to meet the devil and we were unable to as much as pull over for a cup of coffee to collect our thoughts. I drove but it felt like the car was being pulled. I don ’ t know what we expected to find: shit smeared on the walls and cryptic phrases scribbled on it, maybe some sort of journal that documented his descent into madness. What we found instead was – perfect order. Boron had never been neat. His lab had always looked like a bomb exploded in it. Seeing everything organized immaculately down to the books and binders aligned to the tables they sat on in perfectly conforming 90 degree angles - was all the more terrifying. The notes that we did find were written with such tiny letters that we needed to magnify the pages at 40X in order to make them out. 
 
 Hubris will be your doom. Humility your only redeemer. 
 
 Burn it all. 
 
 I felt bad for Boron. I felt bad for his family. I felt bad for how thankful I felt as I pull in to the driveway of my beautiful home. 
 
 “ Dad! ” 
 
 I catch my 11 year old son, Conrad mid-air as he leaps on me the second I come in the front door, my wife and 8 year old daughter making their way to me from the kitchen. 
 
 “ What ’ s up little buddy? ” I ask him, bouncing him up and down on my arms. “ Sweetie? Why are you looking at me like that? ” Leah, honey? Why are you crying? ” 
 
 Conrad is pulling his hand from the back of my neck. I can ’ t place that look on his eyes, the struggle within them, as he looks down at the swarm of beetles crawling up his arm from the hand that was just on his Father's neck.

title: story-69
text:
HI! This is my first piece of writing so please forgive me if it's terrible. Any feedback would be great! 
 
 
 
 It's coming to that time of year again. 
 `` I ca n't Wait!'' I squealed aloud. Everyone in the room looked at me as my face began to burn up. I immediately made my excuses, seems I had said that at precisely the wrong time, yet again, besides I'd heard enough anyway. As I hurried to my room, I smiled over the irony of me attending the annual Dragon Killing Planning ( DKP ) meeting. The meetings themselves were pointless anyhow. All the lords met up, none of them wanting to team up to avoid sharing the spoils, while none wanted to be wiped out by trying to defeat the dragon alone. It all resulted in the same system as the previous year and the year before that and the year before that extra... Well I thought their egotism was reliable if nothing else. 
 
 I collapsed on my princess sized bed and sighed. Not for the first time I wondered why anyone would want to kill Derrick, he's the dragon by the way. Sure he takes the odd cow or sheep, but he always cleans up after himself, and he leaves more than enough silver as payment ( his idea, not mine ), and yet, anytime someone gets ill or goes missing or dies in the forest he's the one whose blamed. Not bandits or disease, but Derrick. Stupid careless peasants. Why ca n't they just not cut down trees if all their gon na do is get crushed by them. 
 
 My mood was dispelled when I saw a familiar scaly nostril hanging down from the top of my window. I live in the furthest room of the furthest tower the palace has. Right at the back. When you look down, there's nothing but air and the odd particle of spray if it's windy enough. Perfect for when you want to meet up with a dragon, away from the prying eyes of the courts. Sure the odd maid is found smashed against the rocks under my window, but then, maids are n't exactly a limited resource, at least not for a princess, and their families are paid handsomely, two silver coins, more than the maids would ever have made. 
 
 Back to the nostril, my bad mood was instantly dispelled as I rushed towards the window, slipping, stumbling and ultimately ruining my new dress in the process. Oh well I thought it was only worth, what, a couple of thousand gold coins. 
 
 As I was saying, slipping and stumbling over the ruined dress I threw my self out of the window and for a brief moment I was weightless. Then he caught me and brought me back up to the window sill. Derrick was laying cat like on the top of the spire its cone roof hiding him from all par the passing ships. He hung his neck lazily down from his perch and looked at me with his dazzling emerald eyes. 
 
 `` So'', his honey like voice drizzled into my ears, `` what are they going to do this time?'' 
 
 `` Oh the same old, send a knight covered in oranges or something'' I shrugged. 
 
 The thin stream of smoke from his nostrils thickened a little, `` Damn witch, cursing me with an allergic reaction to citrus, I miss lemon roasted lamb''. At the thought of food the smoke lessened and a short line of drool crept from his mouth. 
 
 `` Oh yeah there was one other thing'' 
 
 The dragon, pulling himself away from his foodie fantasies inquired. `` What? No, wait, do n't tell me, they'll give the vanquisher double the gold from last year, no, land, a title-'' 
 
 `` You'll never get it'' the princess giggled. 
 
 `` Might it happen to be, your hand in marriage?'' The dragon asked, draping himself around the princess's shoulders. 
 
 `` Eww no.'' Came the immediate reply. `` Their starting a nationwide search for, guess who- 
 
 `` Grisleda.'' 
 
 `` You got it in one'' 
 
 `` That wrinkly curse making old crow, if I so much as smell her I'll-'' 
 
 The clatter of the metal tray cut his rampage short. In front of the open door a young serving girl stood frozen. Both the princess and the dragon, having whipped their heads around at the clattering of the tray, looked at each other knowingly. A few seconds later the splash barely audible from the window went by, unnoticed.

title: story-70
text:
The fugitive had only made it past the first gate when the alarms began to sound. The prison came to life like a giant steel dragon violently awoken by a burglar. Beams of light scorched the darkness as the beating sound of drone propellers filled the sky. The dark figure continued to sprint toward the second gate as the whirling black drones locked onto his heat signature and swarmed toward his location. He shielded his eyes from the dust and debris that filled the air as the drones started to surround him. A pair of prongs struck his right leg and began to spark as an electric charge was delivered by one of the drones. He ripped them out in one pull, wrapped the wires around his hand and used the taught line to slam the buzzing machine into the ground. The propellers of the drone fragmented and showered the area with a hail of shrapnel that destroyed another drone and sent a sliver of razor-sharp metal through the man's left knee. He collapsed as his leg gave out and a web of prongs pierced his body delivering shock after shock. Eventually the body stopped twitching, the whooshing of the drones faded as they returned to their pods and the lights of the prison yard returned to a jaundice yellow. 
 
 `` You took one hell of a beating,'' said a voice as the black rimmed eyes began to adjust to the light. `` Did you really think you would make it?'' 
 
 `` I had to try,'' coughed the man as he wiped the red contents of his lungs from his lips. He narrowed his eyes as the hazy figure of the man looking down on him began to sharpen and he noticed a prisoner label on the man's white coat. 
 
 `` You did n't though. Even with that bionic leg, you could n't have outrun the drones,'' said prisoner Jacob as he motioned down to the twisted mass of metal and plastic that used to be the man's right leg, which clicked and sputtered as servos tried to function despite the damage caused by the drone prongs. `` You're just lucky I can fix it... Samson Cordwell, is it?'' said Jacob as he glanced down at the information display on the the bed. `` Arrested for distribution of malicious propaganda and terrorism against the state. It says you lost your leg in the war against Russia. You veterans were always the worst when it came to augmentation upkeep.'' 
 
 `` You some kind of doctor?'' asked Samson with a grimace as he attempted to move the augmented leg and felt metal grinding against metal. 
 
 `` I was a researcher with a bio-medical group that designed artificial limbs. Your leg is from a rival manufacturer, but I have a pretty good idea of how to fix it.'' Jacob picked up a screwdriver from a tray and inserted it into the leg. 
 
 `` God damn it!'' screamed Samson as the pain receptors shot electrical impulses through the plastic-coated wires and traveled up his spine to his brain. `` What'd they arrest you for? Kidnapping and torturing your patients in your basement?'' 
 
 `` Ha ha oh no, our government is more than happy to let a valuable asset such as myself keep a few skeletons in my closet. They only really have a problem when you drag their skeletons out into the street,'' said Jacob as slowly picked at wires with a pair of pliers. `` Are you familiar with the book of Ecclesiastes, Mr. Cordwell?'' 
 
 `` You kids with your damn religious fantasies. That's what lead to this insane bible-thumping government coming into power in the first place.'' 
 
 `` What has been will be again, what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun. Ecclesiastes 1:9. The state and religious officials at the conference on the future augmentations really perked up when they heard me begin my speech with a verse from the good book.'It's about time these scientists get with the program', some of them muttered. Their applause grew louder and louder as I begin to explain that much of humanity's downfall has been due to a failure to adequately address the issue of unchecked growth of unsuccessful populations.'' 
 
 `` That seems to tow the party line pretty well. The bastards love to demonize the poor as leeches.'' 
 
 `` Yes, they were quite ecstatic to have a leading scientist confirm what they had already believed without scientific basis. I explained how throughout history, as technology and open trade increasingly made the least competitive members of society less valuable to the functioning of the economy and more of a drain on the resources of those who actually produced wealth, these members of an increasing underclass began to demand more and more with a greater inclination toward violence if their demands went unanswered. The last incarnations of this underclass violence were the socialist riots that were crushed by the leader and his militants and lead to his election success in 2028.'' 
 
 `` We did everything we could,'' shouted the gray-haired man as he sat up. `` Those crusader bastards had the corporations bankrolling them and the military arming them. The police just turned away as they gunned down peaceful demonstrators.'' 
 
 `` Which brings me to the skeletons. I stated that there were humane ways to apply Darwinian principles to evolve the human race. I said that the noncompetitive members of society should have been given a basic income if they volunteered to get sterilized. I told them that they had chosen the most primitive, barbaric and evil path to addressing the inequality that was tearing our society apart. Like Hitler, Caesar and all the other tyrants that had torn down democracy in its moment of crisis, they had destroyed the greatest gift a human can possess. They had crushed liberty. They had destroyed millions of their own countrymen and in turn they would be destroyed, just as countless tyrants had been before them. It was at this point that the hall had grown completely silent. The corporate representatives in their shiny black suits turned off their retinal displays with the endless lists of rising stock numbers, the party officials, whose military uniforms glittered with rows of medals, set down their electronic cigars, and the priests clutched their bibles as the calm was broken by a torrent of cries for my execution. I'm still amazed I was n't lynched on the spot, but of course this government is still concerned about appearances, so I was sent to a secret tribunal where I was sentenced to die. And here I am, spending the remainder of my days treating prisoners until they call my name and put a bullet through my brain.'' 
 
 The doctor finished replacing a plastic plate on the bionic leg, which had now gone silent. `` Try it out.'' 
 
 Samson flexed and extended the leg. The wrinkles on his weathered face softened as the pain finally subsided. `` Thanks, doc. She has n't worked this well in years.'' 
 
 `` Helping you has been a great pleasure, my friend,'' said Jacob as he began to place the tools back into a bag. `` Just do n't make this escaping thing a habit.'' 
 
 `` Well, doc, I'd love to make you that promise, but a wise man once told me that'what has been done will be done again' and I ca n't imagine any man can much change his nature much more than the rest of humanity can change it's cursed course.'' 
 
 `` Curse or miracle. It will be done. There is nothing new under the sun.''

title: story-71
text:
The crashing waves knock me around violently, my body flailing at the mercy of the ocean's power. The storm rages on through the night, my prayers in unison with it's seemingly endless tirade. I cling to different pieces of my boat as they diverge through the waters: their destination as hopeless as mine. After hours of being swayed in the dark water, I finally found a large enough piece of my hull to safely ride out the untimely storm. The ocean calms as the sun peaks over the trailing thunderheads. To my surprise, I am just a kilometer away from a small island. I begin to paddle furiously with my feet, my upper body lies exhausted on the battered floating wood. 
 
 I crash into the beach with no energy to spare and the only action I can muster up is a few steps before I crash face first into the sand. When I wake up, I have no idea how long I have been out but the sun has definitely shifted. I stand up, eyes groggy, body covered in sand and try to think of a way to survive. Then I hear a voice near the jungle's edge. 
 
 `` Hello lad! ``, a burly voice echoes out of the shadows of the great canopy that shades the island. 
 
 `` Hey! Help! ``, I yell back loudly, voice hoarse from coughing up salt water all night. 
 
 A giant of a man emerges from the tree tops, jumping straight down into the sand without hesitation. His physique that of a Greek god, his beard nearly drapes to his waist. As he gets closer, it is obvious he is ecstatic to see another human. His lips hinged upright into a grand smile as he picks up pace to greet me. 
 
 `` My good man! You have no idea how long it has been since I've seen another human! ``, his coarse hands feel the size of a catchers mitt as he embraces me. 
 
 I do not mean to ruin his jubilant moment but this is not exactly an ideal situation for me. 
 
 `` Wh -- Where am I? What is this place?'' 
 
 `` This place? Honestly, I can not tell you the name of this place'', he says back, his perfectly angular face still filled with joy but something in his tone is not inline with his emotions. 
 
 `` You do n't know the name of this place, right? Is that what you mean?'' 
 
 `` No, I did not say that, now did I good man? I said I can not tell you the name of this place'', he says in a flatter tone, his voice deeper and more serious. 
 
 `` I do n't understand. I just lost my whole ship in a terrifying tropical storm, my boat got blown to shit and now I land on an unknown Island with some giant man and he says he ca n't tell me the name of the island that he lives on by himself?'' 
 
 `` Yes, that is precisely your situation. You are spot on'' 
 
 `` Well damn... Then please, please tell me how to get off this Island'', I pleadingly say. 
 
 He bellows out a manic laugh, borderline psychotic, especially given the context. I can not tell if he is pure evil or just out of his mind. Either way, the truth will be known to me shortly. 
 
 `` My good man'', he says as his face lights up brighter than when he first found saw me. `` Oh my good man, there is no getting off this Island.'' 
 
 He says it with so much confidence, so much finality, that I truly think he is serious. 
 
 `` What....'' 
 
 `` You can not leave here. I have been here for 300 years... It has been 300 years since I washed up on this beach the exact same way you did''

title: story-72
text:
I come to you to ask a shameful thing. So that you will not kill me for my dishonorable request I will tell you the story in full. Some parts of it you know and trust, some parts of it you know and doubt, but I swear to it all. 
 
 You remember the era of explanation. Every weak young male of the clan was given a starship and sent out into the desert of the universe to build a holding and, perhaps, become strong. You remember when one such man found the ships of another race in the desert of the night. Do you remember how your heart sang? Do you remember the joy you felt when you learned we were not alone in a trackless waist? 
 
 And so, as one does when they find neighbors before unknown, we attacked. We followed the words of the warrior sage, “ When you face a new foe strike his exterior fortifications and learn his strength. ” We attacked a small mining and metallurgical extraction facility. Our hearts sang. What we ’ d always known was confirmed. We were strong. 
 
 We won, of course, we had come with overwhelming force. However, that was secondary. The new race, the humans, had few weapons and they weren ’ t so powerful. Nor were the humans warriors of legend from a physical standpoint. They are smaller than us, and relatively weak. There were few casualties in that first conflict. 
 
 The Humans made fine slaves. We gave them work to do along the lines of what they had been doing before. Then for doing that work we gave them food, shelter, and tokens to trade for further luxuries. They didn ’ t even seem to understand the insult in that. The tale is surely apocryphal, but I will tell it as it illustrates what fine slaves they made. A human was interviewed about his work, and he said that it was fine. He said that the 7 hour day he was made to work was shorter than the 14 hour days he had worked as a miner. That ’ s madness, of course. One can not work a 14 hour day! Even if you could work that long without resting you ’ d need a 30 hour day just to fit in your sleep. 
 
 So the clans attacked more of their worlds. We found mature colonies with 100 ’ s of thousands of individuals and mighty cities numbering in the 10 ’ s of thousands, and we fell upon them from the sky. The first wave, you must have heard, went poorly. They struck at us with coward ’ s weapons and picked our ships out of the sky before they could land! But we were cleaver we circled around to use vectors that approached unpopulated portions of their worlds. We traveled over land from there and when we struck their cities we found them weak. The mighty clans grew more powerful with the fine human slaves, and we saw the way it would be. These humans would be our partners in the vast empty desert of the galaxy. Our subordinate partners, of course, but we were no longer alone in the night and our strength had been confirmed. It was a fine time to be alive. 
 
 The humans sent ambassadors and the ambassadors said we didn ’ t need to attack them. The humans were willing to respect our boundaries. They said they ’ d been in space for a very long time and the galaxy had always seemed empty. They said we could have half of it if we wanted. We told them we had no idea why they were admitting to being cowards, and we said we did want half. We wanted the half they ’ d developed. It ’ s only right that the strong take from the weak. 
 
 The warrior sage says, “ When you know the strength of your Enemy leap for his heart with a dagger clutched in your teeth. ” So clan Black Fang sent scouts deep into enemy territory and found their home world. Or at least they found a world containing over a billion of the humans. 
 
 No! Do not doubt. This was their true number. Tell yourself they were long in discovering space travel and had to tolerate the over-population. 
 
 They struck the world thinking to become the dominate clan. They all died. There were no unguarded vectors on such a thickly populated word. Black Fang ’ s commanders had assumed the oceans would be unguarded, but the coward ’ s defenses covered even those. Black Fang is mighty no more. 
 
 So Iron Claw clan struck. They had wrapped their ships in radar absorbing materials, tuned their reactionless drives so they would leak very little EM, and insulated their hulls such that they leaked only a few degrees above absolute zero. It must have gotten hot in those ships, but it was for nothing. Iron Claw clan is might no more. The humans have better stealth then we do. 
 
 So the most powerful of the clans took rare council. They agreed to act together and split the spoils. They built even stealthier warships. They gathered all the fleets together for a single mighty blow. It was glorious, their ships darkened the sun. The clans are mighty no more. 
 
 The battle lasted ten minutes. Yes ten! I swear, I was there in one of the few ships to withdraw before it was destroyed. The humans had fortified their world while the clans built. The humans had robotic warships, hidden stealth torpedoes, lasers studded throughout their system. The mighty fleet was cut apart and the entire time it was happening we registered more and more launches from their home world. 
 
 The madness of the human ambassadors deepened. They demanded that we surrender. Yes, surrender. They seemed to feel they could make us weak through a display of defensive martial prowess. It is true. I said their madness deepened did I not? 
 
 When we would not be weak they came for us. They fought utterly without bravery. They never landed a ship. They never offered hand-to-hand combat. They destroyed cities from orbit. They EMPed electronics into useless slag. They punched holes in anything that even looked capable of flight with powerful energy weapons. It was the most senseless combat I ’ ve ever seen. Of what value, I ask, is turning the territory you ’ ve defeated into a glassy crater? How do you rule that? What do you gain? You might as well go to some empty world around some empty star and build a city! 
 
 Although it does explain why they tried to keep our ships from reaching orbit when we attacked them. 
 
 On every world they asked the same question, “ Where is your home world? Where is your capital? ” 
 
 The defeated told them, of course, as the defeated do. They went to the home world. I was there in clan counsel when it happened. Their ships darkened the sun. When I said our ships darkened the sun it was hyperbole. When I say their ships darkened the sun it was the literal truth. 
 
 This is the part of the tale you will not believe, so do not interrupt me with your objections. The planet we thought was their home world. It wasn ’ t. It was but a half settled colony. I am told their home world contains over a hundred billion humans. I am told they buildings thousands of stories tall, and hundreds of miles wide. I am told they grow their crops with electric light and that they once almost destabilized the ecosystem of the world by their numbers. 
 
 Can you imagine that? You can ’ t. They had to learn how to avoid killing a whole world. Nor were they lying about being in space a long time. They have millions of worlds like that. We poked a claw at the barest edge of their Empire. 
 
 Of course you don ’ t believe it. I said you wouldn ’ t believe it. But why would I lie? I tell you this to save as much of your world as can be saved. 
 
 So while the clans built, the human worlds built. They made tens of billions of ships. The humans have more warships than we have warriors. They came like a plague of locusts. The sky grew dark. Literally dark as they landed those ships on our defeated home world. When the day ended, I looked to the sky and found our planet had a ring like some world with a failed moon. More of the human ships in orbit. 
 
 “ This is your home world, ” they asked. 
 
 We said, “ Yes. ” 
 
 I don ’ t think they believed us. I think they considered all of our might the martial show of some provincial backwater. I think, maybe, they still suspect we ’ re hiding an overpopulated hive of a world somewhere. 
 
 At any rate, they ’ re going from world to world now and demanding surrender. Here is the dishonorable thing I must ask of you. I will make the request and hope you don ’ t kill me. Give it to them. 
 
 * * * 
 
 Hmmmmm: That was basically as close to Man-Kzin wars wars fan-fic as you can get without writing Man-Kzin wars fan-fic. I did n't really intend that. Humans were obviously vastly more advanced at first contact, and I did n't say the speaker was a big yellow tiger with no grasp of strategy, but the speaker's social structure is about the same. Oh well, Man-Kzin wars are great books 
 
 I did n't really want either side to be wrong. The humans are just defending themselves. Although that was some titanic overkill. I'd like to think the speaker really would have considered our defeated race a partner in the exploration of the galaxy if his race had n't been so hopelessly over confident. 
 
 Perhaps they can still learn something from one another someday. Or maybe the puppeteers will show up...
