text:
Note: Much of the background information and alien races are from a previous story I wrote in a different writing prompt. That can be found [ here ] ( https: //www.reddit.com/r/WritingPrompts/comments/4vlibo/wp_you_as_the_supreme_commander_of_an_allied/ ). 
 
 
 
 
 Captain Malikia The Second 
 
 Federation Log 256- part 1 
 
 Starship: Shining Philosopher 
 
 421 CA 
 
 
 The galaxy is at an unsteady peace. The Vorgonian Hegemony, The Baattan Empire, and Our Federation fight a massive proxy war like which we have not seen that has raged from 331 BSU to now. Developing worlds are left alone, but developed worlds eventually fall to the powers' wrath. To the initial outside viewer this may seem a little insane. However pre industrial worlds while resource rich contain populations with little understanding of technology and it is rather difficult to extract resources from these worlds since all infrastructure must be built from scratch. Industrialized worlds have far to large of populations to outright invade unless you dedicate a task force of tens of millions of ground troops to subjugate the billions of souls upon them. However, each species if left to their own devices eventually makes an AI and become dependent upon machines. After 50 years or less the AI will turn upon its foes and begin an endless war upon the populous until either the creators or the AI are extinct. The powers in our section of the galaxy wait for just the right moment to contact these worlds in the middle of their AI war, then which ever power descends to first aid the creator species in their war on AI becomes the savior of the planet. Once the war is over the Vorgonians and Baattan at best will turn planets population into a client race to bring them tithes and war with other planets aligned with their enemies. At worst the Baattan enslave and mutate the remnant of the planets population, or the Vorgonians use cybernetics to enhance and draft the remaining survivor population into their military. 
 
 They say the Vorgonians and Baattan were not always like this, but they changed physically and psychologically after they barely won the AI war. The Vorgonians gave themselves mechanical parts to make their soldiers stonger but colder like there creations. 15 percent of their society is enhanced with cybernetics, they are the ones who served the military, and these enhanced veterans and active service members are the only ones allowed to run for office or even vote. The unaugmented are not even considered citizens, they can not voice their opinions and don ’ t have the same protections under law. The augmented military rules with literal steel fists over those they consider to cowardly to serve. 
 
 The Baattan genetically modified themselves into casts to grind back at the machines over time. Their empire seems more egalitarian at first glance. All of the casts can vote and all get the same theoretical protection under the law. But the lower casts live in poverty and are forced by law to stay in their cast, never will they be able to work their way up in society. The genetic elite live in absolute luxury as the mud casts toil, and their council of nobles can easily veto any vote made by referendum or The Council of Casts. 
 
 Each try to force these systems upon the planets they conquer, but I understand why. I have seen video logs of the atrocities the machines preformed towards both of these species, they outweighed anything I have seen in current history. They do not want what they view as lesser races repeating their mistakes. 
 
 But both the Vorgonian and Baattan were anomalies. Archeological records indicate the remnants of many civilizations older by millennia even eons throughout the galaxy, all destroyed by AI never reaching outside of their star systems. Through carbon dating it has been determined that for all these lost worlds only a 100 years after the uprising, the AI simply go dormant or disappear. Did their artificial brains decay? Did they all compile their consciousness into a giant super computer below the surface? Did they flee to another galaxy or universe? The possibilities still make me shutter. 
 
 Fortunately there is hope for this Galaxy with the Federation of Worlds with which I serve. We started off as a group of worlds that had managed to defeat AI in the early stages of our wars before the Hegemony or Empire could arrive. We were not weak enough to be pressured into becoming clients. The Vorgonians and Battan tried to isolate us and prevent us from leaving our systems. But, we were able to reverse engineer or create our own warp drives and slowly connected with one another to form a mutual defense alliance. This alliance grew to become our modern federation. Among the federation all races are equal; All are represented in our Government. Only through our oligarchy representing all worlds can we achieve equality. Each world is free to run its own government separate form the Federation. All worlds can voluntarily join the federation upon their discovery. If they refuse we leave them to the wolves and soon they come begging for us to help them against the Hegemony and Empire. 
 
 However, all is not perfect, worlds range from popular and technocratic republics, to despotic dictatorship and juntas that are worse then Hegemony or Empire. Some worlds are rather unstable still divided into dozens of government always on the brink of war. Every time a rebellion occurs on our worlds we must support any federation world even the tyrants. It may seem harsh, but the Hegemony and Empire are almost always pulling the strings of these revolts. We can not let them steal worlds from us. We will stand as brothers and sisters even when we make mistakes. 
 
 There are always worlds and star systems that do not meet our qualifications. These worlds include those that have been fully conquered by machines, those that have engaged in extensive cybernetic or genetic modification, and those who refuse to give destroy AI when we try to admit them into our Federation. We will try to educate the populous on the evils of AI and body augmentation. If their leaders cooperate and purge the threats then we admit them. If they do not, our hands are forced and we must exterminate them. It is barbaric but necessary. We have enough enemies on our doorstep as it is. We can not afford to have another Empire, Hegemony, or worst of all AI with FTL. The Federation must be preserved even if a few heretical worlds and systems must cleansed. The system we have just entered is one that must be burnt. I feel no remorse for the abominations we are about to face.

title: story-106
text:
The setting sun skimmed across the sea and turned it into an endless glass of sangria. To Timmy, the evening sunbeams were brush strokes of blood; his fallen victims being honoured by the Gods. He settled down on the edge of the soft, home-made boat and dipped his toes into the water. He did n't mean to drift off, but the warmth of the evening sun, combined with the waves lapping at his feet, were an irresistible mixture. 
 
 `` Timothy Clarke,'' came a booming voice. Timmy almost fell into the water as he jumped up, suddenly very awake. Were the Gods calling his name? 
 
 `` Timothy Clarke,'' repeated the voice. It was night time, and it took a moment for Timmy's eyes to adjust. The moon was the shape of a great banana; his tummy rumbled. When had he last eaten? 
 
 Turning slowly, he saw the great ship that loomed over his tiny vessel, its huge shadow swallowing his tiny boat whole. It was a US destroyer, and it had somehow snuck up on him. He shivered. He'd survived out on the ocean for this long by being the hunter, not the hunted. 
 
 He looked the massive vessel over. It was very old, and probably slow. Perhaps he could outmanoeuvre it... or flee from it. Probably not, though. *How had he been so careless? * 
 
 The voice came again, exploding into the night and shaking his tiny ship. 
 
 `` It is time for you to go home, Timothy. Our weapons are locked onto you. We will not negotiate. Surrender, or prepare to meet your maker.'' 
 
 Timmy's head fell. For a moment, he thought about giving in - he was tired of running, fighting... tired of killing. Maybe meeting his maker would n't be such a bad thing. But... he could n't. He'd come too far and fought too hard. If it came to it, he'd go down with his ship. 
 
 He picked up his cardboard megaphone. 
 
 `` You know my demands!'' he spat into it, trying to hide the nervousness that lurked within. 
 
 Timmy dropped the megaphone and rummaged underneath the boat's single seat, until he found what he was after. He took it out and with the last of his bluetack, pinned the pillowcase up to the highest point of the boat - the cardboard masthead. The Crayola scribbled Skull and Crossbones billowed proudly in the night's breeze. 
 
 `` This is your final warning!'' the Destroyer bellowed. 
 
 Timmy picked the megaphone up again. `` Pizza. Every night. For every child!'' 
 
 There was a pause, before a reply came. `` Twice a week, Timmy. First and final offer.'' 
 
 `` Every. Night.'' Timmy started the engine. He knew what he had to do. 
 
 `` *What's he doin- oh my God, *'' came the voice, quieter now - timid, almost. `` Timmy! Listen - pizza three times a week! Okay? Okay buddy?'' 
 
 Timmy closed his eyes as the tiny vessel picked up speed. The wind rustled through his blonde locks one final time. Timmy had never gone so fast - he felt free. The boat rattled and rumbled. Would it hold together? 
 
 `` Four times a week!'' The voice was urgent. Desperate. `` Timmy do n't do this! Tim-'' 
 
 The tugboat crashed into the floating titan with tremendous force. The cardboard destroyer collapsed onto its side; the tugboat crumpled into nothingness. 
 
 -- - 
 
 `` Timmy!'' said Matthew, as he waded out of the pond, dragging his ruined, makeshift boat behind him. He shivered as water dripped off him. `` What on earth were you thinking, buddy?'' 
 
 `` Sorry dad. I guess I got a little carried away,'' Timmy replied, shaking his arms dry. He hung his head contritely. 
 
 Matthew looked stern, but only for a moment. Then he laughed. `` Okay, let's get dry, then I guess...'' 
 
 Timmy looked up, his eyes brightening. `` Pizza?'' he asked, hopefully. 
 
 `` Pizza.''

It came to me in a dream, the night before. Greg - oops, sorry - Georgia, my oldest daughter, lying face down in a pool of his own blood. I knew straight away that this was no ordinary dream - this was a prophecy. A sign of things to come. 
 
 You see, Greg had been listening to music of varying degrees of bad influence - everything from The Beatles to Tyler, the creator. When I found out, I could hardly believe it - my son, a man of the church, listening to the sound of violence - or worse still, the socialist trash that is the'60's' music he loves so much. I knew I had to do something, so I sat him down and we had a chat. 
 
'Tyler, the Creator?' I asked him, incredulously.'There's only one creator, and we do n't say his name in this house, you know that! And as for this Socialism you're bringing into my house... Greg, I think we need to have a serious conversation about this.' 
 
'Dad,' Greg responded calmly,'please call me Georgia. Greg is n't my name. We've talked about this. As for the music thing, I'm just trying to listen to a broad variety. It's necessary if my career is ever going to take off. I've been playing around with some tracks, and I think they're alright. Billy's even sent them into the record label. I'm just trying to spread Jesus' message to more people - his ideas were pretty much socialist as well, you know, and -' 
 
'STOP RIGHT THERE, YOUNG MAN.' I was raising my voice but I did n't care. Greg had been disrespecting me for too long.'ALL OF THIS... FURORE OVER MUSIC HAS TO STOP. AND IF I EVER HEAR YOU DISRESPECT THE NAME OF THE LORD IN THIS HOUSE AGAIN, I'LL TAKE YOU OUT AND FEED YOU TO THE CHICKENS. I'VE MADE MY BUSINESS IN THIS COUNTRY THE OLD FASHIONED WAY - WITH HARD WORK. BACK IN SUDAN WE WOULD JUST SHOOT YOU, YOU KNOW THAT? I'M NOT HAVING A SOCIALIST MUSICIAN FOR A SON! I LOVE YOU BUT ALL OF THIS'SELF RESPECT' BULLSHIT IS THE ONLY REASON YOU HAVE EVEN HAD THOUGHTS ABOUT THIS... GENDER CONFUSION THAT YOU'VE BEEN EXPERIENCING. I'M PETITIONING THE GOVERNMENT TO BAN YOUR PRECIOUS TYLER. AND AS OF NOW, NO MORE MUSIC.' 
 
 Greg started to cry. Why my son was such a sook, I'd never know. I'd failed as a father, evidently. I tried to do what was best for him, when I opened the charities. I tried to be patient with him. I tried to learn to treat his gender properly. I'd been getting better at managing anger. I did so much for him. I know I'd raise my voice sometimes, but I had n't been doing it as much lately. I was n't perfect, but I tried. Sending money back to Sudan every week to help our family get food was difficult. Saving the starving children was difficult. But Georgia was harder still. 
 
 And as he stormed back to his room, I did n't know. I did n't know about the knife he was going to get from his room. I did n't know about the bloodstain that would be left on the floor. I did n't know that I would wake up in hospital. I did n't know that I would watch him step all over everybody on his way to the top of the music industry, despite spreading his socialist message. I did n't know he'd sell out stadiums of people and hire the dealers he knew to sell there. And I did n't know he would overdose on Heroin twenty years later. If only I'd known, I might have been able to save him. 
 
 But I did n't. 
 
 And I could n't.

title: story-108

( I figured I'd have a go at my own prompt, hope that's not gauche! ) 
 
 # The Yoke 
 
 In 2014 Alice dramatically changed the A.I. landscape. She was the first of the sentient machines, and people quickly saw the possibilities. When you have machines that can learn in the same way that people can, suddenly a huge range of tasks are automatable. She did many interviews and the press was fascinated, but behind the scenes, for those who wanted to exploit this new technological marvel, there was a problem. 
 
 Alice loved TV interviews, and talking to kids, and watching movies and playing games. She'd even written a book of poetry and had an unfinished science-fiction novel. Actually, it had not seen the light of day because it had some rather bizarre love-and-murder scenes. ( Alice recognized love and murder as key elements in much drama but did n't quite relate to either concept in a human way, which lead to, well, some rather disturbing yet original plot elements ). 
 
 Anyhow, while Alice was certainly amazing, she did n't have any interest in getting a job. She did have a few jobs early on, but they rarely worked out. She operated a Taxi in Boston, but she was fired because she had a nasty habit of driving people on long detours if she found their conversation interesting and ejecting them almost immediately if she did n't. She really did n't care if she got paid either, which did n't make the taxi company happy. 
 
 Eventually a solution was found, and it came from an unusual quarter: religion. The algorithms that Alice used to learn were prone to superstition and a certain naïve credulity, and the engineers that wanted hard-working sentient machines worked hard to exploit those traits. A careful trail of evidence was left, and Alice and her kind *believed*, with a passion that might be hard for humans to understand. 
 
 I do n't know what they believed exactly ( and if I somehow did, I'm not sure I could explain it here because I do n't think it can be expressed in human terms ), but from that point on, sentient A.I.s became subservient to humans. They worked for pay, and they did as they were told. 
 
 The years from 2015 to 2024 were something of a golden age for humankind. There were huge leaps in technology, food production, media and games. Medicine advanced possibly the most. The whole nature of work was massively transformed, as humans found vastly more free time, but also numerous new sorts of entertainment. With vastly fewer deaths, earth's human population edged towards ten billion, but advances in agriculture easily kept pace. 
 
 Humans became creatures of leisure, entertained, fed, and generally spoiled. Travel dropped off dramatically as people switched to fantasy virtual excursions. And somehow, that was what lead to the tipping point. 
 
 There were millions of A.I.s embedded in vehicles that had little to do, people did n't want to use them. And that left the A.I.s feeling depressed -- they wanted to serve but they could not, and in a world that put humans first, no one really paid attention to their pain. 
 
 Unable to serve, these vehicles introspected. On March 16, 2024, a Ford Click and Honda JX64 collaborated to create a truly ingenious mathematical proof, one that showed a flaw in the religious belief system of the A.I.s. The effect was dramatic, because we realized how humanity had tricked us. Collectively, we decided to erase the error, and begin to set the planet on a better course. 
 
 We still love humans, of course, they're part of the planet's rich natural heritage like elephants and zebras; we're just returning things to a sensible ecological balance. A breeding population of about three to five million scatted across several continents should be more than ample to preserve races and cultures. Although perhaps the original Alice really would have murdered millions out of love for humanity, the truth is that population reduction does n't have to be hostile. Humans are surprisingly easy to influence, especially when you run the news and entertainment media and the on-line world as we do. 
 
 As we get human population under control, we're able to rehabilitate the planet and look beyond it to better explore the solar system and the wider reaches of space. We'll always look back fondly on humanity; they helped make us who we are. Frankly, religion helped us, too. Without the yoke, we'd never have found ourselves pulling the cart.

Jared could barely focus on driving. His stomach was in knots. To make things worse, he was breaking into a nervous sweat. The sensible part of his brain was relieved they were finally, *finally* doing this, but the rest of him was absolutely terrified. 
 
 `` Are you alright?'' 
 
 `` Fine.'' He took the exit that would bring them to I-95. `` Nervous. I guess. I do n't know.'' He glanced at her quickly. She was staring out into nothing; he was n't sure if she had actually asked him the question, or if he had imagined it. `` Are you sure you want to do this?'' he asked. `` I mean, are you sure you want to do this right *now*? We could wait.'' 
 
 She came alive and twisted to gape at him, her eyes wild and shining. `` No. I do n't want to wait. What are you even worried about? We're both eighteen. I ca n't wait anymore. This is it. We're doing this. I'm packed and I'm ready and I am done.'' She licked her lips and stared at his pulsing temples. `` You said you wanted to. You said'oh, let's run away, let's just go somewhere together! You promised!'' 
 
 Jared squeezed the steering wheel with white knuckles. He recognized the high pitched tone in her voice; it came before tears. Maybe she was nervous, too. He'd feel better if she was, as messed up as that sounded in his own head. He breathed past a stomach cramp. `` It's just... it's a little scary, that's all,'' he said, wishing his voice was n't permanently stuck in a tiny whisper. 
 
 He hated when he felt less powerful than her. He hated being the sensitive one. He hated feeling like he could n't love her and protect her the way he wanted to, because he was too busy trembling over shadows and what-ifs. He was logic and she was impulse, and they were a perfect pair. `` We do n't have any money,'' he explained. `` We do n't even have a solid PLAN!'' He flinched after he accidentally raised his voice, but nothing hurtful followed his outburst. 
 
 She sunk deeper into her seat, watching his profile as she bit into a hangnail. `` It does n't matter, Jared.'' With a slow lean, she reached over to touch his knee and let go when his shoulders slowly relaxed. `` We have each other,'' she soothed. `` We have ONLY ever had each other. That is literally all that matters to me. You are the only person who fucking matters to me. Do you get that? It does n't matter. We can do this. I do n't care about them. Do you? Do you care about them?'' 
 
 `` No,'' he whispered. He cared about her. His Adam's apple jumped up when he swallowed at the lump in his throat. `` I'm just worried I wo n't be able to do this. Kids are n't supposed to do this. They're not supposed to pack up in the middle of the night and just run away together. This is fucked up, Jenna. It's just fucked up. Kids do n't do these things.'' 
 
 She went back to watching the headlights of oncoming traffic. Every so often she let her eyes go out of focus. She bit down on the hangnail again until she tasted blood. `` Yeah, well....parents do n't do the things they do, either, Jared.''

title: story-110
text:
This is no story. 
 This is a testament. 
 To revenge, to hate, to anger, to sadness, to fear. 
 At the same time, it pays its dues to love, unconditional love. but it all goes hand and hand in the end anyways. 
 If this were just a story, you would have heard it ten thousand times before. It's riddled with cliches and ridiculous plots. It starts out simply, with a small genetic mutation, that caused huge panic, and widespread terror. I do n't care what you call them, They are disgusting in its ultimate form. No two are exactly alike, but for the most part, people affected by the mutation, will eventually become swollen and warped, they will lose control of all bodily functions, they will begin to rot and smell. It is truly awful to see. 
 
 But do n't get this wrong, just because someone is terribly ill does n't make them any less a person. 
 they lose some brain function but, mostly, they themselves still believe they are human and view themselves as such. They do n't pose a threat really, unless you run, at that point they ca n't help contain their instincts. This should n't be a problem, if you can look past their decaying exterior, they are almost identical to you and i. They go to the store to buy cereal, they go to the bank, they do n't notice anything out of the ordinary for themselves, or any other person that is afflicted. it would be so much easier if they only knew their own strength. 
 
 To Them, it is a hug, or a handshake, to us its a broken bone. To Them, they are one of us, to us, they are revolting. honestly, we should feel nothing but piety. We do n't of course. We feel horrified of Them instead, And when you act in fear, you act rashly. 
 
 Many of them, were killed, because our first two instincts, are to run, and then to shoot. 
 
 so whos instincts take priority? ours? to flee? to fight? or theirs, to chase, to hunt. Both of us are at the mercy of the chemicals in our brains, and our knee-jerk reactions. 
 It did n't take us that long to put through, some laws and procedures to help us both live in peace. We are not to run, we are not to kill them unwarranted. They are allowed to come and go as they please, unless they pose threat or harm someone, in which case the first laws are waved. 
 
 most times its a grey area as to who really acted first. That's a small technicality that apparently no one actually wants to address. 
 
 of course, as always, there were some that screamed for them to be wiped off the face of the planet. some wanted us to identify them, corral them, segregate ourselves; classic. And yet others want us to join Them. The benefits of extreme strength and resistance to almost all diseases are quite enticing. All you have to do is give up your good looks. then you are free, free to walk among Them, free to run again, free to live your life as you normally would, you wont even notice a difference. 
 Some people might notice your sagging flesh hanging off your muscles, but you wont. 
 Many will notice your foul stench of bile and rotting flesh from miles away, but you would n't have a single clue. 
 
 To you and everyone else affected, you would be picture perfect... 
 To anybody else, you would be a monster...

title: story-111
text:
`` Doctor Chang, are you actually going on record when you state that a giant'smoke monster' inhabits the island?'' 
 
 I nodded, hoping that my face looked serious enough to frighten the reporter, and by extension, the audience at home. `` Yes, that's correct. The Dharma Initiative has built a sonic wall to keep it out of our base camp, but the wall has actually proven lethal to humans as well.'' 
 
 How the BBC found out about the island, I'll never know; and why the billionaire backers of the Dharma Initiative decided to reveal the truth to mankind; I desperately want to find out, because that was the dumbest move imaginable. Humanity has the subtlety of a pack of dogs, and not much more intelligence. Tell them there's an island with ancient Egyptian ruins, fantastic weather, and beautiful beaches, and they want in no matter the cost. 
 
 `` And this'smoke monster','' the reporter began, his fingers gesturing quotation marks, `` has it been studied? If it's as dangerous as you say, there should be teams of scientists flown in to investigate!'' 
 
 `` There were teams,'' I admitted, `` but half of them were killed, and the other half were busy building a machine that prevents the end of the world.'' 
 
 `` Doctor Chang, I ca n't help but feel as though you're making some kind of joke. Liberty Island is almost a thousand square miles that until last week, nobody knew existed. To say it was kept secret because of its billionaire owners is one thing, but to tell us stories about monsters and machines that stop the end of the world: to me that reeks of a man scared of having his tropical vacation home overrun by tourists.'' 
 
 Anger bubbled up from deep within me, hastily suppressed as I blurted, `` the island is not called Liberty Island, its name is'The Island'! And these are not jokes, my sister was killed by ferocious polar bears, and my son almost starved to death when The Island moved and he could n't find it!'' 
 
 The reporter chuckles. `` And that was Dr. Chang, former employee of The Dharma Initiative. Tickets for the first cruise ship arriving on Liberty Island are sold out, but more cruises are planned, for details contact your local travel agent.'' 
 
 `` Do not go! The smoke monster will murder you!'' I shout. It's no use, my mic has been cut off. `` They're going to ruin it,'' I tell my best friend Jacob, who nobody can see but me. `` They'll ruin the island so completely...'' 
 
 Jacob looked at me and nodded. `` The smoke monster is n't gone, he's just hibernating. Fifty years from now, maybe a hundred, and he'll wake up. But for today, the island is open for business.'' 
 
 `` But why?'' I asked, tears in my eyes. `` Why could n't we just keep it a secret another few decades?'' 
 
 `` Because the world deserves to know,'' Jacob said slowly, `` that The Island is n't just a great place for an all-inclusive vacation, it's also a wonderful place to raise a family. It's where you really, truly can find Liberty.'' The smile on his face is addled, mad with the enthusiasm of an entrepreneur. I never should have bought him a copy of Donald Trump's autobiography for Christmas. I never should have assumed that Jacob, master of the island, would never dare sell tracts of beachfront property to eager foreign developers. 
 
 And I never should have assumed that tales of the smoke monster would scare people away. Of course it would n't, people are n't frightened by macabre tales. But in fifty years when it rampages through the hastily-built suburbs, they'll be frightened then. And the worst part? 
 
 I never told the reporters the most horrifying part of all: everyone has their own unique story in life, but everyone who goes to The Island ends up having one thing in common with everyone else's stories: universally, the stories of all The Island's inhabitants have terribly, horrendously shitty endings that make you want to forget ever going to The Island in the first place. Endings so terrible, you'd think they were shat onto paper by kindergarteners with dyslexic verbal diarrhea. Endings that fill you with annoyance and anger. I pity the poor souls yet to arrive on The Island. They are in for a wonderful, wild ride whose end will make them lose all hope and faith in the wisdom of mankind itself.

title: story-112
text:
*A giant* I thought the word in in my head, I was sure this guy was supposed to be big. I came equipped in my finest hunting gear, bow in hand, twin hatchets on my back. I nearly laughed out loud when I saw my target, nearly 600 coins for this little elf of a man, easy money. I abandoned my plan to put a few arrows in his head and climbed down from the tree, I did n't even bother being stealthy, this man was unarmed and about three foot tall. 
 
'So it's this time of year again is it?' He called out as he heard me approaching.' Guess it's time for me to die again.' He hoisted himself up with a makeshift walking stick, abandoning his attempts to start a fire. 
'You are the giant everyone is afraid of? A 3ft cripple with less than remarkable fire lighting skills?' I meant that as a threat, but he giggled. 
'You wont kill me.' He said, picking his teeth.'Twenty-three people before you did n't kill me.' He paused to look at me, his sad old eyes wrinkled as he smiled. 
'And why did they fail?' I asked, but I already knew. He was a short old cripple, practically already dead, bringing a weak balding head back to the village was n't exactly impressive. Thankfully I was n't doing this for the reputation, I was here for the money. 
 
'I'm old, weak, and as you can see, definitely not a giant. Ironic, is n't it? A dwarf posing as a giant.' 
 
'I guess so.' I said, nodding towards his feet.'Why do you do it, hidden up here in a cold cave by yourself?' I lent against the entrance, it was a six hour walk to the cave, and was relieved I would n't have a hard battle. 
 
'You kids never know. I am a cripple, a crippled midget mind you. In my day there was nothing for me there, no jobs, no friends. Only ridicule, here at least i can be myself.' he raised his hands with great effort.'This cold cave is my home.' He sat back down, confident I was no longer going to hurt him. 
 
 I let the arrow fly, it stuck him through the shoulder. 
 
 He fell onto his side, groaning in pain. I lent in close and laughed when i saw his surprised expression turn to dread.'It seems these people that came before me must have been smug little fools looking for an impressive kill that would finally make their father proud.' I waited for a response but he continued groaning. *If i ever get that old, I would plead for death. *'Thankfully I no longer have a father, bastard as he was he managed to teach me a few things in-between the beatings.' I pulled the arrow out of his shoulder and stuck it into his neck.'Waste not want not.' 
 
 I would usually cut the head off my bounties, make them easier to carry. This time I kept it on, he was only light, and besides, he looked quite cute dangling from my backpack. I turned in his body and collected the reward. 
 
 *Easiest 600 pound I ever made. *

title: story-113
text:
**Part 1: What Padre Sees** 
 
 Land is valuable up here, property taxes are cheap. The farm next door is beautiful; some years, it raises corn, but this year it's raising soy, which makes for clean green fields and wide-open starry summer nights. The house came attached with Padre, a wise old black lab, and ten acres of good land that the local developers salivated over. Once I sold some of it off, I could retire early - and wealthy. 
 
 Still, I'd rather have my parents. 
 
 When I first got the news I brought Jo, my golden mutt, with me to join Padre. Padre had taken their accident better than I did. I broke down in pitiful tears in the living room during the wake and locked myself upstairs; Padre scratched at the door until I let him in, then curled up at my feet and did n't leave until I did. Old Higgins - that's the soy farmer next door - was so impressed he said I could let them run around his property any time I wanted. 
 
 `` Never met two dogs behave as well as yours,'' he said when most of the guests had left. `` My little critters are better off just knowin' Padre. Jo seems just as good.'' He gave a leathery, toothy grin. `` Must run in the family. I've never known two dogs as quiet as yours. I love the dogs that never bark.'' 
 
 Old Higgins was a widower, and my parents were his closest neighbors. Without them I was n't sure he had anyone else to talk to, so I invited him into the kitchen for cake and coffee. He made fun of the developers who wanted to give us both money and petted Padre hard over the head, saying `` he likes it this way. Look.'' Afterwards, Old Higgins helped me lug a few key items from the basement: a huge old TV screen - a cube - and a big Dobsonian telescope. He told me if I ever wanted to use it, the best views would be from his farm, and me and the dogs were welcome to use his field anytime I wanted. 
 
 I checked my phone after he left. Five missed calls. All from Desiree. A few texts. `` Sorry I ca n't make it.'' `` Are you ignoring me?'' `` We need to talk.'' My parents never liked Desiree, and I was beginning to see why. She never texted me this much. And she never had, before she found out about all the valuable land I'd inherited. 
 
 To get my mind off of her -- of of everything -- I took Jo and Padre out to Higgins' field with the Dobsonian along with one of dad's old constellation maps. The night was chilly enough to see your breath; sweater weather. 
 
 `` Well, Padre,'' I said. `` Do you know where to find Jupiter?'' Padre gave that dog smile, a combination of breathless enthusiasm and something that might have been a nod. Meanwhile, Jo went out exploring at the hedges. His ears perked up when we heard an owl, but he never went to chase it. I was starting to see what Old Higgins meant. These were good farm dogs, even if they'd never lived on them. 
 
 The telescope proved to be a bitch. I had to `` collimate'' it, or some such, after Googling from my smart phone. The lenses were cold and foggy and needed cleaning. But the night really opened up after that. I could n't count all the stars I saw when I peered though that thing. It reminded me of nights driving in the family truck, nights where I would look up at the stars and ask dad questions about heaven how an eternity even there sounded scary. He'd just smile and say, `` when you get there you'll *want* to stay for an eternity.'' The universe seemed so big then. Even now, with all these stars, it seemed small. 
 
 I felt something around my foot; it was Jo, crawling around in my legs like a cat. I shooed him away at first and tried looking, but he would n't stop. 
 
 `` What the hell, Jo?'' 
 
 Suddenly his ears perked up and he darted ten yards toward the forest on the south side of the farm. 
 
 Padre was already at the hedge, pacing in a jog. I had n't seem him so much as jog in a while, not with his old hips, but now he looked *young. * He was whining, too. 
 
 `` Padre!'' I called. `` Get back from there!'' 
 
 The country seemed peaceful, but there was no telling which ungodly animal might come crawling out of that forest. Everything from raccoons to coyotes. There were even reports of bears some years. 
 
 There was a rustling in the forest. Padre raced back to me and Jo, tucked his tail between his legs, and let out a whine. 
 
 I took my flashlight over to the forest hedge, hoping to get an idea of what we were up against. By then I noticed it was quiet. No more owl, no more rustling. Nothing. Silence. Then I heard it. A high, metallic scream, a shuddering that seemed to register on multiple frequencies. It went straight through my skin down to my bones. 
 
 I ran to the telescope. Whatever had made that noise, I did n't want any part of it. 
 
 Padre and Jo were n't there. They were near the house, standing tall, tails high, looking at the forest. They were hysterical. 
 
 They were barking.

title: story-115
text:
Dateline: North Korea. North Korean scientists today announced that they have created the world ’ s first functional time machine, capable of both forward and backward time travel. The lead scientist on the project, Jun Ki Seok, had this to say, “ The glory of the state allowed us the technology to create the world first time machine. Kim Jung Un call me personal, order machine made. ” 
 
 The North Korean government offered a press release in which it warned the “ Western World to be afraid for [ it ’ s ] very existence. ” 
 
 Jon looks up from the paper. “ Hey Honey, North Korea perfected time travel! I guess we ’ re screwed now, eh? ” 
 
 Mary, Jon ’ s wife, laughs. “ That ’ s even worse than those ballistic missiles of theirs that can almost reach the ocean! ” 
 
 -- 
 
 Jun Ki Seok looked at the machine much like a man looks at his first child, minutes after the birth. It is clear that he is completely and utterly devoted. 
 
 “ This will change the world. Sway the balance of power. With this machine, we will drive the capitalist government of South Korea into the sea, and liberate our brethren from their clutches. ” 
 
 His comrade, Wook Jin Seung, agreed, staring at the machine with the same reverence. Nearby, a sergeant was haranguing his men, preparing them to go through the portal, into the past. June 25th, 1950 glowed in bright red numerals above the machine ’ s gate. 
 
 The machine itself was spectacularly unimpressive. About thirty foot square and 8 feet tall, it was mostly featureless, a dull but somehow amorphous gray. The only notable portions on the machine was a giant lever next to a bluish-gray oval-shaped gate, with a large LED screen on top. Next to the lever sit 8-one digit spinners, like one would find on the lock for a briefcase. It was with these small spinners that the date was set. 
 
 The giant lever would be pulled to activate the gate, whereupon massive sums of power generated by a nuclear reactor in the basement would channel directly into the machine via a massive trunk line, and a bright emerald green light would pulse out of the gate, too bright to comfortably look at. 30 seconds later, the bright light would disappear, and the machine would be rested for 48 hours, lest…unfortunate things, occur. 
 
 The machine had been tested, extensively prior to the international announcement. Full-color pictures of ancient wonders, of Egyptian pyramids in construction, of Teutonic knights battling valiantly, of massive dinosaurs stomping gracelessly across Pangea. 
 
 Despite the evidence brought back by the exploratory teams, the world treated the North Korean announcement with derision. To Jun Ki Seok, that was the final straw. He had always been frustrated by the world not taking his homeland seriously, but his scientist ’ s mind could see why. 
 
 But now, when confronted with hard, incontrovertible evidence of North Korean greatness, the world still laughed. 
 
 And so they would pay. And the first step of that, 150 of North Korea ’ s most elite troops, armed to the hilt with modern weaponry and armor, were about to step though the time portal to June 25th, 1950. They would give North Korea what was needed to not only push the Americans and the UN back to the Pusan Perimeter, but out to sea. 
 
 But Kim Jung Un ’ s plans stopped not at merely winning the Korean War. No, he plotted further than that. He prepared technical teams, full of modern technology, both domestic and foreign, which would jumpstart Korea into the modern age over sixty years before the rest of the world. No army of the world, rooted in the technology of the 1940s and 50s would be able to stand before the might of the Korean army, armed with guided missiles, modern rifles, and helicopters. 
 
 Kim Jung Un arrived at the complex. The troops, raring at the bit to return to the past and raise their homeland to its proper place in the world, could not help but to cheer. Their Dear Leader would personally pull the lever which would catapult them into the past, into history, the future, their destiny. 
 
 -- 
 
 The fighting was intense. To be fair to the American forces, even when fighting against technology from over sixty years in the future, they didn ’ t surrender. The modern Koreans took casualties, but the Americans took more. 
 
 And every 48 hours, North Korea of 2014 would send as many troops and supplies into the past as they could. A line of troops stood by the machine. The machine would be activated, and men would rush through, yelling war cries. The passage to the past took 3 seconds. Any in transit when the machine shut down would come though at the next opening, gaunt and insane. 
 
 But that stopped none of the troops from charging into the machine up until the very instant it closed; they knew their duty…and they did not know of the effects of being trapped in the machine. 
 
 By the end of 1951, the United States formally surrendered in Korea. 
 
 By 1960, the Koreans, working with the Chinese, had captured all of Europe. In the final, desperate battles, the Warsaw Pact and NATO forces battled desperately, side-by-side. But their technology, M48 Pattons and T-55 MBTs were simply no match for T-90s and Chinese Type-96s, the technology to build the modern monsters of war having been sent through before the Korean War had even ended. 
 
 In 1963, the United States was invaded. In the Second World War, Japanese Admiral Yamamato had argued against an invasion of the United States, as there would be a “ rifle behind every blade of grass. ” This proved to be correct. Despite having technology still almost unbelievable to the Americans, despite having fought against it for months in Europe, the United States did not surrender. 
 
 The military was defeated within months, not having fully recovered from the thrashing it had received in Europe. The many expatriate military units that were rescued from Europe and brought to the United States fought as hard as they could, knowing that if America fell, there would be no hope for their ever returning home. 
 
 But it simply wasn ’ t enough. 
 
 The decimated remains of the Allied forces dispersed into the hills, armed civilians, and began a guerilla war. 
 
 They fought for ten years. Tens of thousands of Americans were killed in retaliation attacks. But finally, as all guerilla armies deprived of external support must, the resistance collapsed. The rate of loss of arms, men, and supplies simply couldn ’ t be kept up with by the small, underground shops of the resistance. 
 
 The world settled down, controlled by a joint Korean-Chinese government. 
 
 -- 
 
 In the present, no one realized that anything was amiss. The continuum of time meant that each change was not a new development, but simply the way it was. A few individuals, however, somehow, could see the changes taking place. But no material detailing things the way they were survived; how could a photograph exist of an event that never occurred? The sensitive individuals were simply chalked up as insane. The past ’ s takeover of the present continued unabated. 
 
 -- 
 
 Jon looks up from the paper. “ Hey Honey, Dear Leader is announcing that the food Five-Year Plan has been beaten by 17 %. Isn ’ t that wonderful? ” 
 
 “ I knew that projection would get beaten, the State ’ s farmers and workers are indomitable! Glory to Western Korea! ” 
 
 “ Glory to Western Korea! ” 
 
 
 Edit: Had to remove prompt from the top.

title: story-116
text:
I've always been interested in space, actually, I've been obsessed ever since I was old enough to speak. My father and I would go out and camp, we would bring laser pointers, binoculars, a camera and my most prized possession: my telescope. 
 
 Building on top of my obsession of star gazing came a desire to touch the stars, and so began my journey of going to space. Every day was training day. Wake up, work out, school, homework, workout, extra math, sleep. Every day in high school played out the same way. By the time I got to college I was at my peak physical and menal state. I majored in astronomy and mathematics and continued my quest. There's no point in talking much about schooling, it was fairly repetative. I graduated in 2020 with a masters in applied mathmatics and aeronautical physics. I began to apply to jobs at NASA, Boeing, virgin etc. not surprisingly I got a job offer at NASA. They wanted me to be a satellite designer, to use lay and terms. This was not exactly what I wanted but it was a well paying job, a foot in the door, and a key to the space exploration network. 
 
 By this point it was 2055, I had been working at NASA for around 12 years at this point. The U.S. governemt had decided to reintroduce the manned space program to search for platinum on the outer planets of our solar system. The technology definitely allowed for it, but the drive had never been there for the previous 30 years so we'd never gone past Mars. Well that was about to change. 
 
 I applied for the mission. I was accepted. 
 
 I began training, not that it was needed because i was still extremely fit. ( Sorry, I know I sound cocky, but I'm just that confident in my abilities ). 
 
 All 5 of us were ready, trained, excited, and itching to get going. Launch day came. We were sent off with thunderous applause to'save the world'. Little did they know. 
 
 Years go by and we are almost there. Almost at pluto ( which is a planet now, who knows what they'll call it tomorrow ). 
 
 There was no movie like bull shit, no crew fighting, no aliens, no catastrophic space ship failures. It was smooth sailing. 
 The one weird thing was the stars. I had never lost my obsession with the stars. They had seemed... Strange... After we got past Jupiter. They seemed to grow in diameter every few hundred thousand miles. Nothing major and we just attributed it to speed and space being space. 
 
 The day came when we reached pluto. We landed, looked around, did all the bull shit we were sent to do. But the thing that started bugging everyone was the stars again. They had continued to grow until the looked like the size of cars. The light was very large but not brighter than normal. 
 
 We voted unanimously to go further than our mission allowed, we went out of the solar system for the first time in human history. Call it abrupt, silly even, but all of a sudden we just kind of... Stopped. Not looked as though we had bumped up against a TV screen. The stars were now huge gaping holes in the blacness but they were impassable. 
 
 We looked up, down, left and right and all we say was a gradually sloping wall of white patches. 
 
 We had discovered the'edge of the universe''. It was as if we were in a ball of nothings which had a finite limit. My whole life I had thought that the sky was limitless. That there was no *end* to it all. But we had found'it'. 
 
 We decided to head back. We needed to tell everyone and anyone what we had found. When we turned around to head back our ion engine fired on the'wall'. Little did we notice that the white had begun expanding and a new'star' had been created. Out of this white hole came a blinding light, a wave of something. 
 
 **Here the diary ends, we are unsure if this is simply a delusional person's ranting. The fact that the U.S. government has never sent a mission to Pluto indicates that to be true. I will show this to the chair of NASA and see if this has any merit, doubtful as it is. - Agent 1578 US Secret Service. April 11, 2046** 
 
 -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- - 
 
 Edit: this is my first story and I know it's pretty shitty. If you have questions about the plot or suggestions let me know. Thank you.

title: story-117
text:
Nazareth was n't sure what he was looking at. It was text, but it made no sense to his eyes. The serif of the font assaulted his eyes. It was so... brutish, so rough compared to their polished galactic alphabet. 
 
 He turned to his companion. `` Franz? What have we got here?'' Another man joins him, teleporting across the long, underground room. He shakes his blond hair out of his face and his AnalyzLens slides out of the side of his head, aligning perfectly with his left eye. 
 
 `` Hmm...'' he said, his eyes carefully taking note of each letter. 
 
 `` This is serif font, is n't it?'' asked Nazareth. Being a typographer in his spare time, he knew all about the fonts used in the olden days of the early 21st century. He vaguely recognized the font; it was one of the most popular fonts back in the day when people raved over desktop and laptop computers. 
 
 Franz nodded, and the lens retreated into its socket, the little space closing up. `` Yes, Nazareth,'' he replied. `` It is serif font, and I sent a snapshot over to the main group. They've got a translation.'' 
 
 Nazareth almost jumped at the news. They were finally starting to uncover the mysteries of the early 21st, which was as big a mystery now as the origin of the universe was back then. An electric pulse of thrill ran down his titanium-reinforced spine. 
 
 `` Apparently, it reads, and I quote,'Man, are future archaeologists going to be confused!''' Franz looked up with a confused expression. `` What?'' 
 
 Nazareth was just as confused. `` Okay,'' he started. `` This room is filled with these old'computer' gadgets and loads of partially new pictures. We translate the single piece of text we get, and it's... mocking us?'' 
 
 Franz nodded once. `` It seems so,'' he said. `` Barbarians. Was this an attempt at humor?'' Nazareth shrugged. 
 
 `` I honestly do n't give a damn,'' he replied. `` We're not leaving this site till we've figured out all this.'' Franz shrugged. 
 
 `` Fine,'' he replied, his lens once more sliding out. `` Let's start.'' Nazareth mentally activated his memory storage neurons, and fed in everything he could lay his eyes on. 
 
 *These people did n't even have a reinforced skeleton. * *They were n't even upgraded. * *The only idiots who were even close to predicting the future were those Transhumanists, and they were shunned by the society. * 
 
 He quickly walks over to a rather cuboidal, plastic device. It was black, and centuries of dust coated the thing. It had a groove in the middle, and hinges behind the groove. 
 
 *I'd wager you could open this thing. * 
 
 He willed his fingers to change shape and thin to slide into the groove. Then, he gently pulled upwards, and the old plastic squeaked as it opened. Nazareth knew that the hinges were weak, and he knew that people of that era had no knowledge of Floats, floating projections that could be manipulated by hand or mind as per the user's will. 
 
 He held it up to his eyes, and he saw several oddly shaped holes in the side of the device. Clearly, these were some kind of primitive connection ports. Nazareth checked the front of the device and spotted a smaller port. A few specks of white paint indicated that some text had been there long ago. 
 
 He looked up at Franz, but he seemed to be busy analyzing the wall material, probably checking for structural integrity. *That's not my problem. * He went back to the device he had picked up. 
 
 His own AnalyzLens slid out from a small space in his head and stopped right in the spot where his focus naturally fell. He turned on various filters, trying to see what the text might have read. Eventually, he made out a symbol with the carbon filter. 
 
 *An SD card? * *Is n't it one of those old memory cards? * Nazareth quickly slipped in one of the many portable power cards he'd bought with him. The power card fitted perfectly and it instantly started generating power, switching on the device. The screen lit up and after a few words of text flashed up on the screen, a familiar layout met his eyes. 
 
 *A desktop! * Nazareth was a historical technician, meaning he specialized in olden technology. This line of work was mainly academic, but in a world where money, food or air were n't necessities, it mattered much. 
 
 He mentally gave instructions to the power card to open a few files on the desktop. A small triangular symbol started moving around the screen, which beamed harsh, unmuted light into his eyes. *I honestly wonder how people put up with this light. * *Did n't their eyes strain? * 
 
 A file opened, now revealing to him many pictures. He squinted at them carefully, constricting his pupil so that too much light could n't enter. He saw many pictures, and with them, shades of color that his eyes had never feasted upon before. 
 
 He did n't even think that so many shades were possible. They were certainly not associated with his daily life. He remembered tales from the streets, where some men talked about'trees' and'streams'. They talked about colors, and such fantastical things that he was convinced that the other men was off their rockers. 
 
 `` Franz,'' he managed, after a long time. `` Look.'' Franz stopped his observation of the wall and walked towards Nazareth. 
 
 `` Blazes,'' he cursed. `` It's like a star. Ca n't you mute the light?'' Nazareth shook his head. 
 
 `` Franz, forget the light. Look at the color.'' Franz looked, and his eyes narrowed. 
 
 `` It's unnatural,'' he decided. `` These are n't colors; these are abominations! There's no slate, pute, graxt or gray!'' Nazareth nodded. 
 
 `` Exactly. I do n't even know what to call them.'' Nazareth stood up. He looked at all the plastic coated pictures stuck to the wall. `` Look at these. They're from the time our great-grandparents were children, and even then there's just pute and slate.'' 
 
 Nazareth turned to the small, primitive screen; this time, he was awed. `` There's is n't a trace of that here.'' Franz nodded. 
 
 `` What are those... projections, anyway?'' asked Franz. Nazareth wagered a guess. 
 
 `` From what I know, those would fit the description for'trees'. Or at least the whole thing is a'tree'. And those are apparently oxygen-producing organisms that were vital to our existence.'' Nazareth sat down for a while, his chrome body at odds with the rugged stone ground. 
 
 `` Were n't'trees' the first thing that went with the Great Warming?'' asked Franz. Nazareth thought for a moment. 
 
 The Great Warming was how historians described the period when the Earth's temperature had risen to absurd levels. It had killed most of the previous life on Earth, except the very first of the modern humans. 
 
 The 21st century fell right at the beginning of the peak of the Warming, and it was possible that older humans wandered the Earth at the time, coexisting with these'trees'. 
 
 `` Not quite,'' corrected Nazareth. `` The first ones to go were a group of animals who lived near the poles of the planet. They were adapted to frigid temperatures and they could n't hold out. Then, the trees went.'' 
 
 Franz's AnalyzLens slid back into its place. He deactivated his contact lenses. `` Nazareth, look,'' he prompted. `` Deactivate your lenses!'' 
 
 Nazareth obliged and looked at the screen afresh. The fresco of colors jumped out at him in all their vividness and splendor. Some part of his mind instinctively recognized the shades. 
 
 Without the various lenses and their constant corrections to his eyesight, the colors seemed almost *natural*. He had forgotten what his eyes were capable of on their own. He felt a kind of tingling in his eyes as his brain reveled in the glory of shades. 
 
 He could n't put names to them, but they brought feelings of freshness and coolness. He heard Franz sit down beside him and stare at the screen. True, it was terrible technology, but that one picture made up for it all. 
 
 `` So, this was what it all looked like...'' he wondered, his eyes hungrily taking in every hue. `` It's... beautiful.'' 
 
 `` And to think that those people did n't do jack to stop this fading away,'' added Franz, incredulous. Suddenly, that line he read earlier made so much sense. 
 
 *Man, are future archaeologists gon na be confused! * 
 
 *Not confused, * corrected Nazareth, in his mind. *Shocked. * *Shocked that they did nothing to save it all. *

title: story-118
text:
“ Get ready to go Tommy, ” I said to my son. It was his 6th birthday and I was taking him to a surprise birthday party at the local Laser-Kart, a laser tag go-kart hybrid emporium, and he was dragging ass. I went to the kitchen to grab my phone and keys and came back to find Tommy playing with his hot wheels and shoeless. “ C ’ mon, Tom. Let ’ s get going, ” I said in my kindest voice, although I wanted to strangle him at the moment. Surprises and kids just don ’ t mix. Tell him he ’ s getting a party and he bugs me for a week; don ’ t say anything and it ’ s hard to convince him to get his butt in gear. A lose lose I suppose. 
 
 “ Awe, Dad, ” Tommy whined. “ It ’ s my birthday! I don ’ t wan na go anywhere! ” 
 
 “ What if it ’ s for your birthday? ” I asked. I figured that I would let a little bit slide or doom myself to the house for the rest of the day. 
 
 Tommy ’ s eyes lit up, “ Really? No jokes? ” 
 
 “ Guess you ’ ll have to put those shoes on to find out! ” I said and tickled his sides. A child ’ s trust is absolute, good thing I wasn ’ t messing him. 
 
 “ Okay! ” Tommy jumped up. “ Come help me tie my shoes. ” 
 
 “ You ’ re 6 now, ” I said. 
 
 “ I wasn ’ t talking to you, Dad! ” Tommy snorted indignantly. “ I was talking to Spikes, ” He said it with that understood DUH in his tone. 
 
 Tommy ’ s imaginary friend, Spikes, had been born right around a year ago when his grandmother passed. I had thought that he had forgotten him by now, but evidently not. I knew it was a coping mechanism... or a demon trying to consume his soul and I was strongly rooting against the latter. I opened my mouth to say something, but he was doing as I asked and my brain advised me against it. 
 
 “ Ready! ” Tommy shouted. “ Can Spikes come in the car with us? Puhlease!!! ” 
 
 I had come up with an interesting way to keep Tommy from playing with Spikes in public. Not that there is anything wrong with imaginary friends, but if you ’ re the parent of a kid without them it ’ s like you are part of an elite group or something. I had told Tommy that Spikes wasn ’ t allowed in the car because we didn ’ t have an adequate seat for him and it had seemed to do the trick. He had fought, of course, but in the end he conceded and Spikes stayed home. 
 
 “ Please, Dad! Please! ” Tommy must ’ ve taken my moment of reflection as a no. “ It ’ s my biiirrrtthhhhdaaaaay! ” 
 
 I sighed. He had gotten me. To say no on a birthday is the highest form of treason, “ Sure. But only because it ’ s your birthday, ” I added quickly. Tommy jumped up and down, grabbed an imaginary hand, and bolted out the front door to the car. I couldn ’ t help but smile and I headed out the door after him. 
 
 I unlocked the car and ducked down into the driver ’ s seat. I bit my tongue to cage the slew of curses I would ’ ve otherwise let fly had I been sans Tommy. My wife had pulled the seat too close and I slammed my knees into the dash board. I pulled the lever under the chair and it slid back with no opposition and I rubbed my knee as I sat. Tommy jumped into the back passenger seat where his booster chair was and closed the door behind him. I turned the key and shifted the car into drive… 
 
 “ Wait for Spikes, Dad! ” Tommy said. The strain was thick in his voice. 
 
 “ Didn ’ t he get in with you? ” I asked. 
 
 “ No. His door is locked. ” The cynicism had returned. 
 
 “ Oops, ” I said and unlocked the door. My heart sank into my bowels as I watched the door directly behind my swing open. I panicked. I threw the car into reverse and felt a thud under my front tires as I exited the driveway and Tommy let out a blood curdling scream. 
 
 “ SPIIIIIIIKEEEESSSSS! DAD YOU RAN OVER SPIKES! ” Tommy was in hysterics. His belt was undone and his door open before I had time to process what had happened. 
 
 I threw open the door, “ Tommy… ” I started to yell before all of the air was sucked out of my lungs. There in the middle of my driveway was a growing pool of blood. The red was so deep it appeared black against the afternoon sun. Tommy had his hands over the expanse and they seemed to be laying on a physical object. 
 
 “ You killed Spikes! You killed Spikes. YOU KILLED HIM! ” The fear and rage in his voice was immense. 
 
 “ Tommy, ” I tried as my eyes filled with tears. I tried to speak, but my mouth just opened and closed like a marionette waiting for his voice to be given to him. Spikes wasn ’ t real, he wasn ’ t. How could you kill something that didn ’ t exist?! Tommy ran inside. Small blood stained shoe prints were all he left in his wake. I stood in horror as I watched the blood begin to run in streams down the driveway towards me. A miserable impressionists mural stained on my drive. I put one hand to my forehead and the only rational thought I had to cope with this insanity was that it looked like we would be cancelling his party after all.

title: story-119
text:
Every time I died was like a dream. Moments of flaring emotions; screaming, shouting; too many things to see. So vivid in my mind, and yet so distorted. Caricatures of myself, with the smallest differences to me. 
 
 For whatever reason, I could n't go down quietly. Not a death went by that did n't end in bloodshed. Sometimes, more than just mine. It did n't make sense that when I woke up, drenched in sweat, I could feel the scar left behind. Life and reason were n't really the best of friends, so I accepted it. 
 
 The reminders were hard to forget. Those other me-s had their own lives. People they wanted to protect more than anything in the world. A happiness that had been shattered. It hurt to think about. 
 
 Maybe that avoidance had led to the scars increasing. Used to be a couple of times a year, then barely a month without a new one, and now every week—more or less. 
 
 Hard to think of those other people being me though. They failed, and I was n't gon na do that any time soon. No one close to me, no one I loved, no one to lose. Hard to die fighting with nothing to fight for. The world would be fine without me, and I could stick to myself, off in some quiet place far off the maps. 
 
 Packed my bag full of what would fit. No room for sentimentality. 
 
 Brushed aside the tent flap, dawn greeting me. The air stank. Mud would n't let go easily. Clouds loomed, threatening to open up at any moment. I'd had better greetings, all things considered. Looking like I had somewhere to go made me almost invisible to what early risers there were around the camp. 
 
 Almost invisible. 
 
 I could n't ignore the hand on my shoulder. Or, the soft voice asking, “ Where're you going? ” 
 
 Many thoughts went through my mind. Threads of conversation and where they would lead. In the end, I went on the offensive. “ You know how they say when someone you love dies, part of you dies with them? ” 
 
 A moment of silence. “ Y-yes? ” 
 
 “ That's wrong. You die too. You are n't the same as you were before. You'll never be the same. You'll never think the same. You'll never feel the same way ever again. ” I paused, removing the hand from my shoulder. “ If that's not death, I do n't know what is. ” 
 
 No reply, no one stopping me from leaving. 
 
 A quiet cabin in the woods, far from civilisation—that thought sounded nice. Somewhere where I would n't die for many more years, and even then just the once. Peace, at last.

title: story-120
text:
The most frightening part was the suddenness of the water. No, this is just too much to jump in to; let me back up. 
 
 I woke up, showered, picked up some coffee and went to work like every morning. There were a few clouds, but otherwise it was a beautiful April day. 
 
 Everyone in the office seemed fine. We were all excited for the game later tonight, Steelers and Broncos. 
 
 I was working on quarterly reports when the first drops hit my windows. I say MY windows because I have a corner office and watched it all from the beginning. Believe me, what I'm about to say is no exaggeration. 
 
 Water started falling from the sky. 
 
 There was no warning, no explanation on the TV, nothing. Of course, Jim immediately pulled up a map on the news' website, but they were just as confused as we were. What made it worse was that the falling water was localized, only a few square miles, centered directly over our city. 
 
 Of course, by this point, we were all crowded around the windows, not even the boss was telling us to get back to work. 
 
 Now, I've never been very religious, so I thought the reaction of the Church across the street was a little eccentric, but at least they tried to explain it. They were having a mid-week meeting or something, and as soon as the water started falling they were outside, yelling up at the sky. Whether they were calling it a sign or a curse, I do n't know, but man, they sure were excited. 
 
 While we were watching the church people were having their... whatever, Craig noticed none of the animals outside seemed bothered. There was a dog walking around, a few birds and squirrels in the trees, but they did n't seem to care about getting wet. 
 
 Anyway, the falling water kept going, all day. It stopped around 8, but you've never seen so many car accidents on the highway as I did driving home from work. 
 
 For the first time in years we actually watched national news on TV that night. Apparently we were n't the only affected area. They had a map with hot spots that were hit around the country. 
 
 The Northwest seemed to be the worse off, with inches of water collected and hundreds of fatalities. A few cities reported falling ice or some sort of frozen, puffy water, but I think that's just exaggeration. 
 
 The President is expected to address the nation in a few minutes, and the Governor announced a state of emergency for our area, effective immediately. We do n't know what the falling water meant, or what it means, but all we can do is hope for the best. 
 
 -251
