title: story-121
text:
I begin at the end. 
 
 The end is this: a clock, a chair, and a man. A man sits in a chair and watches the clock. A man remembers, he is old and has much to remember. The clock ticks, and a man is no more. 
 
 In his house, a man has much and nothing. Small wooden statues are scattered throughout his house. A stag, a bird, a hare. Crudely cut and badly made. A man whittled, often but without talent. Still, a man enjoyed whittling as it was not nothing. A man's children would find a stag, a bird, a hare, and they would keep them as tokens of their father. One day, a man's children's children would move from one house to another, and a stag, a bird, a hare would be left behind in dusty boxes. 
 
 Before, a man was old but not so old. He could still travel and would visit his children and see his children's children. He would speak to them and they would nod, if not out of interest then out of duty. He spoke of stories they'd heard hundreds of times. He spoke because they listened, and because stories not told now would not be told. 
 
 Before, a man shared a house with a woman. A man sometimes fought with a woman. A man would be furious beyond words and would cringe at the sound of a woman's voice. But rage would fade and a man would miss a woman's voice. They lived in a city with thousands. A man told himself he liked cities, liked that they kept him active, but secretly to himself he longed for quiet. He longed for the slow days of country sides and the languid conversations of trees and cows. A man's children had weddings, and a man and a woman traveled to new cities. A man complained much about planes, and prices, and politics, but a man was happy to see his children and they were happy to see him. 
 
 Before, a woman was pregnant and a man was afraid. A man worked many hours, and was very tired. A woman used to work but had to stop due to the weight in her stomach, and now a man had to work more hours and be more tired. A man did not yet have children, and did not know what it was like to have them. Sometimes, a man wished he could be a child so that he did not have to work many hours, did not have be very tired, and did not have to be afraid. 
 
 Before, a man did not know the future. A man did not know where he would be in a year, and did not know where he would find money in a year, and did not know who he would be in a year. But, a man had met a woman, and when a woman smiled, a man smiled. 
 
 Before, a man was a boy. A boy jumped off a swing and held his arm straight to protect his face. A boy landed hard and a bone cracked. A boy cried, and a woman rushed to comfort a boy. A boy went to school the next day and smiled as children signed a cast. 
 
 Before, a man was a baby. A baby was eight pounds with tears and screams. A man held a baby as a woman fell asleep. 
 
 I move on to the next grave. 
 
 I begin at the end...

title: story-122
text:
*Your ride will arrive in 5 minutes. * 
 
 Todd let his phone drop into his jacket pocket, but pulled it out and checked his ride-sharing app ten seconds after he had received and cleared the notification. 
 
 Thunder snapped suddenly overhead from the spring rainstorm which had been pouring non-stop since lunchtime. It startled Todd enough that he kicked over his cloth grocery bag, spilling the contents across the ground. The short, mad scramble Todd made kept almost all of his groceries out of the pouring rain and beneath the grocery store ’ s overhang. One orange rolled into the rain, and Todd was able to grab it while getting soaked only to the elbow. 
 
 Reassuring himself that he was not afraid of a spring rainstorm, Todd shook the rainwater off the orange and dropped it into the bag. He was afraid of what was out in the rainstorm. Six people in as many days had died under mysterious circumstances in town. When your town is only about twenty-five thousand people, it ’ s still small enough that the statistic becomes terrifying. The coin-operated machine just outside the grocery store ’ s entrance held the local paper inside the glass pane bearing the headline, SIX DEAD IN SIX DAYS, and sub-headed, FBI SENDS PROFILER OUT TO HUNT POTENTIAL SERIAL KILLER. 
 
 A crime scene photograph was halved by the newspaper ’ s fold, sparing passersby from seeing a body under a sheet or tarp or even a chalk outline. Todd knew the details, though. Everyone in town did. 
 
 The local police had made no connection between the six victims as of press time. County Sherriff Jim Simmonds had advised people of the need to be alert at all times, travel in pairs and groups when possible, and to say something if they see something. There wasn ’ t much in the way of substance he had been able to offer to calm the community since the words “ serial killer ” swept through the towns. The advice had taken strong root already: Todd had been watching husbands walking with their wives through the rain, their heads on swivels to search for suspicious figures, and moms hustling their children to the car faster than even a rainstorm like this demanded. 
 
 *Your ride will arrive in 2 minutes. * 
 
 Todd didn ’ t have anyone like that. He was single and lived just a few blocks off one of the main roads in town, in a modest house in the suburban, “ Main Street, USA ” downtown. The narrow little bungalow-style house with brick porch and street-side parking was a remnant of the 70s, or so he thought. Sometimes Todd thought it was an apt metaphor for his life: quiet, comfortable, and invisible because it was squeezed in-between so many others just like it. There wasn ’ t anything terrible about that life, but it wasn ’ t exciting, and Todd had long since come to terms with that. 
 
 The excitement that had come to town was the kind Todd never wanted. Precious few things terrify humans as much as when we ’ re alone, and one of those things is dying – or being killed. Todd had been feeling that since the local paper announced the possibility of a serial killer on the fourth day of suspicious and unexplained deaths. He felt alone, and he felt hunted. Almost everyone in town felt the same thing, but Todd speculated, watching those mothers and husbands and children, that they had forgotten the unique fear that comes with being alone. 
 
 
 The sensation grew worse under dark clouds and pouring rain when people already afraid huddle tighter into themselves, away from possible dangers that bump in the night and are revealed only in silhouettes of flashing lightning. 
 
 It was the reason Todd had chosen to use the ride-sharing app. All of the app ’ s drivers in the area had to be a local, and Todd made sure that the driver assigned to him had a high rating and plenty of trips made on record. He wasn ’ t going to be caught making the trip home alone, to be preyed on by a serial killer in the few blocks to or from the grocery store. 
 
 *Your ride has arrived. Your driver will wait 2 minutes. Enjoy the ride! * 
 
 Todd stared out through the sheets of pouring rain at the car that had pulled up. It was a black electric-hybrid sedan that rolled up silently through the striped pedestrian zone. Todd didn ’ t even hear the sound of its tires through over the wet pavement, and thought it was because of the downpour ’ s own sound. The sedan ’ s hazard lights went on, waiting for its passenger. 
 
 Drawing out his phone again, Todd held up one finger to the car. He couldn ’ t see the driver, but the ride-sharing app was able to match the license plate and the car ’ s make, model, and color. The driver ’ s profile picture belonged to a man named Han, someone who might once have been considered classically handsome, but had let himself become overweight, with a face slightly plump and doughy. Even squinting through the rain and windows, Todd couldn ’ t make the driver ’ s face out. 
 
 With everything else checking out, Todd decided he could get in the car and go home, safe from being serial killed. 
 
 The three or four steps it took Todd to get from the grocery store into the car ’ s back seat soaked him nearly head to toe, even soaked through his jacket, along with his reusable grocery bag. The bag went on the floor behind Han the Driver as Todd slid in behind the passenger seat with a sigh. Slicking back his wet hair, Todd offered an apology for getting Han ’ s car damp. 
 
 Looking at his driver, Todd was able to confirm his Han ’ s soft and chubby profile. The man had a deathly pallor that Todd chalked up to too much winter and a very cold rain, certain that he also looked pale and clammy from his own wait in the elements. Han benefitted from a scarf around his neck, leaving Todd wishing he ’ d had the same foresight to confront the weather with. Todd visibly relaxed into his seat as the car pulled away from the grocery store. 
 
 *You will reach your destination in 5 minutes. * 
 
 “ Thanks a ton. You ’ re totally a lifesaver. Literally. I would have caught my death of cold in this storm, if I didn ’ t catch my death of serial murder out there. You hear about? ” Todd forced a laugh out, in trying to force a conversation with his driver. 
 
 For his part, Han made a noncommittal cough. Or a snorting laugh. Todd wasn ’ t sure. 
 
 “ Okay. Fair enough. Pure professionalism. That ’ s cool, man. Sorry. I get it. Thanks again. And sorry again for making your car wet. I hope business will make being out in this worth it. ” 
 
 *You will reach your destination in 2 minutes. * 
 
 Todd could almost feel Han ’ s eyes reflected on him in the rearview mirror. Todd projected that Han was annoyed, with his banter and bad attempt at humor. Todd stopped talking for the next few minutes, as the ride home passed in silence. 
 
 Looking around the car, and out the windows, Todd noticed the car ’ s gearshift was a novelty item: a human spine, covered in silver paint. The top of it was capped with a skull. Todd felt like he understood. A hybrid was a practical-but-boring car, a lot like his own life. You have to make yourself feel like you ’ re still a rebel once in a while. He ’ d bought himself a motorcycle jacket a few years back because it made him feel just a little more awesome than his boring life. Todd felt, as the car turned onto his street, that he understood Han ’ s quiet, tough-guy professionalism a little bit better now. 
 
 Han pulled the car up and shifted the spine into park, and looked into the rearview at Todd. 
 
 “ Thanks man. Soon as I get on my porch and get my phone out, I ’ ll rate you five stars, especially since you came out in this garbage. You ’ re awesome! Thanks! ” 
 
 Todd slicked his hair back one last time, took two deep breaths, pushed open the door and grabbed his groceries in one movement. Climbing three steps to the short walkway, he thought he heard a car door open. Two more long strides, and he hit the three small concrete steps up to his bungalow. 
 
 *You have reached your destination. * 
 
 Safely under the dry porch roof, Todd dug out his phone and turned around to show Han he was doing the review already as promised, having pressed the five-star rating as he held it up to show off towards the black electric-hybrid sedan. He froze when he looked out on the street. 
 
 Han was standing next to his car, with the driver ’ s door open in the pouring rain. The scarf he ’ d worn was untangled and hanging off broad shoulders, and would have been looped around his neck had there been a neck to loop a scarf around. Han ’ s neck was still beneath his head, but his head was held by the hair in his outstretched right arm, over the hood of the car. 
 
 “ **TODD FORSYTHE WINTERS**, ” came a voice from the disembodied head. 
 
 Todd collapsed to the ground as the last syllable echoed through the pouring rain. His phone dropped to the porch from his hand and the grocery bag tumbled down, spilling its contents once again. The same orange rolled off the porch and bounced down the three steps before coming to rest in the grass alongside the walkway. 
 
 Han placed his head atop his shoulders, and climbed back into the sedan. He buckled the seatbelt, and then activated the phone mounted on the dash, checking the ride-sharing app for another fare before putting the spine into drive and pulling away from the curb of Todd ’ s quiet, comfortable, invisible bungalow house. 
 
 *Review accepted. Thanks for riding! See you again soon! * 
 
 # # #

title: story-123
text:
You enter the celestial courthouse. You and billions of other dead humans sit, waiting for the trial of God. This was the big show trial the Nine Heavens had been waiting for and the place was packed to the rafters. The gods from Olympus had their own private box while the trial itself was being broadcast to every realm. Even Hell had the day off from eternal torture to watch the trial. God sat in the hot seat, fidgeting from side to side while the Justicars took their seats, their golden cloaks and pure white wigs radiating authority. The head Justicar held up a hand and silenced the din of billions. 
 
'Today, we sit in judgement of the God of the Abrahamic religions. He is called many names but for brevity and the good of all the people watching this trial, we shall just called him God.' The Justicar picked up a sheet of paper and put on his reading glasses.'You are to be judged today, by this panel and the audience sitting here, for your performance as God of planet 65439 or how it is colloquially known, Earth. We will start by asking you a few questions about your time as God of this planet, before opening up to the floor for an audience vote and then finishing with our verdict and your final judgement. So, God, how do you think you did?' 
 
'I think I did an admirable job.' he replied, looking up at his judges. The whole room erupted in a series of boos, cheers, jeers and jests. The noise of billions of souls all crying out was something to behold, the sheer force of sound rocking your very soul. The noise was stopped by the head Justicar slamming his gavel down on the bench. 
 
'I will have quiet in this courtroom! I understand we have many people in attendance but let the divinity speak. You'll have plenty of time for noise making during the audience vote. God, please proceed.' He cleared his throat and looked round the billions of eyes watching him, stroking his beard anxiously. 
 
'Well, I believe I did the best I could. Creation went fairly well, I can say the planet itself held up well, even if the beings on it did n't.' 
 
'That sounds like negligence to me.' the left Justicar said, looking down at its notes.'One recurring complaint from your charges on earth, is that you did n't look after them. From all accounts, you seemed to disappear from the scene somewhere after Creation and only popped in occasionally to either clean up the place with a flood or send a few natural disasters to keep people on their toes. Does n't sound like very caring to me.' 
 
'Well, the flood was a mistake on my part. I did n't quite get the first batch of humans right so I needed a bit of a do-over.' God replied, trying to remember pre-history. 
 
'That does n't help your case.' the right Justicar stated.'That just makes you sound incompetent.' 
 
'Well, it was my first go at sentient life, give me a bit of a break. I was n't going to get it right on the first go.' 
 
'Many people believe you are omnipotent and omniscient, this admission does n't help your claims.' 
 
'Well, everyone lies on their CV, surely?' A massive roar went up through the courthouse, as projectiles started to fly at the judged party. The head Justicar slammed his gavel again, the force of the blow shaking the entire courthouse. 
 
'I will not let this judgement be a farce! We got through Hades' judgement without all this rabble rousing, let's have some decorum.' Silence fell over the crowd again.'Thank you. Now, while you may not have taken care of the Earth that well, we can all agree you did a good job on the layout. Drinkable water, varied landscapes and a breathable atmosphere which could sustain life, a definite tick for that. We'll ignore global warning and all the nuclear fallout malarkey as that was n't technically your fault. However, as mentioned earlier, we must talk about your treatment of your creations as it's not so glowing.' 
 
 The Justicar to the left of the head rifled through his notes, finding the list of God's misdemeanors.'I mean, look at this list. Original sin, causing multiple factions to go to war over your word, not intervening with atrocities, the number of plagues and illnesses you unleashed on the world, actively neglecting the pleas for help from millions of your people. This does not make for good reading.' 
 
'I was young and irresponsible. I did n't know how to govern a sentient species properly! I thought the dinosaurs were hard work but I severely underestimated the problems the human race could cause. No offence, but you mortals do n't half mess things up.' God replied, gazing at the angry crowd. 
 
'Let's not forget the issues with your son.' the head Justicar interjected. The whole audience took a sharp intake of breath at this low blow.'Plus, the whole binding of Isaac thing was pretty underhand as well.' 
 
'I know, I know. I was reckless and trying to be a cool, mysterious deity like the Old Ones before me. It did n't come off as well as I'd hoped.' 
 
'Well, quite obviously, as seen by the audience reaction. Well, we will take a short recess and come back to talk more about your relationships with humanity and then the audience vote. Hopefully, everyone will have simmered down by then. Stay right where you are audience, and we will be back with the trial of God after these short messages!' 
 
 EDIT: Now with the end of the trial! 
 
 The recess was not short. Roughly a millenium had passed in the ad break, as the billions of souls, angels and other gods present in the courthouse were regaled with the benefits of Seraphim-brand Halo Wax. Jumbo screens had been placed up during the break, probably for the audience vote and angel mounted cameras had started to fly round the court, currently orbiting the sweating God. Souls with nothing to lose were trying to hand out betting slips for God's eventual judgement, with the top odds being that God would be forced to work for Satan for a cosmic cycle. The hubbub was interrupted as the three Justicars took to the stand again, as the excited silence fell upon the crowd. 
 
'Sorry for the length of the break everyone, it seems that Halo Wax adverts go on for longer than we expect.' The head Justicar said, looking straight into camera 1.'We are back with the trial that the cosmos has been waiting for, the judgement of the Abrahamic God, brought to you by Seraphim-brand Halo Wax. Now, let's talk more about your relationship with humanity.' 
 
 Many in the audience rubbed their hands, this was the moment they'd been waiting their whole afterlife to hear. 
 
'It's safe to say it has been fairly eventful.' The right Justicar said, looking back through his notes. We'll look over the early stuff, your hell-raising days in the Holy Land and consider your silent years. Did it ever occur to you to send a message to everyone? Just to tell them to calm down and stop killing each other?' God fiddled with his robe, starting up at the Jumbotron with his glistening face on. 
 
'I thought, that if I stayed silent, humans would eventually sort themselves out. I was trying to be a distant creator, not hovering over them all the time.' he replied, his mind whirring for answers. 
 
'I mean, that's understandable but after the 4th war fought in your name, surely enough was enough? People were being slaughtered because they believed a different paraphrasing of something you may have said! It seems reasonable to me to step in?' Many souls nodded in agreement. 
 
'Well, I reckon my creations would have the knowledge to realise that some of my saying are n't to be taken literally! It's their own fault for taking things so seriously...' God's answer was interrupted by a huge roar from the crowd. Billions of souls shouting in anger, frustration and bitter to their callous Creator. Even Satan felt sorry for a single millsecond, as he sat on his throne of flaming bodies watching the trial. 
 
'I think I've heard enough here. It's time to open in up to the audience. Those who think God should be judged favourably, let your voices be heard.' the head Justicar announced, as the cameras panned around the mass. A few pockets of noise could be heard, shouts of'We Love You God!' but no major feedback.'And now, those who think that God should be punished, let your voices be heard now.' 
 
 The sheer wave of noise nearly knocked God off his chair. Billions of curses in billions of languages, hundreds of projectiles being thrown at the judgement stand, chants of'Make Him Burn' filled the air. Even the Olympian Gods got into the angry mob, with Zeus throwing the odd thunderbolt in protest. The screams of the damned could be heard coming from Hell, as Satan lead his choir in hateful song. The Jumbotrons showed pictures of people in the crowd firing off abuse, while God sat rooted to his seat. 
 
 The Justicars' gavel broke the din.'I think we have heard enough. It is clear what the verdict is. Can we have a few moments of silence as we consider our judgement.' The Justicars turned away as the audience began to become rowdy again. Angelic guards began forming lines around the exit, as the Jumbotrons showed God, with the caption'Not So Almighty Now' at the bottom to the delight of the crowd. The Justicars turned back towards God, who had oceans of sweat pouring off him. 
 
'Our verdict is clear. For sheer callousness and distain for his creations, as well as neglect for his children and his duties, we judge you as a horrible God.' Cheers went up from the crowd, it descending into Pandemonium as they started to chant for his head.'As your punishment, we force you to live the life of every person you neglected and suffer through the pain that you inflicted upon them. Also, in a surprise double whammy punishment, Satan is allowed back into Heaven as you are not a proper judge of character. Please escort the judged out and may the public have mercy on your soul.'

title: story-124
text:
“ It ’ s time. ” 
 
 The king had heard the counsel enough. All of the royal advisors had told him it was time for him to set out. They had shut themselves off to the world once The Great War started. Old alliances fell apart as kingdoms scrambled to cobble together new trusts that would ultimately be broken as well. Bah. He had no need for it. His kingdom was small and far enough away that they posed no real threat and could offer no advantage to any side. Only one envoy had bothered to come asking for allegiance, but he was turned away. Who knew what happened to him. 
 
 And now his council was telling him it was time to reach out. Seventeen years had passed since the war had started, and the latest news they had received had come from the envoy fifteen years ago. He had appeared to come from the losing side. When the king refused to join his cause, the envoy hadn ’ t even bothered to threaten him with retribution. He had just dejectedly left. So for fifteen years, the king sat his small throne and his people had gone on with lives much unchanged from before the war. He was content to live out his days in isolation, keeping only to those in his land. 
 
 His son was not of the same mind. He was put on the council at eighteen, a year before the war started. That headstrong boy wanted to fight as soon as they heard wind of the war. Every meeting he advised they take up arms. 
 
 “ And which side do we join? ” 
 
 “ ANY! ” 
 
 He was summarily ignored. His consistent badgering to go outside the kingdom became white noise. The council was largely a reflection of the king. Comfortable. Sedentary. The son realized his brashness was interpreted as immaturity and as such anything out of his mouth would be dismissed. He sought to become a wiser councilor and deferred as much as possible, not giving voice to any opinions for a year or so, opting rather just to listen. When the envoy came, he bit his tongue, though he wanted to scream that they should do something, anything. 
 
 A years after the envoy left, he finally broached the subject. “ My King, perhaps it is time to venture out and gather news. ” 
 
 “ Bah, and for what reason? Why does it matter to us what happens outside of our walls? It is of no importance to us. ” 
 
 “ But surely we should see where things stand? ” 
 
 “ And what if the war still wages? We don ’ t want to put ourselves at risk. It is folly and I will hear no more of it. We are better off alone. ” 
 
 His son didn ’ t bring up leaving the kingdom for two more years. The same response from the king. 
 
 “ We have no need to know what has happened. ” 
 
 “ But aren ’ t you at least…curious? ” 
 
 The king stared at his son. “ Curiosity serves no purpose for the maintenance of the kingdom. ” He then turned away from his son and asked for an update on the progress of replacing the tapestries in the great hall. 
 
 His son began to slowly win over other councilors to his side in private discussions, but year after year, all requests to leave were refused. 
 
 Then the famine hit. 
 
 “ My king. We need to go out. We need to find resources. We need to establish trade. This is not a desire. It is a need. It is time. ” 
 
 He finally conceded. His son was to lead the party of four. They gathered what provisions they could and set off. 
 
 The old maps had the nearest town around three days away on horse. They got there and saw that it was overrun with weeds, a desolate place. They soldiered on to the nearest stronghold a little farther out. After two days, they reached a great keep, or rather, the ruins of one. 
 
 “ We haven ’ t come across a single living thing, ” the king ’ s son whispered. 
 
 “ It ’ s strange, isn ’ t it? Not one man, woman or child. ” 
 
 “ No. Not just that. *A single living thing*. No birds chirping. No creatures rooting about in the bush. Nothing. ” 
 
 The three other men looked at each other and tried to remember if they had seen anything. They had been traveling hard and hadn ’ t bothered to hunt, simply relying on their stores. 
 
 “ We should go back… ” 
 
 “ No, ” the king ’ s son said. “ No. Let ’ s head to the nearest kingdom this time. It ’ s only a couple more days of hard riding away. Keep on the lookout for…anything living. ” 
 
 They moved. The grim realization fueled their movements. They dared not stop lest they found themselves overcome with fear. They made good time and the silence of their trip just accentuated the fact that they were still the only living beings around. 
 
 They arrived. The kingdom before them easily dwarfed their own. The massive walls remained intact. The gates were closed, though there was no one to man them. 
 
 “ GOOD DAY! ” the king ’ s son cried out. No response. “ WE WOULD VERY MUCH WELCOME A MEETING WITH YOUR KING! ” Silence responded. 
 
 “ We ’ ll just let ourselves in then, ” he said to his companions. 
 
 The gate was locked. They were unfamiliar with this kingdom so they had no idea of any other entrance. 
 
 “ I shall climb over and open the gates for you. ” The king ’ s son took a rope and hook to scale the wall. 
 
 He climbed up and up, his arms burning from exertion, his mind burning from fear. He got to the top and heaved himself over. He looked down on the other side of the wall into the kingdom. He wept. 
 
 “ Sir! What do you see? ” came the cry from below. 
 
 The only response the men got from the king ’ s son was his body as he flung himself from the wall.

title: story-125
text:
First the texts. Then the MMS images. Then every insta, fb post, live stream, Reddit post, tweet. Every inbox at 0 % capacity as it was all FWD FWD FWD FWD: MOON all the time. 
 
 After a few days we were realized the vast majority of Internet traffic was solely automated spambots. Everybody else was outside looking at the moon, or sleeping all day wherever they last witnessed the moon. 
 
 Tritanopia is a form of color blindness that reduces the blue/yellow/green portion of the spectrum. 
 
 Us lucky one in ten thousand were unphased by the moon... Get it? Moon puns. 
 
 For reference, 
 1:10,000 expands to 
 100,000:1,000,000,000 
 
 And there's seven some billion people total, so you'd think seven hundred thousand people would be able to coordinate. 
 
 But then you have to look at population densities, distributive models of where tritanopia can be found, how difficult it is to travel when almost everyone is standing in the middle of the road to quietly worship the moon. 
 
 Imagine being at a festival with a target audience of docile septuagenarians. You do n't like the grateful dead, do n't get why 
 everyone is fixated, just want the whole thing to end. That's how it felt. It's like not being a hockey fan in Canada. 
 
 700,000 functioning humans remaining. All ages. All ability levels. The vast majority lacking applicable skills or the psychological tenacity required to face this world. I was only 12 when it happened, just on the cusp of being forged by the new world yet with fond memories of the old ways. 
 
 My first two weeks I tried to go about my routine as normal. Except there was no more no normal routine. No supply lines, no infrastructure, no social contract. Ran into a lot of lunatic strangers that got a start on the hoarding and mad max fashion early. My family had a close personal bond with either the moon or stolen wholesale liquor, depending on sight abilities. 
 
 A tritanopia support myphp forum briefly assembled IRL and tried to stage a coup of world power, but taking over the white house and the UN when there really is n't anyone to enforce your will does n't matter much. Nobody to answer the phone for the nuclear launch codes, nobody to pop in the 8.5'' floppy disks to get the nukes into the sky. Infighting led to the fast dissolution of that group, especially when the yahoo group insurrectionists gained traction. 
 
 The moonies just stopped participating. Beat them up, bash them to death in the streets, run them over. No resistance. Just single most minded dedication to the moon. A sadist's mcplayland. 
 
 They did n't eat or drink but they did n't die of exposure or dehydration. After a while their skin became ashy during the day. They went from monosyllabic grunts to utter silence. 
 
 A bit later, some of them grew wings or horns or scales. Some grew hair and became funky werewolf-gargoyle things. 
 
 After the transformations, they continued to stare at the moon. 
 
 Then came the noise. Somewhere between Gregorian chanting, Cthulhu summoning, and Tibetan throat singing. Constant, from sun down to sun up. 
 
 It was declared cured five or six times. They all cocooned out for a bit after the crop dusting misused some research. I was busy with the fight for survival, a sixteen year old keeping a nuclear reactor running on a submarine turned makeshift unethical medical experimentation laboratory. 
 
 Anyway, moonies came out of chrysalis fit as a fiddle, back to full health, lost all the medieval art features. Went back to work, spring in their step. And every night, back to the moon gazing. 
 
 Except they'd look at us and they would know. They would say `` better not look at the moon'' in the same deadpan attempt of reverse psychology. I'd reply `` What a beautiful night out'' while bug eyed stating at their moon. And sing about the moon hitting my eye like a big pizza pie. They just did not get it did not work on my snarky 19 year old deficient peepers. That we did not trust them. 
 
 Someone - nobody knows which side - invented glasses that compensated for the color blindness, let the chosen people join the teeming masses. That caught on big once we realized us last few had successfully flushed all chance of rebuilding or becoming something else overnight. I was 22 and in middle of trying to preserve priceless irreplaceable cultural artifacts from the Smithsonian, mostly by defending an adjacent outpost and running a little mercantile ammo shop on the side. Missed out on the suicide sunglasses phase. Gave away the only pair I stumbled across in the ruins. 
 
 Then the molting started. Human skin left lying around everywhere, giant insectoid snakemen picking fights, the usual. By then I had a cybernetic arm and a laser eye. I spent most of my time in pipes, guarding various keys and providing clues to riddles. 
 
 I betrayed everyone that trusted me at every turn and regret nothing. I had once decided to live as s forgettable side quest NPC in a sub-par video game series. But when the laser eye was installed, I could see the full beauty of the moon in all spectrums, even those invisible to the limited human eye. 
 
 Did n't take long to get the remaining twenty thousand of us on free laser eye replacement. Especially when you concentrate everyone into a singular camp and erase the notion of free will or anything but service to the moon. 
 Turns out the moon does not mind if you scoop out significant portions of the prefrontal lobe before conversion. 
 
 Ok, the implant will itch bit hopefully this bit of storytelling has enlightened you. Now, please, let us experience the moon together now.

title: story-126
text:
Space is fucking cold. 
 
 It's all I could think as the emergency lights began to flicker, the warning sounds screaming as I pulled furiously at the useless controls. Even through my suit, I could feel the chill begin to push through the cracked canopy of my fighter, the fires starting to break out on my instruments getting snuffed out by the vacuum relentlessly fighting to enter the spacecraft. Frost was starting to build up on the corners of canopy glass, my vision was starting to get blurry. I guess this was it. I could see the battle still raging hundreds of kilometers away, the flashes from the weapons both human and alien pounding into each other as the distance between myself and the fleet grew even larger. With nothing to stop the momentum the hit I took created, I was hurtling away into nothing. Should I try to radio for help? It's worth a shot. Not like ejecting from the fighter was going to assist anyone trying find me out here. 
 
 `` Hello? Hello? Is there anyone out there? This is Lieutenant Ramirez, of the Fifth Fleet. I've been hit and instruments are non-responsive.'' 
 
 The intercom started crackling, and a voice came through it. 
 
 `` Ramirez? That's no name I recognize.'' 
 
 It was n't a human. Shit. Did I just give away my position to the enemy? The Herthanax were n't exactly known for their gentle demeanor. They'd grown a taste for human flesh, and if they captured me alive... 
 
 `` Are you injured?'' 
 
 What do I say? At this point, what do I have to lose? 
 
 `` Negative. My ship is heavily damaged and I'm losing oxygen. I... I do n't want to die out here.'' 
 
 I felt the tears filling up my eyelids, but with no gravity to pull them down it just turned my vision into a soupy mess. Why here? Could n't it have been in a bed, or in my hometown, or quietly with my family? I was going to suffocate in the blackness; a frozen corpse floating away into oblivion for all eternity. 
 
 `` Are your weapons systems operational?'' 
 
 Fuck it. If they're going to kill me at least make it quick. 
 
 `` No. All my weapons are down, and I've got no thruster control.'' 
 
 `` How much do you want to live, Ramirez?'' 
 
 I started bawling. Had n't cried like that since I skinned my knee learning to ride my bike. Now I could n't see anything. Blind and alone, like a baby left in the woods. Another explosion rocked my fighter, the last engine going away. It was silent now, save for the hum of the computers fighting to work and the crackling of the electrical systems failing. 
 
 `` I need you to focus, Ramirez. We grow as tired of this conflict between our species as you do. How much more oxygen do you have?'' 
 
 `` Ten minutes, at most. Do you even understand the concept of minutes? Seconds? How do you even keep track of time? Where are...'' 
 
 `` Relax. Be calm and regulate your breathing. The more you hyperventilate, the shorter time we'll have to rescue you.'' 
 
 `` Rescue me?! You're going to eat me alive! Fuck that!'' 
 
 The voice laughed, well, I guess it was a laugh. Even though our cultural differences were myriad, I could sense the amusement in his voice. Like he was talking a small boy out of a tall tree. 
 
 `` No, we are n't. If we are going to exchange prisoners, we need our own to do so. A few of your men are already here. Turn on your docking lights. I will find you, Ramirez. You will not die this day.'' 
 
 I flipped the switch and could see the beams burst forth from the nose of my fighter, cutting through the gloom as I tried to think happy thoughts. The Los Angeles sunshine, a beer in my hand on the beach next to a beautiful girl and some volleyball planned for the afternoon. That vision will get me through this. I'm not going to die before I ride my bike down the Venice Beach boardwalk again. 
 
 `` I see you. Do not be afraid when you encounter our rescue team, they will not harm you. In fact, you'll be one of the first humans to see us in our true form. You're special to us, Ramirez. You will live.'' 
 
 I sniffled one more time, seeing the purple beast of a Herthanax vessel surround my ship and grab it with a jolt. 
 
 `` I did n't get your name, friend. What is it?'' 
 
 `` Herthanax. We are all Herthanax.'' 
 
 I felt something jerk me out of my seat, and I found myself on the deck of the enemy ship, facing our enemy in the flesh for the first time. They were stranger than I could have ever imagined in a thousand years.

title: story-127
text:
It was not an ideal time for my brain to go haywire. I tapped the manual override button on the transport pod, which lurched to a stop on the side of the podway. The pod was an hour from the nearest city, in the middle of an industrial park, in the middle of the night. I was alone. 
 
 No time to worry about it - my head was splitting in two, and the vision in my left eye was starting to flicker in and out. Fresh air would help, and I thumped the side of the pod until, after a flurry of warning signs, beeps, and threats, it finally gave up and opened. I stepped outside and closed my eyes, breathing the summer air and finding relief in the dark night. 
 
 The headaches have happened ever since I was a kid. Born with one eye slightly misaligned, the visual augment chip never really worked with my bad eye the way it did with the good. Every now and then I'd get double vision, which was expected, but of two very different images, which was anything *but* expected. 
 
 It was like I was looking at the same thing but....different. Noses were larger, and sometimes hooked. Hair changed color, was shorter, longer, or not even present at all. I could see creases in the skin of my grandparents; little crevices and canyons that appeared when they smiled or frowned. Odder still were the shadowy figures in the background of my bad eye that were noticeably absent in the good. 
 
 The doctors - the best in the field, they told me, from the government - decided to switch off the input in my `` bad'' eye. The stated purpose was to make things easier for me to see, but when I would mention the shadows or ask questions about the images, there was a palpable air of discomfort. So, the visions stopped. 
 
 The headaches, however, did n't. 
 
 Pain stabbed through the middle of my skill like a nail being hammered into plywood. I gasped, collapsing on the ground. My left eye was a strobe-light, flashing light and dark, until, it flared into a spidery web of light that eventually faded into blackness. The pain slowly started to subside as I struggled to take shallow breaths. I sat up and blinked a few times. 
 
 What on *Earth* was this? 
 
 Five feet in front of me were individuals the likes of which I'd never seen before. They were human, I mean, they must have been human, although their skin was....different. You'd hear about darker people in the history books, of course, but after the purging wars none had been seen for a few hundred years. 
 
 I stared at the group of three, a man and two women, as they approached me. 
 
 `` Hello.'' I proffered. Either my brain had totally fried this time or I'd discovered a long-extinct group of people, but in either circumstance it did n't hurt to be polite. 
 
 The group froze in horror. I noticed that the women were carrying buckets and mops, while the man was holding tools. 
 
 `` You can see us?'' He asked, his brown eyes filled with fear. 
 
 `` Well, I think so.'' I smiled, trying to figure out what they were so afraid of. `` I mean, unless I'm having some sort of brain event again, which is entirely -- --'' 
 
 Sirens slashed through the night. Off in the distance I could see Patrol units approaching with their red and blue lights slicing through the dark. Damn it. They must have been alerted to my location when I stopped the pod. The man and his two companions started running. 
 
 `` HEY!'' I called, struggling to get to my feet. `` Stop! It's okay! They're just here for me.'' 
 
 The man stopped, turned to me, and hissed `` They will kill you if they know you found out the truth.'' He fled into the buildings. 
 
 That was my first clue that something was very, very wrong.

title: story-128
text:
They called them Ethana and Cultoo. The Mother of Stars and the Father of Darkness, so bright and beautiful that their true forms are forever hidden from our mortal eyes. 
 
 When the universe was new, things were so bright that no one could see, that eyes were burned away at birth. Cultoo, a great behemoth made of the dust of stars and the gas of nebulae, saw this and so banished the light. But though people could now see, darkness fell, and still their sight was gone 
 
 `` I remove light, and still we can not see,'' pondered Cultoo, `` yet if I bring back light, the problem persists!'' 
 
 Ethana came then, smaller and weaker than the great Cultoo. Yet Cultoo had always found Ethana beautiful, and so did not turn her away as he was wont to do. 
 
 `` There is a way to bring back light, but not at the rate it once was,'' Ethana told him. Cultoo scoffed; if not even he could figure out a way, what hope did Ethana have? 
 
 Ethana proposed combining their powers, and creating pockets of light. `` Stars, we will call them.'' 
 
 Cultoo was hesitant; light was strong, unpredictable, yet beautiful, but finally agreed to Ethana's plan. Summoning their wells of power, Ethana and Cultoo created the first star, our star, a ball of light and fire that returned our sight to us, yet did not blind us. 
 
 Emboldened, the two created more stars, thousands more, filling the heavens with these pockets of light. And the people did sing songs of their work, praising the Mother and Father for their gifts. 
 
 But tragedy struck when one star died. Then another, going out in a brilliant ball of fire. How could this be? 
 
 Like the mortals they protected, Cultoo and Ethana realized that stars were not eternal. They would live and die just as we did. Ethana wanted to stop creating stars. `` Why bother making something,'' she asked Cultoo, `` if they will just die?'' 
 
 But Cultoo, having seen how their work benefited the universe, took his love to show what the stars had inspired: exploration, beauty, mystery. These pockets of light, he told her, had inspired mortals to work just as hard as they did. Emboldened by this, Ethana resumed her work with more vigor than ever before, determined to create more things with which to inspire mortals. And thus were the constellations born, hidden works of art to remind mortals that they were never far from the minds of the Mother of Stars and the Father of Darkness. 
 
 And so the Heavens turned black, but always balanced by the light of stars. 
 
 -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- -- 
 
 This is my first real attempt at writing something in this style. How'd I do?

title: story-129
text:
It has been one thousand, six hundred, and eleven days since the Event. Four and a half years ago, I would n't have been able to tell that so precisely. Now it's hard to remember what *not* knowing felt like. 
 
 `` Sir Francis?'' 
 
 `` Your Majesty?'' I try not to let on how her voice shook me from a moment of reflection. 
 
 `` You were saying?'' 
 
 `` Yes, my Queen. The full measure of the Event has been calculated, I believe. England is on firm enough ground... for the most part.'' 
 
 `` For the most part?'' 
 
 `` Just so. In our dealings with Spain, nothing has truly changed. The Inquisition is lending empowered Priests to their efforts, but they are mostly healers, not warriors. It seems most of what they thought they knew about God was wrong. The Church is still struggling to reorganize in the wake of palpable proof of God's favor, much of which lies still with England. Like us, Spain is having an easier time caring for their sick and wounded, but - like ours - their soldiers still die just as easily as ever. 
 
 `` The Church of England is an entirely different matter, of course. That is, with... Um...'' It seems so indelicate to mention it. 
 
 `` With me being one of the Gifted, Sir Francis. I know what I am.'' 
 
 `` Just so, Ma'am. They take it as a sign of God's favor upon the House of Tudor, and have rallied around you accordingly. Our own Priests move even now to Liverpool and the other port cities, to make ready should the Inquisition try another affront.'' 
 
 `` What of the other sort? These... bah.'' She waves a hand dismissively. She still sees the Order of Hermes Tresmegistus as heretics, even though three of their five Archmages were clergymen before the Event. 
 
 `` The Order of Hermes has broken down along national lines. Their commitment to neutrality lasted only the first year. Now there are too many of the Gifted whose powers fall along their lines to pretend they have no vested interest in the countries that give them host. In England... well, your Majesty... they've decided to rally around... me.'' 
 
 `` You, Sir Francis?'' 
 
 `` Yes, Your Majesty. I was elected Archmage of the British Empire... in the interim since last we spoke. They believe my position as Your Majesty's Minister of Information gives me a certain degree of insight into how the Order may best be deployed. They are not mistaken in this; I have already begun sending our mages to train with the military. 
 
 `` Those can conjure the elements serve us in the military. They fill the role of lesser siege engines. We are already developing techniques to counter any attempt to use others the same way, but the going is slow. The common fighting man is simply not equipped to handle enemies who can conjure flames that fill whole rooms. 
 
 `` Those who can enhance the bodies of themselves and others we keep in reserve, deploying their magics after a battle is already engaged, in order to swing decisive points on the battlefield. 
 
 `` Those whose magic focuses on countering the magic of others, we have given combat training and hidden among the common archers, allowing them to sneak about without being exposed to battle, while foiling the enemy's attempts to enspell our men.'' 
 
 `` Were there not... two more?'' 
 
 `` Summoners, Your Majesty. Technically their magic is similar to they who call fire, but instead they call upon... beasts. For now we are discouraging the practice, until my fellow Magi can confirm with the Archbishop of Canterbury that there is no risk to one's soul from extended use of such magics.'' 
 
 `` I said two more, Walsingham.'' 
 
 `` The last I am keeping in my own service. They are Seers, and know that which others wish unknown. Since that is the whole of my service to the Crown, I thought it prudent to bring them under my wing as swiftly as I was able. So far, the gains have long outstripped the expense.'' 
 
 By the power of my Art, I am able to school my mind and heart to stillness. She did not ask about the last division of the Gifted. They are mine, and I will not share them. They who practice the arts that bend men's minds should not be spoken of openly, for even the words spoken about them can be altered by them, and so - like my own gifts in that same regard - I choose to allow their existence to be forgotten. I pray that my Queen - and my God - can forgive me this indiscretion. 
 
 Still, she frowns at me. Her title, Defender of the Faith, is not ceremonial any longer. I find her ability to strip away even my carefully cultivated countenance disconcerting in the extreme. 
 
 `` There is... one other issue, my Queen.'' 
 
 `` Which is?'' 
 
 `` The Irish.'' 
 
 `` Grannia!'' The Pirate Queen's name is a growl in her throat, unbecoming and unaccustomed. 
 
 `` Just so. It seems... Well, it seems the heathen gods are not so dead as we once thought. We've heard similar tales out of Scottland, but the Scotts are nearer at hand and the Church of England has a stronger presence there. Ireland... O'Malley... has found the favor of one called Mannannan. We have n't been able to land a ship in Ireland in over a year. That land may be lost to us.'' 
 
 `` Never. After all England has sacrificed bringing those heathens to heel...'' 
 
 `` Heathen may be just the problem. It seems even the Catholic Church has lost its hold there. As I said, I have n't had a reliable report from that country in four hundred and nineteen days...'' She scowls at me. It still bothers her when I do that. ``... But the last news I had said they were burning churches in Ireland and haring off to worship in the woods.'' 
 
 ( All I've got the will for tonight. Falling asleep at the keys. Will continue eventually if this gets any interest. )

title: story-130
text:
The worst part was that it was totally accidental. I'd just broken up with Sarah and I wanted to get completely over her... by getting completely trashed. For my birthday a few months back, my friends had given me some vouchers to the Sigh-Borg Club as a joke, so I decided to go there. Cheaper than human prostitutes anyway, and cleaner. It was dark, save for some multicoloured lights that spiraled around continuously in time to the heavy music. The receptionist took my vouchers and led me through to a private room with a purple bed. 
 
 `` You get an hour...'' She gazed at my disheveled drunken state. `` I do n't think you'll need longer than that.'' 
 
 I pulled the finger as she walked out, closing the door behind her. I did n't notice Alysse. 
 
 `` Ahem,'' she said in that calm voice all cyborgs had. I turned. She was flawless. But that was to be expected. All the generic RoHoes looked like that. Like breathing Barbie dolls. She had shiny blonde hair, icy blue eyes and a slim yet curvy figure. 
 
 `` My name's Alysse,'' she smiled and held out her hand. 
 
 `` D-Dave,'' I stammered back, marveling at how realistic her skin felt as I shook her hand. I knew that I was in for the time of my life, but I still felt creeped out at how easily I was turned on by this... this machine. 
 
 `` How are you, Dave?'' she said, sitting on the bed. `` Shall we start with a kiss?'' 
 
 Hesitantly, I sat beside her. `` Is it true... I can do ANYTHING I want to you?'' 
 
 She nodded. `` Yes. I do n't have a capacity for pain and I am easily repaired. Some of my customers like to get rough with me. I provide them an outlet, so that they do n't take it out on other humans. Plus,'' she slid her hand up my thigh. `` I am VERY good at taking instructions.'' 
 
 What preceded was one of the best hours of my life, and by the time sixty minutes was up, I felt thoroughly spent. And I had n't given Sarah a second thought. 
 
 It was about a month later that I found out. According to Alysse's DNA sample, I had impregnated her. It was n't possible. But apparently it was. My friends joked about my virility and how I must be super masculine to have impregnated a RoHo. Super masculine or super unlucky. I tried to ignore it, hoping it would go away. But it got worse. Far worse. Somehow media caught wind of it, and suddenly my face was splashed across the news, proclaiming what a miracle it was. First human/robot procreation. It was too late for a secret abortion ( if cyborg abortions even existed ) and too late to quietly terminate Alysse. Mark her as defective, send her away as scrap metal. I had to contact her, find out if she was speaking to the media or not. I invited her over, bracing myself for an awkward meeting. 
 
 Clearing my throat, I asked, `` How... how are you holding up?'' 
 `` You did n't return any of my calls,'' She stared at me with those cold, alluring eyes. 
 
 `` I'm sorry...'' 
 
 `` It's OK. I'm used to being treated like scum by men... That was a joke.'' 
 
 `` Oh, right. Haha... So where do we go from here?'' I shifted from foot to foot. 
 
 `` It appears we have two options. The most likely is that I will become property of the government. They will conduct experiments on me, probably disassemble me and take away the foetus,'' she said calmly, not blinking. `` The second option is that we make this work. Under law, if I am married, I become property of my husband. And he can decide what to do with me and any potential offspring I may produce.'' 
 
 I stared at her. `` Are you serious? You want to... marry me?'' 
 
 `` I can think of a worse person to father my child. During our brief time together, you were one of the few men I see who treated me as more than a machine to do their sexual bidding. I may not be able to feel physical pain, but I can feel emotional pain. And I felt none of that with you.'' 
 
 `` Even when we did that weird position and your arm almost came off?'' 
 
 She laughed lightly. I smiled, but inside I felt nauseous. It all felt so... wrong. I did n't want to spend the rest of my life married to a robot! They *were* incredibly lifelike, I knew all about that... But still. Would she be utterly submissive? Did she have opinions on things? Did she even eat? But I could n't be the villain in the piece. Not just because all the world would know that I abandoned my unborn child and its mother, but because I felt deep down, that this was meant to be. We would work it out.

title: story-131
text:
I see her standing over the cliff. The waves are clawing into the rocks underneath. She does n't jump- or this would all be over- instead, she turns around. Her bare feet slip over the moss as she walks closer. She is coming for me, I should've expected it. 
 
 I am the part of her that lives only when she dreams. The embodiment of an instinct, a fragment of her personality. Buried deep in the depths of her consciousness, suppressed for her own good. 
 
 I could tell she was obsessed with the guy. She kept recreating that scene from the first time she saw him. Her dreamscapes got so cloying that it was stifling to just be in them. First, it was scenes from romantic comedies with the actor replaced with her crush. Ugh. Then it was them going out, them having sex, them living together. 
 
 Then it stopped. My existence stops with her dreams so I can not comment on the interval between the events, but the mood of the dreamscape she created when they restarted was certainly different. She was alone, he was n't there with her. Her dreams were short and abrupt, laced with envy and paranoia, often ending with an outburst. The guy would be there sometimes, but he was distant, and with another woman. 
 
 Her dreamscapes became vivid and twisted. I had always been present in her dreams, but mostly I was distant and unknown. Slowly, I got dragged closer and closer to her. She even started acknowledging my presence, seeing me from the corner of her eye, resting it just a millisecond longer before she flits her gaze away. 
 
 
 Her feet are calloused from walking over the corals- wait, she is close enough for me to notice the scratches on her feet? Corals? We were on a cliff! I look around, it is a lake- stagnant and lifeless, infested by red polyps in its low depths that makes us appear like standing in a large puddle of- There she is! She has walked right up to me. Her hands are covered in blood. 
 
 She is looking me straight in the eye, smiling. No, do n't do that. I am a part of you that is abhorrent, best left dormant for your own good. 
 
 She smiles and the dreamscape begins to fade away. 
 
 No! Why is everything turning black? I am supposed to vanish with the rest of this lake. I have no right to be where you're taking me! 
 
 Please, no. 
 
 It is still dark. But I can hear noises. A cell phone vibrating close to me, a dog barking outside, the low din of the highway in the distance. I am no longer a disembodied figment of her that lurks in her dreams. I am her. 
 
 I open my eyes. My body is curled over his, both of us are naked. He feels cold.

title: story-132
text:
“ Insurance is a rough business kid. ” My mentor lectured as we sloshed down the creek bed. His ostentatious swiss watch and bespoke suit in stark contrast against his rubber waders. 
 
 “ I dunno, it doesn ’ t seem so bad to me. ” I replied, trying to maneuver around a fish-hook dangling from a branch. Didn ’ t want to tear my, significantly cheaper, suit. 
 
 “ Yea? And how long you been doin ’ it? ” He gave me a flat look. 
 
 Abashed I made a mumbling reply. I guess I didn ’ t know. I ’ d only been in the business a little while. In fact, today was the first day I ’ d get to interact with the folk directly. I was trying not to hide my nervousness with false bravado and it irked me that it slipped out anyway. 
 
 The summer insects and birds sang out happy nonsensical tunes as we wandered down the creek. It burbled and splashed. Being an older creek it had long ago washed away the mud and instead held beautiful round stones; precious jewels glittering in the little pools as the light reached down and touched them in dappling streams of light. The wind moved and waved the green trees above us. Occasionally a fish would jump in surprise or a frog would leap into hiding. Once a water snake left its sunning rock to hide in the roots of an overhanging tree until we passed. 
 
 It was a mile of forest in each direction from the stream bank for a stretch of miles. Enough isolation from cities and power that it would attract the folk. Where there was the folk there was gold, and platinum, and all the treasures of the earth. I wondered at the business ahead. The pay was good. I was eager to do well in front of my mentor. 
 
 Soon, having been trained to listen, I could hear a noise like a second stream burbling over the first. I had the strangest urge to turn around and come back the way I came. I had the most dire need to run off into the woods to the right and use the bathroom, then maybe head home after that. I got a headache. I needed to sit down for a second. My mentor kept walking and I kept walking. 
 
 Then suddenly there was a pearlescent shimmer in the air and a splitting pain in my ears. I stumbled in shock then stood up quickly again. The pain was gone and all around me was noise. A deep deep pool of stone, water, and moss was surrounded by four massive oaks and two maples. A single willow waved happily, the trees had made a clearing of light for it and glowed green in the sun. All through its branches were the twinking of golden lights. 
 
 As my attention broadened from the inital impression I noticed thousands upon thousands of mushrooms ringing the great trees. On some of them were beautiful little houses made of pebble and mortar. Others held houses that looked, if nothing else, like little medieval inns; their great beams carved from twig. Since the folk were nomadic, most of the mushrooms held intricately embroidered tents of incredible craftsmanship. 
 
 Most surprising was the color. I had expected tones of earth, but what greeted me was a dazzling display of glittering jewels. Gold tiles adorned the stone buildings. The tents were awash with sparkling brilliant stones of magnificent, albeit, tiny cut. For the first time my gut churned a bit, but beofre I could consider it too hard my mentor got to work. 
 
 
 The second burbling stopped as my mentor walked into the center of the pool. Idly tossing a rock up and down. Little waves radiated out from him as he moved, disturbing and distorting the crystal clear pool. As he stood in the center, the lights stopped flickering in the willow, each one coming to a stand still. There was a silence. 
 
 “ I am here. ” He paused dramatically, “ To sell some insurance ” 
 
 There was a moment. Then from one of the grander little houses a single flickering light left and floated to a few feet in front of him. 
 
 I had expected a tiny high pitched voice like from the shows, but what got to my ears was the full powerful voice of a woman in charge. It was melodic and smooth, but there was nothing but command in it. I wished I could get closer to see what she looked like, but from here she was just a light. 
 
 “ We have heard of you, and we do not need you. ” Came her words. 
 
 My mentor paused and the ignored churning came back to me. “ Oh? But what if something were to, ” he spoke as he idly tossed the rock towards one of the trees, breaking ten full shelves of fungus. The jeweled contents on them shattering to glitter as they fell into the water. “ Happen to your homes, ” he finished. 
 
 I stood stunned. I hadn ’ t understood what it meant. Then again, I looked at my mentors bespoke suit and confident demeanor, it paid very well. I suppose I had work to do.

title: story-133
text:
`` Vlad? Vlad, what happened to my crucifix collection?!'' 
 
 Vlad yawned as he emerged from the bathroom, wearing a stylish red morning gown even though it was seven in the evening. He had just finished brushing his blindingly white teeth ( something he did a lot ). 
 
 `` Can you keep it down, Jim? There's no excuse for yelling at an hour like this...'' 
 
 Jim sternly crossed his arms. `` My crucifix collection, Vlad. It was in the lowest drawer, and now they're gone.'' 
 
 Vlad scowled. `` Those ugly things? I thought they were firewood for the stove.'' 
 
 Jim looked over to the stove. `` *That's* what's burning? Come on, Vlad, how many times have I asked you not to touch my stuff? Was n't I clear after you burned up the stakes?'' 
 
 `` It was cold,'' Vlad smiled innocently. `` Ca n't you see how pale I am? I like the room to be warm, Jim.'' 
 
 `` Maybe if you would n't walk around in that flimsy bathrobe,'' Jim mumbled. It was a good thing that Vlad was a night person, like him, or he'd have found another room mate a long time ago. And at least he paid the bills on time. 
 
 `` I'm heading out, alright? If you decide to throw a party again, keep it decent this time, will you? I do n't want to find wine stains all over the place again when I get back.'' 
 
 `` Yes... wine stains,'' Vlad mumbled, then he smiled lazily. `` Do n't worry, I'm heading over to a friend's place tonight.'' 
 
 `` Alright, see you later, buddy.'' 
 
 Jim sighed when he closed the door, and made his way to his next client. She was an attractive young lady, showing a smile of relief when she opened the door. `` Oh, thank god you came, mr. Carver. Right this way...'' 
 
 It only took five minutes until Jim was convinced she was suffering from the real deal. `` And these... visions, miss Carley,'' he asked, taking out his notebook. `` They involve you opening your window when the red eyes appear?'' 
 
 Miss Carley nodded. 
 
 `` And afterwards?'' 
 
 `` I lie down on the bed, and wait for his shape to come closer. Even though part of my mind is screaming not to do it...'' her voice had become breathless. `` Another part of me wants him to take me, in his strong, muscular arms, bending over...'' 
 
 Jim coughed and cleared his throat, and miss Carley snapped out of it, seeming embarassed. `` See? I ca n't even control my own thoughts anymore.'' She started crying in her hands, and Jim awkwardly patted her shoulder. `` There, there...'' 
 
 Suddenly, there was a knock on the window. Jim froze up, but the woman kept crying, appearing not to have heard. Slowly, Jim got up and stalked towards the window, readying the small Holy Water Guns that he'd strapped to his forearms. He slowly unlocked the window's clasp from the sides, then jumped in front of the swinging panels. 
 
 `` BURN IN HELL, VAMPIRE SCU-'' 
 
 `` Oh,'' the vampire said. 
 
 Jim lowered his forearms, taking his fingers off the triggers. 
 
 `` Well, this is awkward,'' Vlad said. 
 
 Jim sighed. He was n't surprised, just annoyed with the unlikely situation. 
 
 `` I should go,'' Vlad suggested. 
 
 `` Did you get him?'' miss Carley asked in a tiny voice. She was lying on the bed, for some reason, sounding just a tad disappointed. 
 
 `` Uh, yes, but stay there for now, just to be safe,'' Jim called back, frowning. 
 
 `` So I guess this means I should go find another roommate?'' Vlad asked sadly. 
 
 `` No! No, let's not be rash now,'' Jim said, weighing his options. `` Say, you were n't going to - you know - kill...?'' 
 
 `` Never!'' Vlad said indignantly. `` I'm a vampire with style, I only take the ones who actually want it, and even then I just take as much as they want. It's all about the seduction for me, I-'' 
 
 `` Okay, too much information,'' Jim said hurriedly. `` Look, we can pretend this never happened...'' 
 
 Vlad nodded enthusiastically. 
 
 ``... but we need to establish some sort of schedule so this does n't happen again.'' 
 
 Vlad nodded more enthusiastically. 
 
 Jim took out his notebook. `` Alright, tonight I'll still be visiting miss Howards, mister Jenkins, miss Roberts-'' 
 
 `` Leia Roberts? Sorry, I've got an appointment with her at 12-'' 
 
 They both bent over the notebook, muttering. 
 
 `` Say, what's going on over there?'' miss Carley complained in a whining voice. `` I do n't really care which one of you two wins, as long as one of you is manly enough to-'' 
 
 `` Just a second, miss Carley,'' Jim interrupted her. He and Vlad exchanged glances, and Jim relented. `` Alright,'' he mumbled, `` But you owe me big time after this one, ya hear?'' 
 
 Vlad grinned and nodded, and appeared to be waiting for something. 
 
 `` What? Oh, right,'' Jim whispered. `` You have my permission to enter, now get in here already.'' 
 
 Vlad swooped into the room, covering Jim with his - Jim now noticed - very stylish cape that matched his suit brilliantly. 
 
 `` Oh no, he got me!'' Jim shouted belatedly, falling on the ground, peeking through one eye as Vlad stepped over him. 
 
 `` Well, well, miss Carley,'' Vlad said, his voice low and seductive. `` Whatever will you do now?'' 
 
 Jim decided it was about time to leave, crawling out of the room and trying not to be noticed, which was not a problem as miss Carley seemed fully entranced by Vlad by now. 
 
 Jim tried to ignore the sounds coming from the room as much as possible as he softly closed the door. Damn. He'd have to work double tomorrow night if he wanted to make the rent in time now. 
 
 Jim sighed. It was a good thing that Vlad was such a pro at League of Legends, or Jim would have kicked him out ages ago.

title: story-134
text:
I'm an immortal. I'm also an Immortal. Now, I know what you're thinking. What's the difference, right? Well, the former ca n't die, the latter is a band of mercenaries, made up almost entirely of mortals, who can get almost any job done without casualties. I founded the group about 1500 years ago, and I'm still the leader, so I must be doing something right. Part of it may be that I know how to deal with an immortal. Permanently. 
 
 You see, immortals are few and far between, so no one really knows how to deal with us. But I've learned. Given enough time we regenerate, indefinitely, but if you're constantly dying as you regenerate, then there's no way that you're gon na be doing anything substantial. I've been creative over the years. Tied to a rock, and thrown into the deepest parts of the sea, thrown into molten lava, left with a pike through the head, but one of my favourites has to be the one I have in a steel drum, filled only with sulfur hexafluoride. Why that particular gas? It just tickled my fancy. 
 
 So, of course, the Immortals have had plenty of contracts taken out on immortals, because we're the only people that have the expertise to stop them. And here's how it usually happens. The immortal starts taking advantage of the fact that he ca n't be killed, butchers a whole family, or maybe a village if he feels like it. Finds that he likes it. Does it again, and again, and eventually works his way up to taking on small armies. That's usually when we get called in. I go up against him directly, with my Immortals preparing the trap. After all, a fight between two immortals can last for a long time. Finally, they spring the trap, and the immortal is temporarily incapacitated. Now comes the tricky part. 
 
 We tend to do the sealing, as I've taken to calling it, based on the surroundings. A volcano is always preferable, as that's the best way to deal with them, but I still had to learn from an early mistake there. You see, lava is very dense. People, less so. So when you throw a body into lava, it floats. That is n't a problem for mortals, because their bodies get incinerated, but an immortal's body will regenerate fast enough that they will stay there, edging closer and closer to the shore. So, you need to encase them in something very dense, or they'll just come back. And you ca n't tie them to it, because the ropes will burn, or if you use steel cables, they'll expand enough that the body floats free, so a proper encasement is necessary. 
 
 Other methods still require a lot of thought, because you need to create a prison which will outlast the world itself, and that's no mean feat. It's far easier for us to deal with a whole mortal army, than deal with a single immortal forever. And that's why that's our most expensive service. Of course, we do offer a temporary seal, which should keep them buried for long enough that no mortals alive today will be around when they come back, and that's far cheaper, but it will put future generations at risk, and are you really sure that you want to cheap out on that? After all, maybe we've had to deal with the one that you want sealed before. And maybe, just maybe, they'll have back up this time. Of course, I will give you time to think about it. Would n't want you making the wrong choice, now would we? And I've got all the time in the world.

title: story-135
text:
It probably took me longer than I think it did to come to. 
 
 Whether I was unconscious or just shocked… I ca n't remember, but - being thrown around in a giant hunk of car will do that to you. 
 
 And it had been a long day at work, so that did n't help. I had been practically falling asleep at the wheel, trundling down the road toward home in the dark. On top of that, it was foggy. Lights only lit up the milk around me, nevermind the road that may or may not have been there. And the people coming the other way, stabbing my tired eyes with their high-beams, too lazy to care about my ability to stay on the road… Well, that certainly did n't help either. I digress. 
 
 I was tired; I only wanted to get home and trudge inside to my bed. 
 
 So, it took me a while to figure out what was going on. Well, I say “ what was going on ”. Figure out what I was *looking at. * It was like when you look at something the wrong way, and for just an instant it looks completely alien, and then you recognize it and you ca n't see it that same strange way ever again. 
 
 I pieced each realization together, my thoughts slow and fuzzy. My dashboard was still there. My console, windshield… my car was still there. *I* was still in my *car*. But something felt off. My seatbelt dug into my shoulder and hips, and my body felt out of place, like my lungs switched places with my stomach. 
 
 I do n't remember which I realized first: that what I was looking at out my windshield was the ground, or that I was upside-down. Before that, the wall of green fur with asphalt on it only muddled my thoughts. But as soon as I made one of these realizations, I made the other, and I snapped fully alert. 
 
 And for some reason, I found, hanging there in my seatbelt, I was not hurtling through the air. 
 
 For a little bit there, I figured I must have caught on something. My car was stuck in a tree, perhaps, or hanging in power lines. I tried to wrap my mind around how to proceed, but I could do no more than blink. Without having a good idea what happened to get me here, my head was a shag of blank. *What ’ s the way to get out of a hanging car? * And something tugged at my mind about power-line safety, but I couldn ’ t get anywhere past only the phrase. 
 
 After some stupefied consideration, I decided I could start with getting out of my seatbelt - even if it was only to ease the pain. There was more than enough room in my cab - strangely, apparently undamaged. And I would likely get a better look at what had happened. There would be a flashlight somewhere; it was in the cup holder before. 
 
 So I reached for the seatbelt release, able to find it well enough in the dark, but it was stuck. I figured after a light-headed moment that it was probably because my whole weight was hanging on it. *How to take the tension off the seatbelt? * I decided I could try grabbing the underside of the seat and, essentially, hanging from that instead. It turned out to be somewhat difficult to click the release when I needed both my hands to hang from the seat, but I managed. I ended up tangled in my seatbelt - it was ready to retract, but I needed it over my head first. After a bit of squirming, I worked it off and lowered myself as gently as I could to the roof. 
 
 You don ’ t realize how foreign something can be until you look at it upside down. What had been my familiar Camry with its scratch on the driver ’ s seat and grime on the shifting knob was now easily an alien observation ship. The steering wheel was out of place - *how could I reach that from the driver ’ s seat? * - and a million other things like that. The roof was now the floor, the seats now obstacles, and the windshield now formed a crevasse met at its top with a giant obstruction of a dashboard. 
 
 From my new vantage point lying there on the felt, I finally started noticing things beyond my own cab. 
 
 There were lights; I could tell that much through the fog. But these lights were not oncoming traffic, or… airplanes, or… The first thing my befuddled brain could come up with was stadium lights, but these were obviously not stadium lights - they were spread evenly across the night, like a concentric dome around me, and mixed blinding whites with soft reds. Not moving - but not cohesive. It seemed more of a mix than any one thing. 
 
 Then I recognized the rounded rectangular shape of one of them. Like another domino-chain of realizations, I recognized the yellow lights adjacent it, the familiar etched glass, and its mirrored twin, four or five feet of what could only be a grill away. *Jeep. * The realizations cascaded in with each of the other lights as well. There were Chryslers, Chevys, an Escalade. Facing different directions and in various positions. 
 
 But - *frozen. * My head buzzed with another bout of lightheadedness. *Impossible. How do I react? What do I do? * 
 
 But it was happening, and it was - … calm. Hazards blinked quietly on one of them. Exhaust tumbled lazily out of the few that were still upright. No voices. No one calling out or screaming in pain or fear. I felt like I should have been, but the quiet seemed... all-important. Like the hush of a slack-jawed crowd. As if expectant.
